An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based). Additionally, the research calculated the branching fraction of this decay, which was found to be (3.8±0.5±0.3±0.3) × 10^-4, and the normalization factor $f_{B^0_s}/\eta_{CP}S_{B^0_s}$ which was found to be 1.106±0.066±0.033, consistent with predictions from lattice quantum chromodynamics. The research also led to upper limits being placed on violations of CP and isospin symmetry in the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay system. The results were found to be in line with theoretical predictions from the Standard Model. The effective lifetime of the $B^0_s$ meson in the $K^+K^-$ final state was found to be larger than the $B^0$ meson in the $K^-*\mu^+\mu^-$ final state by a margin of 0.026 picoseconds (0.011 picoseconds) at a 95% confidence level. The research also led to the creation of distribution shapes for $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decays, which were in line with the predictions of the Standard Model, however, nowhere in the analysis were any peaks or threshold enhancements found, suggesting that the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay system follows the predictions of the Standard Model across the board. This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the control variable affecting the diffusion coefficient, particularly with the presence of rough inputs; it establishes the convergence of a specific numerical discretization method and provides an alternative solution using a stochastic simulation technique known as the Monte-Carlo method. The paper first presents the mathematical formulation of the problem and then discusses the challenges associated with modeling fractional Brownian motion. The main section describes the numerical approach, including the application of finite elements to solve the state equation and the associated convergence proof. The paper also explores alternative methods of modeling diffusion driven by fractional Brownian motion. The conclusions highlight the feasibility of modeling fractional Brownian motion in stochastic control problems through the use of stochastic simulation techniques, particularly for rough basin cases where traditional methods fail. The results demonstrate the capability of the method to yield accurate solutions even in domains with rough boundaries. The paper also compares the outcomes with those obtained from the finite element method, demonstrating the validity of the proposed approach. The most significant contribution of this research is the proof of the convergence of the numerical solution to the desired outcome within the applicable space. The paper also explores alternative methods of modeling fractional Brownian motion, considering its non-stationary nature, and concludes with suggestions for enhancing the numerical scheme, particularly in relation to mapping the rough movement of the system and potential applications in modeling fractional diffusion equations. The results provided in the paper are derived from a one-dimensional model, and further research is required to adapt the approach to higher dimensions. The paper also includes results from a model with fractional kernel, indicating the method's feasibility for complex movement modeling. The research offers a viable numerical solution for partially observable stochastic control problems and paves the way for exploring more intricate models. The paper is relevant to the field of numerical analysis, particularly within the context of stochastic systems, and the results presented could contribute to better modeling and understanding of related physical phenomena. The approach proposed also offers a viable alternative to modeling systems driven by external inputs, particularly in cases where traditional methods fail due to the coarse nature of the input. The research has the potential to be extended to additional modeling frameworks and could be applied to various types of stochastic systems, also enabling the mapping of rough movement within such systems. The paper includes an illustration of a rough basin case, demonstrating the capability of the proposed method to yield accurate solutions even in domains with complex boundaries. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and the cosmic magnetic field's influence on cosmic ray paths. Our research suggests that the arrival directions of the most energetic cosmic rays may be influenced by local environments, in contrast to lower-energy cosmic rays. The implications of our discoveries on beyond-Standard-Model cosmic ray components and the magnetic field are also explored. The statistical methods employed in this analysis have been made publicly accessible to facilitate replication and further investigation. In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in a classification application involving the detection of tumor cells within whole-slide images. By simulating a FL environment with a large, diverse dataset of cancer images from various sources, we compared the results of training models using both a federated approach and a centralized approach. Our findings indicate that federated learning can produce models with similar accuracy to those trained with centralized data, while avoiding the need to collect extensive training datasets at a single location. This has significant implications for the development of more reliable and accurate image analysis models in histopathology. To further explore the potential of federated learning, we also examined the impact of different data management practices among the participating institutions on the training process. Our research demonstrates that federated learning can effectively accommodate varying data quality and management practices, leading to improved models through the efficient utilization of available training data. To facilitate the adoption of more advanced deep learning architectures in this field, we have made publicly available the code used in our study. This code serves as a foundation for developing high-performance, interpretable models that can be trained via federated learning. To build upon this work, we suggest exploring other innovative deep learning techniques, such as attention-based mechanisms and exponential family autoencoders, that can enhance both the accuracy and interpretability of the models. Additionally, we believe that federated learning offers a promising solution for addressing data disparities and improving model performance in this field. To move forward, we need collaborations with research institutions and medical organizations to test our findings with real-world applications and evaluate the performance of more advanced deep learning architectures using publicly available datasets of digitized tissue samples. In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with limited success due to its slow convergence rate and inability to adapt to changing channel conditions.  To improve this result, a decision feedback equalizer with an increased number of trellis stages was implemented, resulting in a 20% reduction in BER from 0.4 to 0.32, but still failed to provide sufficient improvement for the desired low BER level.  To overcome this limitation, a weighted least square filter was added in series with the FDE, yielding a significantly improved BER of 0.1 following the initial application of FDE.  To minimize water coverage on the optical cable and reduce energy consumption of the data terminal, an automated system was developed to manage the cable depth and temperature, ensuring optimal operating conditions for the data transmission system.  To monitor the water coverage and cable temperature remotely, a wireless communication system was incorporated, utilizing GPRS to provide real-time data and system status from any location in the world.  To prevent power failure on the data terminal, an automated backup system was implemented, ensuring continuous operation and data transmission without interruption.  To provide an additional security measure for the remote system, a secure VPN was set up using a DSL modem, enabling two-way communication and ensuring the integrity of data transmission.  To minimize water coverage on the cable and reduce energy consumption of the data terminal, an automated system was developed to manage the cable depth and temperature, ensuring optimal operating conditions for the data transmission system.  To achieve this, a linear actuator was controlled by an automated system to maintain the optimal cable depth, thereby minimizing water coverage and reducing energy consumption.  To regulate the cable temperature, an automated system was developed to manage the cable temperature based on its depth, water temperature, and ambient temperature, ensuring optimal operating conditions for the data transmission system.  To demonstrate the effectiveness of this automated system, experiments were conducted over various underwater paths resulting in a maximum BER of 0.1 achieved at a data rate of 72Gbit/s over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.

Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. We've applied this technique to two prominent time-series tasks: time-series classification and anomaly detection and demonstrate its superiority over current best practices and methods aimed at improving TCNs. The code is openly accessible, enabling widespread adoption of our dilation optimization technique. Moreover, it includes an interactive visualization tool that enables users to explore and annotate their own time-series data. The code can be found here: https://github.com/hjdwu/Smart-TCN. These tools, specifically tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our work equips ALBA with an additional feature: given an inductive formula, it returns the maximal subclass of DLEs models of the formula. Alternatively, this maximality can be expressed in terms of the algebraic language using the technique of Salitre and Kurczenko. Building on this, we utilize the ALBA algorithm and its output to achieve the same result using the game theoretic perspective of the Drzewiecki trees, thereby extending the realm of application beyond DLEs. Furthermore, our approach grounds these diverse techniques in the same uniform framework, allowing us to establish the maximality property as a corollary of the correspondence theory. This innovative connection between ALBA and the trees enables us to import key properties, including the computability of the correspondence map in the game theoretic framework. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research and present a corresponding algorithm for determining the truth status of each data entry. Additionally, our approach can incorporate various strategies for handling exceptions and aggregating data. A complementary algorithm is also provided to determine the truth status of each data entry in the absence of null values. A key aspect of our research is that all proposed solutions can be applied to real-world scenarios involving large datasets. A notable feature of our framework is that it yields interdomain comparisons for data entries, allowing different data sets to be compared on an equal basis. A corresponding experimental design has been devised to evaluate our approach through a series of pressing problems, including data quality assessment, query validation, data merging, and interdomain comparison. This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. Our research found that the TV-PARX model produced more accurate and robust forecasts than alternative models, including the traditional PARX model with fixed parameters. Our findings suggest that score-driven models that adapt to changing conditions provide the best forecasting results for count-based time series data. Our research also highlights the importance of selecting an appropriate scoring function and model formulation to achieve optimal results. Finally, we have implemented the TV-PARX model in an R package called "tvparx" to facilitate its use across various applications. The package is now available for download from the CRAN website. The TV-PARX model can be particularly beneficial in modeling and forecasting count-based time series data sets that exhibit non-stationary characteristics, such as shifting patterns, irregular fluctuations, and prolonged cycles. The research demonstrates that the TV-PARX model yields superior forecasting results for such data sets when compared to traditional models, and provides actionable insights for managing critical count-based events, such as corporate defaults and infectious disease outbreaks. The TV-PARX model is highly versatile and can be applied across a broad range of count-based time series data sets that present similar challenges. The associated R package allows researchers and practitioners to easily implement the TV-PARX model and generate accurate forecasts for complex count-based time series data sets. The package also includes a user-friendly graphical user interface that streamlines the forecasting process and enables the creation of high-quality forecast visualizations. The research is particularly relevant to economists, epidemiologists, and other researchers who analyze and forecast count-based time series data sets, and can be applied across various industries that deal with critical count-based events. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across various categories, environments
and object instances. In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful of
demonstrations, can generalize to new object instances, and outclass a competitor
approach using symbolic object descriptions. The code is available at: https://github.com/ivanpascan/ndf_object_manipulation.

The SiD's robust silicon vertex and tracking system, complemented by its high central magnetic field, ensures precise momentum measurement. The detector's finely granulated calorimeter system, designed for particle flow analysis, delivers accurate energy resolution across a wide energy range. Given the approaching construction timeline for the ILC, the time has come to reassess the design choices made during the design phase and incorporate the recent breakthroughs in technology into the review process. This review will discuss R&D prospects and participation opportunities for the SiD's development areas. Nevertheless, due to the inherently long development periods for detector components, involvement in the associated R&D is strongly encouraged to ensure a smooth construction process for the ILC, allowing it to operate effectively by the scheduled start date in the late 2030s. This review will outline potential collaboration paths for various development projects, advocating for early involvement to ensure a successful construction phase, given the significant time gap between design completion and the actual construction phase. This review aims to stimulate discussion, encourage participation in associated R&D, and explore potential collaboration paths within the SiD community to guarantee a smooth construction process for the ILC, allowing it to operate effectively by the scheduled start date in the late 2030s. This will ensure that the detector is constructed with the latest technological advancements, thus maximizing its scientific potential. This review represents the initial step in this endeavor, and further discussion among the SiD community is necessary to define the prospects and participation opportunities for the various development areas effectively. This review will be continuously updated to reflect the evolving development projects, participation opportunities, and associated R&D breakthroughs, with regular reviews scheduled to ensure the validity of the information provided. This initial version of the review will focus on highlighting potential collaboration paths for various development projects, encouraging early involvement to ensure a successful construction phase for the SiD detector, given the significant time gap between design completion and the actual construction phase, anticipated to commence in the mid-2020s and conclude by the scheduled ILC start date in the late 2030s. We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for O(N) universality classes in classic scenarios. Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. Alternatively, we have previously found $|z_c|$ to be around 2.03, 1.68 for $N=2, 4$ although these earlier results have a larger systematic uncertainty. Moreover, we have confirmed that the critical behavior at the Yang-Lee edge shares the same universality class as that of the critical pure gauge QCD phase transition despite some uncertainties in the latter's critical temperature and order parameter. Consequently, this implies that any non-monotonic behavior in the QCD phase transition could be attributed to the Yang-Lee edge singularity. Finally, we have assessed that the proposed chiral Yang-Lee edge universality class holds in the three-dimensional SU(2) $Z_3$ symmetry model with global symmetry of order 2, albeit with significant uncertainties. Nonetheless, this predicted non-universality is corroborated by worm algorithm and functional renormalization group results. The anticipated chiral Yang-Lee edge universality should hold across all fundamental and simple gauge theories in 3D, potentially enabling the inference of QCD's critical temperature and order parameter solely from pure gauge theory data analyses. Ultimately, our study anticipates that any discernible deviations in the QCD phase transition that have conventional interpretations could be explained by the Yang-Lee edge singularity. Consequently, we recommend re-evaluating the interpretation of observed features in QCD's critical behavior with temperature. Moreover, we propose that the proposed chiral Yang-Lee edge universality could serve as an indication of the existence of Yang-Lee edge critical behavior in continuous second-order phase transitions in statistical physics. Lastly, our investigation sets the stage for a deeper exploration of the Yang-Lee edge critical behavior in QCD, encompassing studies of critical exponents, edge critical behavior, and potential tricritical points within the QCD phase transition landscape. Ultimately, our research anticipates a pivotal role for trimer models and relativistic fermionic models with SU(2) symmetry in testing the proposed chiral Yang-Lee edge universality class through tricritical universality classes

This specific inequality is an improved version of the Billy-Bartlett inequality and is applicable to any positive definite matrix. Our new inequality yields a tighter bound and is more versatile, allowing us to derive a broader range of convexity results. Our findings can be applied not only to sparse linear regression but also to more complex settings, such as multi-task and group Lasso models. Our approach can be used to provide theoretical guarantees for recovery consistency in statistical inference and is a crucial component in designing efficient algorithms for non-convex optimization methods, such as gradient descent. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to estimate the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The code is available online at https://github.com/zwang84/Refine-Pose-Estimation.

Peridynamic theories have seen a significant expansion in their application across multiple disciplines, due to their ability to model and track discontinuity formation within materials. Bond-based Peridynamics, despite its modeling restrictions, has become a widely-used approach in numerical simulations because of its ease of implementation and intuitive connection to real-world physics. This paper delves into the aspects of bond-based peridynamic models, providing a thorough examination of the theory and its numerical representations. Various bond-based PD integral kernels have been presented along with their distinguishing characteristics, leading to discussions on their implications and common traits. A closer examination was conducted on the role of non-locality in determining motion, the interplay between kernel structure and material non-penetration, as well as the influence of PD kernel choice on modeling fracture. To further illustrate this, simulations of brittle fracture in rubbers and steels were showcased, highlighting how selecting the ideal PD kernel can capture the unique characteristics of different materials. Finally, this research emphasizes the necessity of balancing modeling complexity and precision in choosing PdKs, and suggests that the study of PD kernels can contribute to a deeper comprehension of materials and their fracture mechanisms.

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple
inverse covariance matrices, as shown in Danaher (2013) and Tomasi (2018). The
GGLasso package supports the resolution of diverse formulations and notable
subcases like Graphical Lasso with latent variables, Group, and Fused Graphical Lasso. Moreover, it provides an efficient and user-friendly interface for users to focus on model selection issues rather than programming concerns. The library is paired with an interactive RStudio viewer that is ideal for communicating statistical findings to non-technical audiences. The development of GGLasso is ongoing, and it is available at https://github.com/cristiancunyat/GGLasso. The latest version of the library can be downloaded from the Python Package Index under https://pypi.org/project/GGLasso/. The source code for the paper is available at https://github.com/cristiancunyat/GGLasso_paper. The paper is hosted at https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGLasso/index.html. The GGLasso library is comparable to other prominent graph learning libraries such as highperformance Spark-GAN (Zhang 2021), the R function "gglasso" (Dietzenbacher 2021), and the Python library "scipy.optimize" ("minimize"). However, it excels when dealing with large-scale covariance estimation projects due to its direct integration with the Python scikit-learn library, specifically "MiniBatchGradientDescent" and "LogisticRegression", within the Graphical Lasso with latent variables framework. Consequently, the GGLasso library can take full advantage of multi-core processors and accelerate large-scale covariance estimation projects by a factor of up to 50 when utilizing multiple CPU cores. Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been scrutinized and assessed, focusing on deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on configurational averaging. Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. Furthermore, research found that an optimal method could be identified that boasts extremely low bias in comparison to other alternatives. Through the analysis of alanine dipeptide simulations, both with and without solvent, higher precision was achieved with no decrease in computational efficiency, allowing for large time steps without compromising conformational exploration. Ultimately, the most efficient method demonstrated enhanced molecular sampling, yielding overall improvements of at least 25% in feasible time steps in vacuum and reductions of at least a factor of ten in configurational average errors in solvent simulations with larger time steps. The newly developed method demonstrates the potential to significantly enhance molecular dynamics simulations. The source code is available upon request.

We tackle the persistent issue of exponential stability for a stretched Euler-Bernoulli beam on a star-shaped graph with three equal branches. The outer points where these branches meet are fixed while rotating. The inner point is capable of moving in two ways, with rotational movement influenced by an external friction. A detailed analysis in a Hilbert space reveals how the spectrum's asymptotic distribution and structure evolve. Specifically, we identify the role of eigenvectors and their characteristics in relation to the system's exponential stability. Further, we demonstrate how the asymptotic distribution of eigenvalues and the behavior of eigenvectors aid in determining the stability of this system. Ultimately, we establish conditions for exponential stability by influencing the branch eigenvalues through the external friction. This breakthrough condition is expressed in terms of the discrete Dirichlet eigenvalues of a particular differential operator. To further investigate this operator's properties, we are compelled to introduce an extension of this operator to a full space, analyzing its spectrum and structure in comparison to the original, reduced operators. This analysis enables us to derive new formulas that relate the branch eigenvalues to the system's stability. Consequently, we are able to define an explicit condition for exponential stability solely in terms of the branch eigenvalues. This condition, however, is still indirect. We resolve this by investigating a related, simplified problem that allows us to establish the desired condition directly. We then apply this insight to the full star-shaped beam system, revealing how the external friction's behavior at the inner point significantly influences the branch eigenvalues, ultimately driving the system towards exponential stability. Nonetheless, we observe that stability can never be achieved through friction alone when the beam branches are extensible in the tangential direction. We are compelled to introduce additional external forces to achieve exponential stability in this scenario. We then establish a general approach to formulate these forces, leading to a condition that guarantees exponential stability. We validate our analytical findings through numerical simulations, employing a Runge-Kutta method to integrate the dynamic equations and demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach in achieving exponential stability. We also analyze the behavior of our model when subject to external forces modeled by a Volterra operator, revealing how the asymptotic distribution of eigenvalues and the corresponding eigenvectors aid in determining the system's exponential stability. Our new method, MultiLayer Eigenvector Connectivity (MLEC), is an algorithm that calculates eigenvector centrality in multilayer networks. In contrast to existing techniques, current approaches only consider a limited version of the network. MLEC takes a broader view, accounting for all layers and their connections, making it the first comprehensive implementation of eigenvector centrality for multilayer networks. While similar variants exist for single-layer networks, our implementation represents a pioneering effort. We demonstrate the advantages of MLEC through a key insight: it can be applied to detect central nodes across different network configurations, such as separate networks, merged networks, and networks with interconnected components. In particular, we show that MLEC offers a solution to a longstanding problem - identifying the most connected nodes in multilayer networks. To further enhance performance, MLEC includes an optimization technique that reduces computational time. Through extensive testing on real-world datasets, our algorithm demonstrates high efficiency and precision. Notably, MLEC has a high potential for application in the analysis of collaborative behaviors among entities in multilayer networks. The source code for MLEC is openly available online. In addition, we introduce a new dataset consisting of multiple layers for the sporting event, the European Premier League, which can be utilized for research purposes. This dataset showcases the capabilities of MLEC and demonstrates the benefits of employing eigenvector centrality in multilayer networks. We tackle the issue of non-blind deblurring and demosaicking on noisy raw images using a learning-based approach tailored to handle these images directly, with an innovative new component that simultaneously demosaicks and deblurs them in an interpretable way. To train this model, we utilize real-world camera data transformed into raw images through a realistic process, mimicking real-world camera functions. By doing so, we demonstrate the advantages of our single-stage model over traditional approaches combining demosaicking and deblurring modules, according to objective performance metrics. Additionally, our method is capable of removing a camera's intrinsic blurring effect, which effectively enables deblurring of sharper images from actual pictures. Experimental results show that our model produces significantly better images compared to the input raw images, matching the quality of images obtained through traditional approaches after demosaicking and deblurring. Moreover, our model's ability to deal with diverse blurring types and demosaicking difficulties in real-world scenarios is highlighted through a scientific experiment. The model's simplicity and performance make it suitable for various computer vision tasks requiring image enhancement. To facilitate further research, we are releasing the dataset and model publicly.

This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. A well-known hypothesis posits that gravity at a quantum level must be devoid of universal symmetries. We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories. These $\theta$-terms generate nonlinear connections between axion fields and quadratic gauge field strengths which can be used to break many universal symmetries. If we consider charged states as part of the scenario, additional universal symmetries may be destroyed, yet we found that the $\theta$-terms yield a Witten-like effect that diminishes the range of charged states through the creation of charged magnetic monopoles and dyons from the vacuum. Ultimately, this leads to significantly constrained effective field theories that are capable of bearing universal symmetries. The theories we studied contain an Antigravitational Glue scenario which may be relevant to the study of gravitational particle physics. The full range of our findings can be applied to the context of string landscapes where vacua are distinguished by their universal symmetries. In such an environment the $\theta$-terms emerge as the primary driver of symmetry breaking, resulting in scenarios such as the Antigravitational Glue scenario, where gravitationally neutral forces like QCD dominate the behavior of the string landscape. This often misplaced trust is the foundation on which our objective is built – namely to minimize the reliance on device hardware and software components for users to safely run any Android application. 

We present a novel multi-domain hardware design for cost-effective componentization of critical security functions, which entails splitting the device's system architecture into several secure, independent segments. 

Each hardware segment contains its own operating microkernel, which runs various security functions as guest operating systems. 

We further develop a suite of hardware modules consisting of several secure regions, which can be allocated dynamically according to changing security requirements without needing significant hardware adjustments. 

We choose the Qualcomm Snapdragon 425 SoC as our platform and successfully partition the CPU, memory segments, and other components into multiple secure domains. 

We showcase six distinct security applications that can operate independently or jointly on our multi-domain platform, achieving this by developing customized hardware and software solutions which result in only a 1.45x performance overhead when compared to the unpartitioned device.

We investigated the challenges of robust reinforcement learning in scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally manipulates rewards and transition probabilities. The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously considered methods. We established a key finding that no reinforcement learning algorithm can discover an optimal policy better than $O(\epsilon)$ under these circumstances. Interestingly, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can be robust when the corruption is bounded and is capable of finding an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. We developed a Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, capable of tolerating unbounded reward corruption, and achieved an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy. The FPG algorithm represents a pioneering solution to robust reinforcement learning in scenarios with significant adversarial interference. Moreover, we verified the effectiveness of an FPG implementation utilizing a neural network on MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks. The results demonstrated that the learned filters can recognize patterns indicative of adversarial influence and facilitate the discovery of robust policies. The FPG algorithm showcases a groundbreaking solution to robust reinforcement learning in scenarios with substantial adversarial interference. Moreover, we found that the learned filters are capable of identifying patterns associated with adverse influences and facilitate the discovery of robust policies. The FPG algorithm successfully mitigated the impact of the adversary and enabled the natural exploration of optimal policies in scenarios with significant adversarial interference. The FPG framework opens up new research avenues for robust reinforcement learning generalizing beyond corruption bounds. Our investigation focuses on a 2D electronic lattice from a non-symmorphic wallpaper group.  We're examining a herringbone lattice with two types of glide symmetries in perpendicular directions using Dirac cones as test signals.  With this approach, we determine the irreducible representations of the lattice in the Brillouin zone, identifying those that contain Dirac cones.  The results demonstrate that introducing a dimerized potential disrupts the equilibrium state, giving rise to varying amounts of Doping across distinct sublattices.  A corresponding study using a Heisenberg spin Hamiltonian shows that all Dirac cones can be destroyed through adequate adjustment of the spin parameters, with possible exceptions in certain highly doped cases.  This finding is verified by exact diagonalization and a Monte Carlo simulation, revealing that nearest-neighbor interactions are sufficient to eliminate the Dirac cones and transition to a gapped state.  The underlying reason for this phenomenon lies in the incompatible local magnetic moments that arise around the Dirac cones, forcing a transition to a gapped state to avoid magnetic instability issues.  This magnetic instability instability could be a common trait of Dirac materials, with potential implications for understanding their behavior under external perturbations.  We propose a simple scheme to visualize the evolution of Dirac cones in parameter space, defining a magnetic disorder parameter that quantifies the disorder resulting from competing local magnetic orders and provides valuable insight into magnetic materials.  As exemplified by our study of the Ni-based spin Hamiltonian, this disorder parameter enables an intuitive understanding of magnetic disorder in Dirac materials, offering a practical tool for identifying materials with stable Dirac cones and exhibiting magnetic instability.  We also find that in our model, coupling the spin Hamiltonian with a simple electron phonon interaction leads to a spin-lattice phase diagram influenced by the disorder and both the spin and lattice temperatures, with potential implications for understanding spin-lattice phase transitions in other materials.  Finally, we suggest that our approach can be applied to any two-dimensional electronic lattice using Dirac cones as test signals to study the interplay between lattice symmetry, competing local magnetic orders, and electron phonon interactions.  As a demonstration, we adapt our methodology to the square and kagome lattices, identifying distinct spin-lattice phases in the Ni-based spin Hamiltonian when these lattices are compared to the herringbone structure.  Our research provides a framework for exploring the intricate relationships between lattice symmetry, magnetic order, and electron phonon interactions in two-dimensional electronic systems.

Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Specifically, we analyze the quadrature squeezing properties and sub-Poisson statistics of SPCCSs, and compare their values with states generated using beam splitters and parametric amplifiers. We also determine the conditions under which SPCCSs exhibit nonclassical phase properties. Our findings show that the states generated using a parametric amplifier possess greater quadrature squeezing and sub-Poisson statistics than those produced with a beam splitter. However, both types of SPCCSs display analogous success probabilities and nonclassical phase properties. We propose applying SPCCSs in robust phase-sensitive quantum metrology protocols, describe how to engineer these states using quantum-optical catalysis, and examine the impact of optical interferometer malfunctions on state quality. SPCCSs offer a promising foundation for developing new applications in quantum sensing and communication.

In this study, we investigate the potential for learning tumor shapes from CT scans alone by using deep learning methods that can process raw image data and derive models of the tumor's surface. We contend that these models should account for variations in pose and be robust to limited training data. To address this, we developed an end-to-end network that can generate surface-based tumor descriptions from CT scans and trained it on a relatively small dataset of 120 cases, comprising CT scans and corresponding surface models derived from endoscopic data. This network not only considered raw image data but also generated surface-based tumor descriptions that could be compared to endoscopic data and yielded models of the tumor's shape. To mitigate external influences on the network and focus it solely on the task of tumor identification, we trained it as part of a larger system that could derive models of the tumor's surface, descriptions of the surface, and features of the image simultaneously but in isolation from one another. This approach resulted in models that could be used for comparing two surface-based descriptions and evaluating the similarity or difference between two surface-based descriptions or an image and a surface-based description. On a small validation set of 20 cases, the network performed tumor identification tasks comparable to those of human experts but with less variation and training was achieved in essentially an unsupervised manner by manipulating the network in response to its own output and adjusting it based on the desirability of producing different models of the tumor's shape. This led to the development of a system that could model multiple views of the tumor's shape and evaluate the similarity or difference between two such models. Moreover, this system allowed for the automatic generation of models of the tumor's shape from CT scans, model-based delineation of the tumor, and comparison of models of the tumor's shape. All of these capabilities were demonstrated on a clinical dataset of 50 cases. This study offers a novel approach to learning the shapes of tumors from CT scans alone and paves the way for similar applications to similar complex challenges in medical imaging. Whether this approach can be scaled up for use in actual medical practices remains to be seen.

The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and a major obstacle in the exploration and extraction of petroleum. A technique called geosteering can help optimize well placement and reduce costs by ensuring the drill reaches the desired subsurface layers efficiently. However, implementing geosteering requires accurate formation phase and depth data, which can be obtained through a process called time-depth conversion. This process is typically performed using a pre-drilled well's known time-depth data and a technique called neural network-based interpolation. Yet, current methods only consider data within a certain range, called the support domain, which can lead to inaccurate conversions when dealing with uncertain well-log data. To address this limitation, a new approach using neural networks that handles the entire input space and can incorporate the additional information from formation phase data to improve time-depth conversion results is presented. This proposed method is evaluated using synthetic and real-world data sets, which show significant reductions in error rates compared to traditional approaches. Consequently, it has the potential to enhance geosteering operations and reduce drilling expenses. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the benefit of utilizing well-log data in time-depth conversion and lays the groundwork for integrating the approach into complex neural network architectures that can model well-bores and sample collections. Ultimately, this work has the potential to contribute to better well-placing strategies and improved subsurface data modeling. Lastly, the associated code and data sets are publicly accessible for replication and extension. Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. 

One possible solution involves leveraging human-generated search queries on an image-centric platform, such as Wikipedia's "MediaWiki" or Flickr's "Flickr". Users submitting these queries have essentially specified what they are looking for in those images. Assuming there is a connection between a search query and the associated images, we can utilize this query as a suitable evaluation metric for automatic image description systems. 

This approach's validity depends on the accuracy of matching search queries with images containing the described concepts. Several factors complicate this task, including: 
1. Limited knowledge sharing between visual recognition models and natural language processing components, given current multi-modal systems' architecture limitations.
2. A significant discrepancy between search queries and actual descriptions provided by users, potentially leading to inefficient system optimization. 

To address these challenges, I propose modifications to both the training and evaluation processes of automatic image description systems, involving the integration of a search query recognition model that is trained independently. This recognition model's goal is to identify concepts recognized by the visual recognition model and assess its performance based on overlap with the reference data's semantic components. 

Experimental results indicate that this approach yields a notable improvement in system performance when evaluated using the proposed method, incorporating external search query data, rather than relying solely on the current dataset. 
Additionally, I observed a notable disparity between search queries and actual descriptions provided by users on the Flickr dataset, leading to inefficient system optimization. 
A model that focuses on optimizing the overlap with search queries, rather than descriptions, yields a notable improvement in system performance. 
This approach's validity is further supported by an independent evaluation using Wikipedia's MediaWiki data. 
A notable model variation, incorporating a joint multi-modal model that optimizes both search queries and descriptions, yields no significant improvement in system performance. 
This suggests that search queries, rather than descriptions, contain the most valuable information for system optimization.

Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. However, we did not observe increased dissemination of misinformation in areas with low population density or those experiencing significant recent population changes. Our research suggests that misinformation targeting specific local concerns or interests is less likely to spread widely, but a larger, more stable population can facilitate the broad circulation of all news. In conclusion, the extent to which misinformation spreads varies significantly across regions, and is influenced by the political and cultural environment more so than the underlying platform design. This research raises important questions about the role of technology in addressing online misinformation dissemination. Lastly, our study offers several practical recommendations for mitigating misinformation dissemination, including the targeting of local content with fact-checking initiatives and the development of more effective algorithms to limit misinformation circulation. In conclusion, we highlight the significance of exploring the intricate interplay between technology, society, and politics when investigating online misinformation dissemination. We introduce a groundbreaking, efficient, and user-friendly detection algorithm called HALFADO. HALFADO uses a limited number of human judgments to effectively identify anomalies in real-time, high-frequency data streams. Implementing a precise detection system is crucial for empowering human teams across the digital world by providing reliable decision support. As these systems have profound societal implications, transparency into how they operate is a fundamental human right.

Conceptually, our method builds upon a well-established machine learning technique, leveraging its established theoretical benefits, but takes a semi-supervised approach, combining the strengths of human intuition and computational capabilities. In practice, HALFADO improves upon traditional expert systems by integrating their capabilities into a single comprehensive system.

We showcase the algorithm's performance in two complex scenarios: (1) detecting derogatory language on a social media platform and (2) detecting financial fraud in real-time transaction data. HALFADO's development challenges the misconception that advanced machine learning methods are only achievable with significant computational resources and extensive human annotation. The code for HALFADO is openly available, providing a versatile framework that can be adapted for numerous complex data classification tasks. Furthermore, we highlight potential directions for further enhancing the algorithm.

Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, the research discovers notable differences in speech content, with classifications ranging from instructions to neutral conversation. This work provides valuable insights into the characteristics of human speech used for robotic demonstrations and can serve as a starting point for investigating other human-robot interaction modalities. Ultimately, it aims to contribute to the development of more human-like robotic learning systems that can effectively combine auditory and visual feedback from a single human instructor. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. The main contributions of this work can be summed up as initiating a novel multi-target CDR task, proposing a ground-breaking MSDCR framework, and introducing an influential open dataset for single-item recommendation in a real-world scenario. The source code and the dataset used in this research are available online at https://github.com/hongzheng1996/MSDCR.

Intel's Optane DC Persistent Memory Module (DC PMM) has reached commercial viability as the first commercially available nonvolatile memory DIMM. It offers fast, byte-granular data access similar to DRAM, combined with power-fail safe storage. In-depth performance evaluations have shown Optane DC PMMs to excel as primary memory and persistent storage accessible by user-level applications. Various modes and benchmarks were used to measure Optane DC PMMs performance under different scenarios, including comparison to DRAM, which revealed the following results. When used with a DRAM cache to mask their relatively slow bandwidth, applications with small memory footprints are largely unaffected. Those requiring more storage may experience some performance degradation but still benefit from retaining more data in memory. In file system mode, especially with optimizations tailored to the Optane DC PMMs load/store interface, significant performance improvements were achieved, up to two times the performance with certain applications. Furthermore, user-level applications with Optane DC persistence outperformed those using the file system approach, resulting in substantial time savings. In specific instances, user-level applications with Optane DC persistence outperformed those using the file system approach by almost two times. In situations where data processing is highly optimized and memory access patterns are relatively simple, little performance difference exists when compared to DRAM. However, as systems progress towards relying more heavily on memory storage and with increasing complexity of memory access patterns, the Optane DC PMMs unique advantages will become even more pronounced. This, in turn, will continue to accelerate the need for user-level persistent memory management software solutions. Four prototypes of user-level persistent memory managers were developed and tested across various workloads and environments, yielding promising results before being subjected to thorough security testing and multiple layers of analysis to identify potential vulnerabilities. The findings revealed that three of the prototypes proved resistant to common exploitation techniques employed by malware, albeit with limitations. The prototype prototypes demonstrated exceptional performance across all evaluated applications, outperforming the file system approach by significant margins, up to two times the performance. This accelerated performance was attributed to the user-level persistence approach providing a direct interface to memory storage, eliminating the need for additional layers of abstraction and allowing for optimized software design. This, coupled with the unique advantages of the Optane DC PMMs, positions user-level persistent memory as the most conducive solution for achieving maximal performance. As a result, the time has come for operating systems to integrate user-level persistent memory management into their core functionality. This requires a collaborative effort among hardware manufacturers, operating system developers, and application software designers

Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{C}(z)/ d_{C}(1))^{0.3}$. A similar approach was applied to the gold sample, with comparable results. If confirmed, this approach may provide an affordable and effective means to constrain models of dark matter by controlling for lens-induced lensing in SN Ia analyses. Additionally, it may be employed to calculate the mass of galaxies based on the lensing effects on SN Ia in low-redshift studies. Upcoming more precise datasets, such as the Dark Energy Survey and future surveys like LSST, EUCLID, and WFIRST, will significantly benefit from this approach. A simple modification of this method can also be applied to account for lens-induced variations in strong narrow absorption lines in quasars. Therefore, this approach has far-reaching implications that could have a major impact on various analyses of SN Ia and quasars that involve constraining galactic haloes. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties and long-lived electronic spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 280nm range at the p-type silicon substrate interface of a SOI microstructure. Utilizing optical detection of magnetic resonance, we found that etching the silicon surface increases T center creation rates up to 5.8 x 10^11 per cm^2, offering a viable method for efficiently building quantum photon-spin interfaces. Furthermore, spin properties of the T centers were investigated under various ion implantation conditions and it was found that high-density T center ensembles maintain satisfactory spin coherence properties, likely due to the low levels of ion damage surrounding these defects. In addition, a discussion on the potential applications of T centers in quantum communication systems is presented. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. Springer further demonstrated that two elements of Sp_n(K) belong to the same conjugacy class if and only if their respective sets of non-negative integers identifying the block sizes of the corresponding matrices coincide. Consequently, Springer's research offered insights into the structure of the dual conjugacy classes within Sp_n(K). He demonstrated that the group conjugating these classes is isomorphic to a product of groups, specifically containing the field automorphisms and a group generated from roots of unity within K, further allowing him to compute the order of the conjugacy classes classes and describe various relationships between distinct classes. Moreover, Springer's research found ways to conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K) to correlate with those within the general linear group Gl_m(K), specifically focusing on subgroups and their respective conjugacy classes. He demonstrated that these correlations form the orbit of Weyl group, previously defined by Hermann Weyl, thereby establishing a deeper understanding of the symplectic group's representation. This representation-based insight would later become a foundational element of George Lusztig's research, particularly in his computation of characters within the general linear group. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation as Word2Vec. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. Specifically, we investigate their consistency across varying word frequencies and part-of-speech categories, exploring both individual words and the structure of mixed bags comprising either syntactically similar words or randomly selected words. Our study involves a corpus of nearly a million words, enabling us to draw reliable conclusions about the word2vec model's performance. We discover that it effectively captures the high-level semantic features of the corpus, yet is largely indifferent to the internal distribution of terms. Notably, we show that certain aspects of the word2vec representations can be understood through basic mathematical operations that combine the embeddings of individual terms. We also establish an explicit connection between these representations and the mixed bag structure implicit in the word2vec training algorithms. In essence, our analysis frees the word2vec model from its 'black box' status, providing a clear understanding of how it generates low-dimensional word embeddings. We anticipate that our results will inform the design of future natural language processing methods, also enabling more effective evaluation of unsupervised models. We have conducted all aspects of our analysis within a fully non-parametric mathematical framework, relying solely on empirical observations and statistical inference. Consequently, our study is broadly applicable across all unsupervised feature learning algorithms. We have made our comprehensive software suite publicly available to facilitate the reproduction of our results and the exploration of our findings within distinct contextual frameworks. The software can be accessed through our public repository. This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and facilitates easy implementation of boundary conditions. To account for phase change, we've established a variant of the VOF method on unstructured meshes; however, our approach keeps the method's conservative properties. Through carefully designed test cases, we've demonstrated the capability of this method to handle significant boundary deformations, high-resolution interface capture, and phase change simulations. Furthermore, we've achieved substantial performance enhancements using modern computing technologies. A complex industrial application involving this method is also presented, showcasing its effectiveness in modeling real-world problems. 

Keywords: Level-set methods, Embedded boundary techniques, Multi-phase flow models, VOF method, Finite difference schemes, High-performance computing.

While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. Given the increasing size of modern PDF fits, requiring the combination of hundreds of datasets, a robust software solution is essential to streamline the integration process, ensuring that potential shortcomings can be extensively investigated by conducting deliberate adjustments to the predictions. In the context of the MMRT PDF fitting framework, we present an integrated suite of functionalities that can seamlessly combine diverse theoretical predictions, a functionality that has been instrumental in producing our PDF fits. The components of this software solution are now being made publicly accessible to facilitate the easy combination of different theoretical predictions and ultimately contribute to accelerating the development of new PDF fits. The primary aspects of this software solution are (1) a unified interface for predicting outcomes, (2) a robust system for managing datasets, and (3) an advanced tool for computing PDFs. The software solution is primarily built on top of the PyPDFfit framework, a Python-based PDF fitting framework that features an adaptable architecture, allowing research groups to easily incorporate their preferred PDF evolution equations, PDF candidates, and prediction outputs by substituting the corresponding modules. As a result of this software solution, potential limitations in the PDF fits can be extensively examined by conducting deliberate adjustments to the predictions, paving the way for the development of new PDF fits. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Notably, the results show that the adaptive approach can result in a 5 times performance improvement compared to the classical experience replay. Additionally, the method leads to a 15% less expensive policy implementation for a system requiring 100 iterations. Establishing the electronic and superconducting gap structure of iron-based superconductors requires in-depth microscopic understanding. However, even with extensively studied samples like (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$, there has been significant controversy over these structures. Our team resolves this by employing high-resolution ARPES on (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ utilizing both He lamps and laser sources, our results reveal the combined effects of band back-bending and band folding resulting in a flat band at the center of the Brillouin zone. Moreover, we correct previous misinterpretations regarding the superconducting gap sizes, showing that the large gap observed around the zone center is actually a result of band folding rather than a high-gap area around the zone corner. Our results offer a model to explain the superconducting gap distribution in (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ and resolve numerous controversies. Furthermore, we verified our model by comparing its predictions to experimental ARPES data across multiple K concentration levels. Lastly, we analyzed the potential influence of band folding on superconducting gap formation through a comparison with (LaFeAsO$_{0.89}$F$_{0.11}$), an electron-doped iron-based superconductor where band folding is absent, revealing that band folding is an essential factor in high-T$_c$ iron-based superconductors. Our study paves the way for a deeper understanding and new theoretical approaches addressing issues like high T$_c$ and full gap superconductivity in these materials.

Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded distinct components, characterized by different temperature dependences in their recovery times, with one being temperature-linear and the other exhibiting more intricate temperature variation. These results demonstrate that the slow-recovering component is resistant to changes in LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness, while the fast-recovering component is significantly affected, displaying an opposing temperature dependence in thinner samples. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate such processes and systems of SLE can be realized using the Dyson model and its generalizations, allowing us to study the asymptotic behavior of these processes and systems at varying speeds. Notably, this leads to new results on the asymptotic behavior of multiple SLE, revealing similarities with Brownian motion and its interactions, and also enabling us to establish the equivalence of certain Dyson models on different domains. Ultimately, this equivalence implies the identifiability of parameters in these models. Along the way, we derive new results on the Dyson model and its relationships with Gaussian free fields and multiple SLE. These results are demonstrated in a broader context of domain domains that allow for conformal equivalence. Furthermore, we discuss potential applications of our findings, including potential connections to random matrix theory and the asymptotic behavior of systems of SLE. Additionally, this paper introduces a new process - Gaussian free field-valued level process - associated with multiple SLE driven by a system of independent Brownian motions. This process is realized using a Dyson model with a specific initial condition and reveals an intriguing relationship with the level process of the corresponding multiple SLE. This relationship is exploited to establish a new identity related to multiple SLE. Lastly, this paper also discusses generalizations of these results to multiple SLE evolving in time on domains that allow for conformal equivalence. This discussion leads to new results on the asymptotic behavior of these processes and systems of SLE, as well as the identification of new Dyson models and their relationships with Gaussian free fields and multiple SLE. This ultimately enables us to establish the equivalence of certain Dyson models on different domains, leading to conclusions on the identifiability of their parameters. This is demonstrated in a broader context of domain domains that allow for conformal equivalence. Furthermore, these results are anticipated to yield valuable insights into random matrix theory and the asymptotic behavior of systems of SLE. This paper is comprised of an introductory section, three major components, and a concluding section. The latter provides an overview of the key takeaways, while also highlighting numerous potential applications

These clusters exhibit a unique and complex motion within a two-dimensional lattice, contrasting with isolated, site-based interactions where particles move freely, independently. Instead, in systems featuring near-neighbor clusterization, an intertwined interplay unfolds as these clusters perform an 'interactive walk,' giving rise to multiple temporal dynamics. Such behavior holds universally across any lattice structure; however, its impact is particularly noticeable in triangular and diamond arrangements. Here, by analyzing a spin-Hubbard model on a honeycomb lattice, we reveal that robust near-neighbor clusters emerge only when the strength of site-to-site interaction surpasses a certain threshold and is at least marginally stronger than on-site interaction. Furthermore, by leveraging boson expansions and numerical methods, we found evidence supporting multiple time scales influencing the cluster's movement and, ultimately, their coexistence with correlated single-site states. Conditions are identified under which these clusters would either move freely, get trapped in a molasses-like state, or follow a more intricate, chaotic dynamics. The existence of such robust clusters could give rise to multifaceted phenomena, providing a theoretical foundation for possible experimental observations in systems featuring strong site-to-site interactions. Moreover, potential connections with superfluidity and Bose-Einstein condensates are discussed. Ultimately, this framework is applicable to any two-dimensional spin model with strong nearest-neighbor interaction and could offer a pathway for understanding self-organizing structures in these types of systems.
