Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific technique addressing this challenge is the splay-tree-based approach; however, its efficacy is compromised due to significant storage and retrieval costs associated with the underlying data structure. In contrast, structural memory algorithms offer efficient conflict resolution methods with minimal storage requirements, albeit often resulting in heightened node traversal costs. We introduce the Remove-Win design framework, which leverages a combination of splay trees and structural memory algorithms to develop efficient protocols for resolving concurrent updates. By generating unique prefix patterns for each update operation and tailoring algorithm configurations, Remove-Win achieves optimal performance with minimal storage requirements and low node traversal costs. Moreover, we demonstrate that a system utilizing the Remove-Win design can recover from conflicts caused by multiple concurrent updates with low latency. Furthermore, our analysis and experimental evaluations confirm that the Remove-Win design ensures both low latency data access and high performance data retrieval. In addition, we provide theoretical evidence that our design can achieve optimal performance measures. We also apply the Remove-Win design framework to develop an efficient protocol, referred to as the Multi-Win algorithm, capable of handling any number of concurrent updates without coordination. We demonstrate that this algorithm can effectively resolve conflicts and recover from all possible conflict scenarios. We also present the design of a distributed key-value store system called WinStore, which employs the Remove-Win design framework and can handle concurrent updates without coordination, resulting in a high-performance data retrieval system with low latency data access. We evaluate WinStore and show that it can provide both low latency data access and high-performance data retrieval with minimal overhead. Furthermore, we evaluate WinStore's performance under heavy load conditions and demonstrate that it can achieve high concurrency levels and effectively handle a large number of concurrent updates with minimal latency. We also compare WinStore with other distributed key-value stores and demonstrate that it can achieve similar performance levels. We also compare WinStore's performance under different deployment scenarios and demonstrate that it can effectively handle a large number of concurrent updates with minimal latency even when deployed on a single machine. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions for various traits and potentially associated biological pathways. Furthermore, we've identified candidate genes associated with different functional elements, such as promoter regions and regions affected by histone modification, that could serve as targets for follow-up studies. In conclusion, our approach has been proven effective in uncovering the genomic elements that underlie the associations found in genome-wide association studies and has provided valuable insights into the nature of these elements. Our research findings are accessible through our web platform enabling researchers to explore our results, download data sets and learn more about our approach and its applications. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered. As a result, the population of black holes in the galaxy's center may be overstated, while also implying that the majority of LMXBs, including some considered black hole candidates, actually contain neutron stars. To differentiate such neutron star binaries from black hole candidates, a new scheme of classification is proposed based on the velocity of their primary components and the hard X-ray spectrum of their outbursts, expecting to identify at least half of the black holes among the LMXB population. To explore the possibility of using this test, the line velocity approach can be utilized by analyzing the star systems' velocity in the plane facing the Earth or the velocity perpendicular to this plane. 

Using the sample of wide binary star systems from a study by Hernandez et. al. (2019) and considering effects from small angle approximations, a new statistical approach was applied to simulate how velocity measurements are affected by the orientation of these star systems. 

Under the assumption that Newton's specific gravitational theory is accurate, a mathematical simulation showed that a large binary star system would have a smaller velocity distribution than expected (an anisotropic velocity distribution) if it contains two stars that are widely separated. However, this anisotropic velocity distribution becomes less noticeable as the line of sight changes.

Since this anisotropic velocity distribution is consistent with an irregular velocity distribution caused by the movement of the Milky Way galaxy, further analysis was conducted to eliminate the effect of the galaxy's movement on the star systems' velocity distribution.

After accounting for the galaxy's movement, the anisotropic velocity distribution disappeared, indicating that the actual mechanism contributing to the irregular velocity distribution is random and unrelated to the orientation of the star systems. The results showed no significant discrepancies in velocity between the two groups, indicating that the actual cause of the irregular velocity distribution is random and unrelated to the orientation of the star systems.

This brief research extends a discovery made by Diamond--Sasaki, relating 
geometric modularity of non-algebraic weights to algebraic weights and vice versa. 
Our investigation demonstrates that non-algebraic weights geometric modularity 
entails geometric modularity for multiple algebraic weights, which has clear 
consequences. Moreover, we prove that geometric modularity of several algebraic 
weights may imply geometric modularity of a non-algebraic weight. This 
connection bridges Diamond--Sasaki's findings to earlier generalisations of 
Serre's conjecture, specifically focusing on weight aspects. Our primary tool 
is the geometric Blakebox package, particularly the part utilizing Ragsdale's 
description of geometric Galois representations. By applying this method, we 
analyze local allof E_k(A_s) at wild primes and make connections to 
geometric modularity, thereby making novel contributions to the field.

THz radiation enables the precise stimulation of vibrational frequencies in molecules and crystals, leading to the introduction of inertial influences on electrons. By drawing a comparison to classical mechanics, where circular motion generates Coriolis and centrifugal forces, analogous effects arise, specifically spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, and the interplay of these forces with the spin-orbit and the redshift of energy levels. These effects can persist for a few picoseconds following the initial stimulation, and potentially amplifying their magnitude could make this approach a promising means of controlling localized quantum states and chemical reaction barriers via vibration. Investigation of this approach involves calculating the differences in energy between initial and persisted states to determine the magnitude of this effect for various molecules and crystals. The results show that, despite some of these effects being too small to be significant, others could potentially be large enough to influence local quantum states and chemical reaction barriers when vibration is extensively amplified during its normal operation. Moreover, some of the calculated energy differences display an inverse relationship with the frequency of vibration, meaning that lower frequency vibrations could lead to larger energy differences, or more substantial shifts in energy levels. This implies that targeting low-frequency vibrations could be a more effective strategy for controlling localized quantum states and chemical reaction barriers via vibration. The primary limitations of this approach are the possibility of vibration being damped by other means, such as light, and the availability of suitable molecules that exhibit distinct energy differences due to vibration. Nevertheless, this concept offers a foundation for exploring innovative ways of controlling localized quantum states and chemical reaction barriers in molecules and crystals. Furthermore, it is feasible that some of the calculated energy differences could be adjusted by dipoolar fields to the desired levels needed for chemical change or quantum state change. Lastly, this approach could potentially be expanded to other physical phenomena that can be stimulated by THz radiation, leading to new avenues for the control of matter. The specific examples analyzed here involve the spin-rotation coupling of conduction electrons with respect to core spins in NiO and LaMnO$_3$, local alignment of superconducting pairs with respect to the vibration of oxygen in HgBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{7+\delta}$, the centrifugal field coupling of Cu$^{2+}$ ions in La$_2$CuO$_4$, and the interaction between vibration and spin-orbit in La$_2$CuO$_4$. The results demonstrate that this approach can yield novel insights into the interplay between local quantum states and chemical reaction barriers in molecules and crystals

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. This research investigates the interrelationship between that number and the minimum number of nodes needed to achieve an edge-free representation. An exponential-time complexity exists in determining if breaking fewer than half the nodes results in an edge-free representation, whereas determining if breaking fewer than two-thirds the nodes results in an edge-free representation exists in the space of NP. It's also established that the latter case possesses a lower bound of NP-complete, as well as a higher bound of NP complete for large random bipartite graphs compared to randomly selected nodes. An exponential-time complexity exists in determining if breaking more than three-quarters the nodes results in an edge-free representation, whereas this bound is of particular interest because it represents a significant improvement over previously existing methods which required re-drawing edges in the original context. The newly developed approach to removing edge crossings relies on a node-cutting method which involves determining the minimum number of nodes to break in order to achieve an edge-free representation. This new approach exists outside the realm of application to general graph types but exists within the scope of bipartite graphs. Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI tasks, particularly in image recognition tasks, yet some challenges remain unresolved. The issue of processing continuous visual data streams and dealing with unbalanced datasets in the learning process continues to persist. Past research has tackled these issues independently, despite their concurrent presence in real-world applications. In this work, we address the challenge of learning incrementally from datasets that are not only unbalanced but also grow over time. We examine algorithms that rely on fixed deep neural network architectures and employ bounded memory to retain examples from previously encountered classes throughout the learning process. Given the constraint of limited memory, older classes are learned from fewer examples compared to newer ones, further exacerbating the initial dataset imbalance. Consequently, a scoring bias emerges, favoring newer classes over older ones. We experiment with a comprehensive range of score calibration methods to counter this bias. The evaluation was conducted across three datasets, utilizing two scenarios representing varying degrees of dataset imbalance, and testing three distinct memory capacity constraints. The findings indicate that most calibration methods yield beneficial results, and their effectiveness is particularly pronounced when memory constraints are tighter – a scenario that holds practical relevance. Moreover, our research discovers that incorporating the usual distillation component into incremental learning algorithms is unnecessary. By removing it, a simplified fine-tuning approach emerges as a more robust foundation for tackling imbalanced incremental learning challenges. The code and models are freely accessible for use at https://github.com/etoro-research/incremental-learning, enabling the community to build upon and improve our proposals. Overall, our experiments yield tangible improvements through the reduction of newer class bias via simple techniques, paving the way for further research into a fundamental issue affecting the majority of deep neural network algorithms. Consequently, more research is needed to fully mitigate the bias and address other core challenges associated with incremental learning. As such, our code, model repositories, and evaluation benchmarks are designed to support collaborative research aimed at creating more robust deep neural network algorithms capable of adapting to complex, ever-changing visual data streams. As we advance the state-of-the-art in deep neural network research, it is crucial to address the fundamental challenges associated with the algorithms themselves before fully leveraging their potential.

A localized alteration in knot diagrams is referred to as an unknotting operation. It can be performed in one of three ways: by reversing the direction of a non-crossing knot segment, or by altering a double cross in a knot diagram. The primary objective of unknotting operations is to transform a given knot into an untangled state via a sequence of localized changes. Unknotting operations have been utilized in prior research to characterize distinct classes of knots based on their complexity. The current study expands upon this concept by introducing a new ordering of unknotting operations, which involves determining the minimal number of operations required to transform one knot into another. The basis for this new ordering is rooted in a specific collection of unknotting operations that can be performed in a localized manner. The proposed ordering is complex and multifaceted, reflecting the intricacies of knot diagrams. It is demonstrated that it possesses distinct properties, such as translational symmetry and the inclusion of trefoil knots as a maximal sub-class. The relationship between this new ordering and Melnikov's ordering system is also discussed. The interconnection between unknotting operations and the braid theory of knots is explored, revealing an interesting connection involving the creation of double crosses. The study of unknotting operations is seen as an integral component of knot diagram dynamics, a broader framework that encompasses the evolution of knot diagrams over time. The potential applications of this framework are also considered, including the investigation of unknotting processes that are driven by forces, as well as the analysis of knots that can be untangled through gravitational interactions with other objects. In the field of Computer Science, matrix-based problem design holds significant importance. Various disciplines like computer graphics, graph theory, and machine learning extensively employ matrix operations to resolve complex issues. Consequently, matrix multiplication, the most frequently used matrix operation, can pose a computational bottleneck when applied to large matrices. To mitigate this limitation, the integration of parallel computing techniques, such as CUDA and openMP, has become essential. This study compares the efficiency of matrix multiplication implemented with these parallel APIs on central processing units and graphics processing units. Our findings indicate that GPU-based execution yields superior performance, especially when multiplying large matrices, although this comes at the expense of increased memory usage. Furthermore, our research reveals that the optimal matrix size for optimal performance on these platforms is 1024 x 1024, and that parallelization techniques can optimize matrix multiplication even on central processing units. However, this achieves a maximum 2.5 times improvement in computational speed at the cost of increased memory consumption. This study's results can serve as a reference for developing matrix-based applications that require optimal performance on modern computing platforms. This research is complemented by a publicly accessible code repository for matrix multiplication development, which is highly adaptable and may be utilized as a base for various matrix-based projects. The code is freely accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/aleksandrbaykov/MatrixMultiplicationComparison. In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks to be performed that would be beyond the capabilities of any single agent. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on a scenario where agents select between two tasks of varying difficulty that are randomly distributed and partially known. It has been found that a stable state of cooperation, characterized by a straightforward linear pattern, can be achieved when there is a wide range of possible task difficulties. Furthermore, it was discovered that the most advantageous action for each agent in response to an approachable strategy profile can be complex and nonlinear when the distribution of task difficulties is not uniform. A computational method has been established to calculate a cooperative equilibrium through learning within the set of linear policy options. The effectiveness of this approach was validated through the successful identification of a linear equilibrium strategy and a compound equilibrium strategy that exhibits a complex, nonlinear pattern. Additionally, the findings were applied to the development of a model that can predict the time required for a system to reach a cooperative equilibrium. The model's ability to make these predictions was verified through multiple trials. It should be noted that the environment and algorithm used may result in equilibria that are suboptimal. Trials were also conducted to compare the performance of the learning algorithm in relation to the complexity of the environment. It was observed that under conditions of low complexity, the algorithm converged at a rate comparable to that of an algorithm that leverages prior knowledge of the distribution of task difficulties. However, under more complex conditions, the algorithm converged at a significantly faster rate than expected. It is anticipated that these findings will contribute to a deeper understanding of cooperative systems characterized by learning agents that execute random tasks. Moreover, these results are hoped to pave the way for future research into scenarios where the distribution of task difficulties is not necessarily linear and where the skills required to perform these tasks follow a more complex pattern. Ultimately, the ultimate goal is to establish a broader theoretical framework that can explain cooperative equilibrium strategies in a more comprehensive manner. Alongside these analytical findings, experimental trials were conducted to compare the performance of different learning algorithms in cooperative multi-agent systems, and it was observed that the complexity of the environment can significantly impact the efficiency of these algorithms. It is anticipated that a deeper theoretical understanding will provide a foundation for designing more effective cooperative solutions across a diverse range of applications. As precision strategies advance for future colliders like HL-LHC, FCC-ee, FCC-hh, ILC, CLIC, CEPC, and CPPC, accurately controlling theoretical predictions becomes essential. We examine the potential role of amplitude-based resummation in achieving this level of control, with case studies at the LHC, future colliders, and even in quantum gravity. Although the resummation approach is computationally demanding to match leading logarithmic accuracy, we show that it can significantly improve theoretical precision, consistently across different colliders and processes. However, the challenge remains cost-effective, given the computational requirements. To address this issue, we suggest several possible solutions to enhance the performance of amplitude-based resummation, including leveraging machine learning techniques, adapting existing lattice QCD methods, or exploring the application of quantum gravity, which could potentially reduce the computational cost while maintaining theoretical precision. If successful, these approaches could make amplitude-based resummation more feasible across various processes and colliders. Nonetheless, further research is necessary to evaluate the viability of these solutions and develop the field of amplitude-based resummation. Object detectors, in particular those that utilize Feature Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in the framework. This paper reexamines FPN within the context of detection systems and sheds light on its success through an optimization lens. It identifies that incorporating FPN results in distorted backpropagation pathways, limiting each backbone network level to focus on specific scale ranges. Consequently, two practical approaches are presented to empower each backbone level to consider all objects within the detection framework. Firstly, introducing auxiliary objectives facilitates direct propagation signals during training. Secondly, constructing the feature pyramid more reasonably can circumvent irrational backpropagation paths. Comprehensive experiments validate the analysis and demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods on the COCO benchmark, resulting in substantial improvements of over 2% across one-stage, two-stage, anchor-based, anchor-free, and transformer-based detectors. The code has been made publicly available.

Complex, multi-dimensional data is often analyzed with conditionally specified models, which rely on implicit assumptions at their boundaries. Unfortunately, current methodologies lack a systematic approach to assess these extreme assumptions due to complex copula and marginal forms. In contrast, this research introduces novel tools to measure the implicit assumptions of conditional models concerning their boundaries. These tools allow us to derive explicit formulas for approximating extreme assumptions related to the distribution of a single variable and new results for a two-dimensional distribution. Additionally, an innovative method is introduced to enhance the convergence of tail assumptions by modifying the original model through a scaling factor, which can be applied to both single and multi-dimensional distributions. A new metric is introduced to measure the distance between two conditional distributions based on their implicit assumptions at the boundary, enabling comparisons between different models. Finally, an innovative approach is proposed to estimate the parameters of conditional models by targeting these assumptions, rather than the original model. This research is grounded in the context of extreme value theory and provides novel solutions to longstanding challenges affecting the analysis of multi-dimensional data. Several innovative methods are proposed and demonstrated through theoretical and empirical developments, which offer feasible solutions to prominent issues affecting the analysis of complex, multi-dimensional data. In practice, these methods can be applied to derive new results and address existing problems, leading to potential applications in various contexts. In theory, these methods uncover new insights, paving the way for further research and in-depth mathematical justification. We aim to tackle the Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) challenge, which poses a difficulty in language understanding, by evaluating and comparing various contextualized methods. WSD entails determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context. We test and contrast Contextualized Embedding (CE) techniques like Hierarchical Recurrent Neural Network (HRNN) and MultiTask Learning (MTL) for WSD resolution on two datasets. Our findings indicate that HRNN outperforms other CE approaches and traditional methods like Supsense and SemiSupsense. We also observe that incorporating additional tasks and hierarchical structures to the word context improves WSD performance. Moreover, our experiments show that the underlying mechanisms of contextualized models play a crucial role in resolving WSD. We hope to contribute to further research and development of WSD challenges by providing the results of our comparisons and analyses. All code and data used in this project are available for download at https://github.com/aliugh15/Contextualized-WSD.

Reasoning about and sequencing unordered events is a crucial skill to understand real-world procedures, which often require grasping temporal common sense and incorporating various forms of information. Real-world procedures are commonly communicated through a combination of written text and visual aids. The ability to accomplish this task is essential for complex tasks like planning sequential tasks and summarizing instructional content from multiple sources. Although humans can easily understand and sequence unordered multimodal procedural instructions, the same cannot be said about current machine learning models. In our research, we assess the ability of machine learning models to understand and sequence unordered multimodal instructions by compiling datasets from widely-used instructional manuals and gathering extensive human feedback. Our findings show that these models not only perform much worse than humans but also struggle to efficiently use the information provided in both textual and visual forms. In an effort to enhance the performance of machines on this task, we introduce sequential-aware pretraining techniques that make use of the sequential connections present in both written text and visual aids, leading to significant improvements exceeding 5%. Through an in-depth analysis of the model's performance, we discover that the primary benefit of these techniques becomes apparent when the instructions are presented in a sequential fashion, demonstrating that machines can still benefit from them even though they assess instruction sequences independently. As a result, this research contributes not only a method to enhance the performance of machines on sequential tasks involving communication but also a large-scale dataset for further research and development. This dataset, known as the Multi-Modal Instructional Sequence Ordering Dataset (MISOD), comprises over 110k instructional sequences with corresponding ordered paths and is comprised of sequences from widely-used instructional manuals, coupled with widely-used image datasets. MISOD is available for download at https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/master/misod. The relationship between this derivation and traditional network measures is explored through correlations. Neural language models have largely surpassed $n$-gram models due to better language knowledge capture, but our findings suggest that n-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs. Building upon this observation, we aimed to create a neural model that retains the advantages of n-gram models. Consequently, we developed a large-scale n-gram model, named BigFreeBnB, which achieves exceptional performance across various language tasks with minimal computational expenses. When combined with a neural model, the hybrid system significantly improves results in both low-data and normal-data settings, as evidenced by our models' performance on datasets like Gigantic Miniature, IMDB, and ADE20K, as shown in the main body sections 3, 4, and 5 respectively. Moreover, BigFreeBnB's effectiveness is further demonstrated through its application in generative tasks, such as generating novel sentences, questions, and answers. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. By expanding the range of poses they can handle, our technique opens up applications for faces that rotate freely in images, such as in video sequences. In these cases, our approach produces realistic results even with the absence of actual pose information. Based on extensive testing, our model represents a significant advancement over current methods, all of which are designed for limited pose ranges, in accordance with the AFLW200-3D dataset's capabilities. Consequently, our technique offers greater flexibility in the production of high-quality, realistic faces. The novel strategy of our system also makes it possible to create a suite of face analysis and reconstruction techniques that operate directly in the 3D domain, free from inherent ambiguities associated with 2D projections. The implementation of our system involves the introduction of several groundbreaking 3D face processing techniques, such as pose estimation, reconstruction, and alignment. Speech enhancement plays a crucial role as an initial pre-processing step in audio signal processing technologies like speech recognition and synthesis. Despite the advancement of deep learning-based speech enhancement models, they are hindered by their large size and difficulty in tuning. This paper introduces an semi-supervised speech enhancement framework that incorporates a limited professional dataset into an extensive non-professional dataset. The framework consists of two segments: professional-to-non-professional speech enhancement models are developed using a deep unsupervised domain adaptation method, and the use of a professional dataset as additional training data in a supervised setting. This approach is evaluated using two datasets and two evaluation metrics, showing significant improvements over baseline methods. The findings suggest that the proposed framework achieves enhanced speech quality, particularly in low-snr conditions. Moreover, the results indicate that incorporating professional data into non-professional data improves speech quality and reduces the discomfort associated with altered speech. This implies that the model is not only enhancing speech quality but also retaining the original speaker's identity to some extent. The proposed method demonstrates the potential to enhance speech with an acceptable degree of naturalness and consistency. This has significant implications for the broader applications of speech transformation technologies.

A negative pressure room (NPR) in biolabs and infectious-control hospitals must meet stringent safety standards set by bio-safety levels (BSLs) to prevent potentially deadly pathogens from escaping into the surrounding environment. These facilities maintain negative air pressure relative to the outside space by using specialized systems to contain the microbes. Modern building management systems utilize differential pressure sensors (DPSs) to regulate and monitor NPR's air pressure. However, these sensors are vulnerable to manipulation through tailored audio signals, allowing an attacker to compromise the facility's primary containment system. Our research reveals that critical NPRs can be vulnerable to cyber attacks using the Bluetooth protocol, exploiting the limited security measures in place. A demonstration shows that a distance record for Bluetooth transmission can be achieved, potentially allowing an attacker to access and compromise facilities located on separate floors. Our findings highlight the importance of implementing robust security protocols to prevent unauthorized access and ensure the containment of life-threatening pathogens. Moreover, this research emphasizes the need for regularly updating security measures to account for evolving wireless communication technologies. Lastly, our study recommends the use of randomized pressure readings and secure communication protocols to prevent attacks and protect public health.

A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. As a solution, we propose adjusting the design of existing auction-based pricing mechanisms to account for the inherent riskiness of storage units, thereby allowing them to provide more stable and flexible services to the grid. By making these changes, we believe a larger pool of risk-aware storage units could be engaged in the grid, ultimately leading to lower costs and enhanced stability requirements for energy supply. Empirical evidence from our research indicates that up to 50% of hidden costs associated with energy storage could be addressed through this approach. Furthermore, storage units' willingness to participate in flexible pricing schemes correlates with their level of risk awareness, with a notable 15% increase observed in one market. Our study highlights the significance of storage units' risk awareness in influencing their behavior and suggests integrating them more seamlessly into the grid, with implications extending beyond low-carbon energy systems. Ultimately, our work provides a foundational framework for investigating the interplay between energy storage technology, grid pricing mechanisms, and the inherent risk preferences of storage units, with scope for applying this research to other contexts involving time-based auctions and risk-aware agents.

To better understand these experiments, various factors are re-cast in dimensionless forms to define a parameter space in which circulation patterns are mapped and classified. Notable patterns and trends emerge when varying rotation rate, as well as the rate at which heat and motion are transferred and released in the atmosphere. Similar patterns in circulation are found to occur under both laboratory and atmospheric conditions, revealing similarities between atmospheric circulation and circulation in fluids under strong gravitational forces. Deep neural networks (DNNs) benefit from being trained on optimal subsets of annotated data. Active learning algorithms achieve this by pinpointing data samples that are essential for improving DNN performance. The method is particularly advantageous in large-scale industrial settings where labeling costs are exorbitant. The emergence of self-supervised pretraining underscores the significance of leveraging unlabeled data for enhanced model performance. Integrating active learning with self-supervised pretraining allows the exploitation of vast amounts of unlabeled data in tandem with targeted annotation of crucial samples. 

Our investigation combines active learning and self-supervised pretraining in the context of ImageNet. The evaluation reveals that results on modest, commonly used benchmark datasets do not reflect actual performance on large-scale datasets like ImageNet due to an uneven class distribution selected by the active learning method. Existing AL algorithms failed to surpass random sampling among our evaluated benchmarks, including small and large-scale scenarios. In order to address the issue of class imbalance, a novel variable-kernel margin-based active learning algorithm was proposed. The new algorithm selectively recruits diverse samples with varying importance weights, leading to an imbalance-detecting score that identifies classes with low scores. 

In evaluations on small and large-scale scenarios among the DAQA benchmarks, the proposed algorithm yielded superior results compared to state-of-the-art active learning methods that failed to outperform random sampling. Moreover, the proposed algorithm demonstrated superior performance on unseen classes in OCO and achieved comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods on small-scale scenarios while outperforming them in large-scale scenarios in the CUB dataset. Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as they demonstrated distinct behavior. Those of larger size displayed a unique Hall plateau pattern with an additional plateau arising from helical edge states formed when a magnetic field is applied. Conversely, smaller-sized samples showed an unusual transition from the edge state to the helical state at their corresponding critical thicknesses due to size constraints. Notably, this transition was accompanied by an unexpected increase in longitudinal resistance. Additionally, both types of samples exhibited positive and negative differential resistance peaks associated with the formation of magnetic Landau levels within their energy gaps. A theoretical model incorporating both edge and helical states proved capable of explaining these findings. Experimental results were also found to align with those predicted by the model when considering the energy gap and magnetic field levels. A notable aspect of this work involves the discovery that the positive differential resistance peaks can be utilized for controlling magnetic field-induced resistance in HgTe quantum wells. This finding has significant implications as it may enable the development of magnetic resistance-based devices. Furthermore, our findings also suggest that size constraints play a crucial role in determining the transport characteristics of these quantum wells. This is particularly evident when comparing the edge and helical state regimes in large and small-sized samples, where the latter demonstrates a significant increase in negative differential resistance when transitioning from the edge to helical state regime. This increase in negative differential resistance in small-sized samples can be attributed to the longer carrier mean free path when compared to the size of the sample, leading to an enhanced interaction with the magnetic field and resulting in the observed increase in negative differential resistance. This work provides new insights into the transport characteristics of HgTe quantum wells and has significant implications for the development of magnetic resistance-based devices. It also highlights the potential for optimizing device performance through precise control of the quantum well's thickness and applied magnetic field. This approach could be applied not only to HgTe-based devices but also to other types of two-dimensional materials exhibiting Dirac cone-like energy spectra. In this work, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework centered on ODE neural networks, which reinterprets classic optimization techniques within a gradient-based context. This framework leverages ODE neural networks to recognize patterns in data and establish a mapping to optimize variables. By doing so, it bypasses the need for traditional methods of optimization and learning. Our model features an end-to-end differentiable structure, which allows for the direct extraction of features and subsequent classification. We also derive an explicit formulation for updating ODE neural network parameters and demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by applying it to a range of tasks, including supervised learning, feature extraction, and commodity domain adaptation, with minimal required parameters. Our framework significantly outperforms both traditional methods and other meta-learning architectures across multiple metrics. The implementation of our method is available online.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. The results show that the system achieves a significant reduction in errors and outperforms conventional transfer learning methods. Furthermore, the proposed system is capable of mitigating dangerous predictions with an error reduction of over 40% in some cases. This suggests that the system holds promise for creating safe and reliable machine learning models. However, the method does rely on human input of high quality. Additionally, the approach is computationally efficient and can be applied to a range of machine learning architectures, including neural networks. Despite its advantages, the system has a few drawbacks, including the requirement for significant human effort to correct errors and refine the model through various iterations. Moreover, the approach has a tendency to produce conservative predictions that, while safe, may not always be accurate. Moreover, the method requires substantial human input to create high-quality safety guidelines. This input is crucial for the system to function effectively and learn from its mistakes. Furthermore, the guidelines need to be designed in a way that allows the refinement agent to handle exceptions through the incorporation of specific rules that can be processed efficiently by the agent. Additionally, the system has a limitation where the scoring agent's reliability metric is only applicable to predictive models. Consequently, this constraint limits the approach's potential applications to areas like transportation, healthcare, and finance. Finally, the system's performance is hindered by the artificial errors inserted in the training datasets, suggesting that it may struggle with real-world datasets containing diverse and complex errors. Nevertheless, the proposed system presents an innovative collaborative approach that focuses on developing safe and reliable machine learning models using a combination of human input and artificial intelligence. This approach has the potential to play a key role in creating robust AI systems capable of addressing critical challenges in various fields

In x-ray image analysis, identifying prohibited items contributes to maintaining public safety. However, the difficulty lies in detecting low-contrast, color-less objects which can result in unsatisfactory performance. Until now, there have been limited studies in this field due to the absence of high-quality specialized datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel dataset named High-quality X-ray (HiXray), which contains a comprehensive collection of 8 prohibited item categories and comprises 102,928 high-quality images. These images are extracted from real-world airport security inspections and annotated by experienced security personnel. Moreover, to enhance the accuracy of prohibited item detection, we introduce a Lateral Inhibition Module, which emulates the human ability to disregard irrelevant information and focus on distinguishing characteristics. By incorporating a flexible module and leveraging Bidirectional Propagation and Boundary Activation modules, LIM successfully minimizes noise and accentuates identifiable features from multiple directions. Experimental results on HiXray and OPIXray demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing detection approaches. The dataset and model are publicly accessible, paving the way for further research and advancement in prohibited item detection. A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. Additionally, we establish the relationship between $J_n^T$, the colored Jones polynomial, and its counterpart based on biperiodic links. Lastly, we propose an analogue of the volume conjecture for $J_n^T$.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance. Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques in context-gloss pairs to enhance the efficacy of WSD. A comparative analysis of different context-gloss augmentation techniques is conducted, revealing that the application of back translation to definitions produces the most satisfactory outcomes.  The findings provided in this study can serve as a foundation for investigating other NLP tasks that involve disambiguating words with multiple senses. This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the framework of graph-based data. However, applying DP to graph data poses significant challenges due to interconnected data points that can form complex relationships. This issue is compounded by a lack of universally accepted DP formulation in graph-based contexts. This problem further exacerbates the difficulty in conducting private machine learning on graph data. This work also compares and distinguishes different graph-based learning tasks from those that incorporate graph neural networks. In this research, we propose a method to automatically generate complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping technology in simulation. By using a set of control points to create a parametric road design, we define a driving task that an equipped vehicle must perform. Modifying the control points significantly impacts the road's overall shape and layout. Our approach leverages optimization techniques to identify a set of control points that creates challenging driving conditions, causing the vehicle to veer off its intended path. We validated our method with three distinct search configurations, focusing on balancing testing speed and practicality for evaluating autonomous lane-keeping systems. The results showed that our approach could find stressful driving scenarios in a reasonable time, even when restricting the search to more manageable sizes. However, there was a trade-off between finding challenging tests and the time it took to find them. Ultimately, our method proved effective in creating difficult driving scenarios for lane-keeping system testing and had potential applications in evaluating other autonomous vehicle functions. The source code for this research is available online. The findings described in this paper led to the development of a public dataset containing challenging driving scenarios along with the underlying control points that define them. The dataset consisted of over 10,000 highly stressful tests, alongside a smaller set of 500 scenarios that were particularly demanding in terms of lane management. The data was generated using a multi-objective optimization algorithm that balanced the challenge level with practical considerations for use in evaluating autonomous lane-keeping technology. To facilitate user discovery, product recommendations are often accompanied by descriptions. The rise of personalized music playlists through automatic recommendation introduces the challenge of creating descriptive metadata. This paper introduces an innovative approach called music captioning, which leverages audio content analysis and natural language processing to effectively summarize the tracks within each playlist. We explore various captioning techniques, including a custom-designed model that combines multi-scale feature extraction and a neural conversational framework, yielding an 11.9% increase in effectiveness according to user evaluations. Our approach demonstrates a balanced combination of efficiency and quality, producing descriptive metadata that is not only audibly relevant but also aligns with the overall playlist theme, as validated by both objective and subjective assessment. Furthermore, we observe a notable 28.8% improvement in captioning accuracy when considering the music genre, as evidenced by both internal comparisons and external metrics. This innovative approach to music captioning paves the way for enhancing automatic music recommendations with descriptive metadata, potentially leading to increased user engagement and comprehensive music exploration tools. Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach for describing interacting Bose gases within a specific phase-space framework. This method extends previous hydrodynamic methods, enabling the simulation of non-equilibrium quantum fluctuations and their subsequent behavior as these fluctuations dissipate into thermal resonances. Building upon this framework, we derived stochastic hydrodynamic equations that directly relate quantum forces to classical friction forces, and demonstrated that our approach can be applied to various systems by specifically analyzing one-dimensional interacting Bose gases, including obtaining exact stochastic hydrodynamic equations at the level of quantum hydrodynamics. Furthermore, we compared our results to both experimental data and quantum field theory predictions, and found excellent agreement when considering the momentum correlations of boson field operators, and at low and intermediate densities. The accuracy of our approach supports the feasibility of studying quantum fluctuations in interacting Bose gases, and could be particularly useful for simulating systems that require many-body quantum fluctuations to be understood, such as superfluidity and quantum phase transitions. The developed method is versatile, and could be applied to other interacting quantum systems, such as Fermi gases once quantum field theory for fermions is incorporated into the approach. The explicit equations derived from this framework could be used to analyze the dynamics of Bose gases at extremely low temperatures, and the developed approach provides a framework for studying the effects of quantum forces on the behavior of these systems. The implemented method is highly computational efficient as it can be directly integrated from initial conditions, and the accuracy of the approach could be evaluated by applying it to systems with known quantum field theory descriptions. The research is currently limited to equilibrium and near-equilibrium situations, but has the potential to be extended to more complex scenarios in the future. Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation. This model incorporates two contextual networks that target start and end times separately, leveraging contextual features from the entire video sequence to guide the generation of proposals. Each context network consists of a spatial network that extracts spatial context and a temporal network that extracts temporal context from the video sequence, with both contexts being learned using a dual-stream scheme. All context networks work in unison to generate proposals that are reviewed and refined through a comprehensive evaluation protocol. Experimental results show that our DCAN model achieves exceptional performance on the ActivityNet dataset, outperforming top-notch baselines by a significant margin and setting a new benchmark for action proposal evaluation. The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma remain somewhat enigmatic despite detailed documentation. A recently investigated explanation suggests that these structures form when magnetic field eddies caused by edge-localized modes trigger the development of a PTM seed island. However, this study instead seeks to provide an alternate explanation based on observations of edge plasma turbulence. A distinct feature of plasma turbulence is the existence of persistent structures known as blobs and holes in the scrape-off-layer. Measuring the currents within these coherent regions has shown that they follow the direction of the magnetic field. Here, the relationship between these turbulent filaments is likened to ELM filaments, which comprise 'blobs' with enhanced plasma density and interspersing 'holes'. To further this theory, a computer model simulating current within a q=3 surface has shown magnetic fluctuation similarities to those detected by JET in-vessel coils. This implies that the manifestation of a PTM is closely linked to capturing 'holes' on such a surface post-ELM, producing corresponding magnetic readings. Conversely, the detection of 'blobs' captured on a q=4 surface would produce the signature magnetic fluctuations associated with a PTM. This theory suggests that the energy sources driving the development of these turbulent filaments could provide a more fundamental explanation for the origins of PTM. Furthermore, it is proposed that PTMs will only arise when 'holes' are captured on a q=3 surface or 'blobs' on a q=4 surface, offering a potential explanation for the variability in PTM frequency across different JET shots. Lastly, this theory predicts that PTMs will continue to occur as long as edge-localized modes persist and modify the plasma edge so as to repeatedly give rise to turbulent plasma configurations conducive to the generation of PTM magnetic signatures. As a result of this investigation, the term 'palm tree modes' is formally proposed to encompass all magnetic field fluctuations arising from the interaction between edge magnetic field lines and coherent filaments in the plasma scrape-off-layer. Finally, projections are made on the expected behavior of PTMs in relation to the occurrence frequency of ELMs and the resulting changes in plasma configuration. 

This work has significant ramifications for the understanding and study of PTMs and their relationship with ELMs, requiring a review of ongoing research in preparation for upcoming tokamak devices such as JET's full power phase and the ITER device. This research focuses on resolving collision avoidance for non-holonomic robots moving at constant speeds in a two-dimensional space, leveraging dynamic vortex potential fields and their gradients to create cooperative behavior between the robots. A variable repulsive force field, sensitive to velocity and position of nearby robots, is introduced to prevent the emergence of local minima, and only activates when a robot approaches a potential collision with other mobile robots or stationary objects. It's demonstrated through kinematic analysis that a cooperating robot can evade non-cooperative robots moving at constant speeds or actively attempting to collide, under conditions specified by potential field parameters, and this cooperative approach is verified through experiments using a mobile robot platform. Adjusting the field parameters is shown to allow multiple cooperative paths between obstacles, and the approach is found to prioritize speed over efficiency in practice, and may not always opt for the most direct route due to the influence of vortex fields. Though this method does not guarantee global optimality, it produces consistent results in the context studied. The proposed method is compared to alternative collision avoidance strategies, and potential improvements to vortex fields, such as adapting to changes in the robot's dimensions, weight or sensing capabilities, are identified. Recent advancements in wireless communications research have led to increasing interest in the Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology. Comprised of passive reflective components that can modulate the characteristics of incoming waveforms, such as phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization, an IRS offers a means to actively control the characteristics of wireless channels. Given its promising properties, researchers are looking into the potential of incorporating IRS technology into radar systems to optimize target parameter estimation. This paper provides a theoretical basis for implementing IRS technology in radar systems, with a particular focus on scenarios where the line-of-sight (LOS) link between the radar and target is obstructed or weak. We investigate the potential of utilizing IRS technology to create a virtual non-line-of-sight (NLOS) link, enhancing radar performance and target parameter estimation. Through numerical simulations and comparative analyses under both optimized and suboptimal scenarios, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the IRS-provided virtual link in target parameter estimation when the LOS link strength is lower than a relative strength of $~10^{-1}$ in comparison to the NLOS link. Furthermore, our results indicate that over 90\% of the target parameters can be estimated accurately when the IRS-provided virtual link has a relative strength greater than $10^{-3}$. Additionally, we observed that our optimized approach enhances target parameter estimation accuracy by approximately 20-40 times over the suboptimal scenario across various signal-to-noise ratios. Overall, our research findings validate the potential of IRS technology to revolutionize radar systems, enabling reliable target parameter estimation in obstructed or weak LOS link scenarios. Moreover, we propose an advanced algorithm called the Minimum Mean Squared Error (MMSE)-IRS, achieving a 90\% accurate estimation within 5-6 iterations. Moreover, our research extends beyond target parameter estimation, providing a foundational framework for various other radar-related applications, such as active detection and remote sensing. Ultimately, our study paves the way for the integration of IRS technology into modern radar systems, leveraging its capabilities to optimize target parameter estimation when the LOS link is obstructed or weak. However, further research is needed to fully explore the limitations and potential of IRS technology in such scenarios.

Discovering vulnerabilities in programs through fuzzing is a crucial process, but measuring its effectiveness is still an unsolved issue despite the progress made. A widely accepted evaluation standard in software testing is mutation analysis, assessing the ability to detect artificial flaws, and it encompasses a variety of measures that evaluate the ability to trigger and detect faults of any difficulty. However, the traditional mutation analysis approach is impractically costly for fuzzing due to the need for independent evaluation of each mutation. This study presents the application of modern mutation analysis methods, combining multiple mutations to assess the effectiveness of fuzzers for the first time. An evaluation framework for fuzzers has been introduced and utilized in conjunction with various popular fuzzers and testing subjects. The evaluation results indicate that contemporary fuzzers can detect mutations in only a small percentage, but this outcome serves as a motivation for future research to address (1) the enhancement of fuzzer performance in detecting sophisticated failures and (2) the development of more effective techniques for triggering mutations and faults. Like other aspects of fuzzing, this evaluation framework is an open research area and invites contributions from the community. Following the success of pretraining techniques in learning representations, various methods utilizing pre-trained models in continual learning have been developed. Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by implementing mechanisms for continual learning with minimal or no updates to the backbone models. In this study, we challenge the necessity of complex models by comparing a basic alternative we devised. We propose that a pre-trained feature extractor can achieve high performance in continual learning tasks, including the Split-CIFAR100 and CoRe 50 benchmarks. To test this, we conducted a straightforward comparison: a single-headed, task-free baseline uses the frozen pre-trained model to extract image features and calculate their corresponding mean features for every encountered class. It then determines class predictions by comparing the nearest neighbor distance between test samples and mean features of each class, resulting in a Nearest Mean Classifier (NMC). This basic approach achieved 88.53% accuracy on the 10-Split-CIFAR-100 benchmark, outperforming state-of-the-art continual learning methods using the same pre-trained transformer model. The proposed NMC was also robust in sample-efficient scenarios and comparable to state-of-the-art methods in the CoRe 50 benchmark. The straightforward comparison we conducted has significant implications for the ongoing research in continual learning, suggesting that the complexities often added to the task-free baseline may be unnecessary. To facilitate future research, we have released the code and model weights used in this comparison, along with the dataset and evaluation protocols employed. It is now publicly available on the Continual Learning Repository. It is hoped that this comparison, along with the tools released, will contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the role of complex models in continual learning. It will also provide a baseline that researchers can use for comparing their models to a simplified, task-free baseline that achieves high performance. We define a new concept of relative 1-homotopy type for mappings between a surface and a metric space that contains a specified set of Jordan curves, and investigate its properties. This enables us to prove the existence and local smoothness of the surfaces with minimal area within a particular relative 1-homotopy class in certain types of metric spaces. Furthermore, we establish that when the ambient space has a certain topological characteristic, maps that are relatively 1-homotopic are also relatively homotopic. These findings also hold for closed surfaces and improve previous results of several mathematicians. Additionally, we present an example demonstrating that in certain environments, surfaces with minimal area may not be smooth. Moreover, we develop an alternative approach to computing the energy of maps between surfaces based on their values and gradients, and demonstrate that this method aligns with the classical definition when evaluating points. This new framework leads to an improved understanding of the regularity properties of surfaces with minimal area in certain environments. Consequently, we can eliminate the need for certain topological assumptions in certain types of metric spaces. For instance, in compact, smooth surfaces embedded in a three-dimensional Euclidean space, we can remove the requirement for proper immersion. These developments allow us to establish stronger regularity properties for surfaces with minimal area without relying on Reifenberg's theorem. Lastly, we present an improvement to an earlier result of several mathematicians regarding the structure of sets with minimal volume and boundary within a volume-controlled environment. This new result is achieved through a combination of our new approach to relative 1-homotopy type and the earlier result's methods. This work is a preliminary step towards a more comprehensive investigation of sets with minimal volume and complex boundary structures. It involves defining the concept of relative biharmonic maps and developing new properties for maps within specific relative 1-homotopy types. Ultimately, this research is aimed at resolving a topological obstruction in the field of minimal surface theory. This involves establishing the equivalence between sets obtained through homotopy extension and those acquired through homotopy lifting in relation to maps that are relatively 1-homotopic. This new understanding may also yield improved results for the volume of sets defined through homotopy types, potentially leading to new volume estimates in minimal surface theory. It is further anticipated that these new properties and concepts will give rise to novel approaches to investigating the topology of sets and surfaces. Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus, which has a low-spin structure, have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, characterizing their properties. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate pattern of shapes existing together, where a high-energy prolate 0+ state at 3463 keV, and a collective 2+ state just above it, 286 keV, marked a first in Ni isotopes. This discovery of the prolate 0+ state resolved a long-standing debate regarding the 0+3 state's configuration, and demonstrated how close the ground state and low-laying excited states are to various shape-consistent wave functions, needing small amounts of prolate or oblate correlations to define their individual identities. Moreover, by comparing 64Ni to its neighboring isotopes, researchers found that the Monte Carlo shell model correctly ordered the relative energies of different shells, and that the small changes in energy differences between these shells were responsible for the appearance or disappearance of specific prolate or oblate states in 64Ni. Lastly, this work highlighted the importance of determining all excited states thoroughly, to fully comprehend the complex structures of isotopes like 64Ni.

Deep Neural Networks with vast parameters have faced challenges in real-time deployment, prompting the utilization of Teacher-Student architectures in knowledge distillation. Initially used to achieve comparable performance with smaller student networks, these architectures have now been applied across various knowledge learning objectives such as knowledge distillation, expansion, adaptation, and multi-task learning. Current research leveraging Teacher-Student architectures has successfully combined multiple knowledge-learning objectives with efficient, lightweight student networks. This distinct survey delves into the specifics of Teacher-Student architectures with multiple knowledge learning objectives and systematically explores knowledge construction and optimization processes, as well as analyzing various Teacher-Student architectures and learning schemes that produce robust and representative knowledge. Moreover, the paper summarizes and explores the practical applications of Teacher-Student architectures across various purposes, such as classification, recognition, and generation, before examining promising research directions, particularly on the design of Teacher-Student architectures, the quality of knowledge, and the theoretical studies of regression-based learning. With its in-depth analysis, this survey is poised to provide invaluable insights for industry practitioners and the academic community on the utilization of Teacher-Student architectures in multiple knowledge learning objectives.

We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which stands for Finite state Automata Bucket Elimination. Our method essentially buckles down the complex function representations to their most basic forms, allowing for straightforward computations along the way. We examine FABE in relation to its more sophisticated counterparts, particularly when dealing with dense, random, and structured graphs. Our results show FABE to be significantly faster and more reliable than the current state of the art methods, notably when handling large-scale, highly connected graphs. Furthermore, we find that FABE tends to use less memory than the established methods, which can be attributed to the relatively small size of finite state automata when compared to other methods. In scenarios where FABE falls short, such as with non-function data or highly asymmetric graphs, we find that it can still offer some level of performance over the basic Bucket Elimination approach. Lastly, we explore various aspects of FABE's performance, discussing both the underlying principles and the potential areas for further improvement. The FABE implementation is now available online for download.

Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation levels. Our research incorporated momentum transfers resulting from the absorption and emission of photons, as described by a modified version of the optical Bloch equations. Furthermore, our analysis provides a framework for accounting for photon recoil in multiphoton transitions and could be applied to other systems using multiple beams by incorporating momentum transfers resulting from multiple interactions. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol found that for these two systems, anisotropy's influence could be disregarded, allowing a simplification of the jamming theory for shear. Furthermore, by combining this with an anisotropy-free model for shear, researchers were able to predict the viscosity function that governs the thickening transition, revealing that shear and anisotropic forces can cause distinct transitions at distinct volumes, specifically at $\sim0.58$ for shear and $\sim0.62$ for anisotropy. The proposed framework also accounts for long-range forces, introducing a novel theory that explains the origin and characteristics of shear-induced criticality. The discovered relationship between viscosity and volume can be examined in a state of stationary flow; however, the proposed framework requires further exploration in scenarios with changing volume and in gravitational fields. By delving into the interplay between friction, anisotropy, volume, and long-range forces, this study provides a foundation for a unified theory of state transitions, offering a chance to investigate force diagrams for complex systems involving multiple components. Moreover, by identifying shear-induced criticality as the primary driver of the shear thickening transition, this research offers a novel perspective on the long-debated issue of shear thickening's origin. In addition, the proposed framework brings forth fresh questions regarding the interplay between long-range forces and confining conditions during state transitions, as well as the potential for universal behavior in systems undergoing multiple transitions as they change volume. Ultimately, this study suggests that a deeper comprehension of complex systems necessitates a separate examination of distinct interactions to ultimately integrate these studies through the proposed framework. By examining the interplay between long-range forces and confining conditions during state transitions, this research provides a foundation for a unified theory of state transitions, offering a chance to investigate force diagrams for complex multi-component systems and paving the way for a thorough exploration of the proposed framework's broader implications. Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{sl_2}(n)$ of the diagonal embedding of the Lie algebra $U(sl_2)$ within the tensor product of $U(sl_2)^{\otimes n}$. Furthermore, $sR(n)$ can be presented through generators and defining relations, mirroring those of the special Calogero-Sutherland algebra. Additionally, a specific deformation of the algebra $sR(n)$ is constructed, along with its irreducible representations. These deformed representations exhibit Casimir elements that remain unchanged, and their weights are shown to align with those of the Calogero-Sutherland model. A notable $so(3)$-basis, termed the $sR_3$-basis, is introduced and demonstrated to possess desirable properties. Lastly, the introduction of a deformed U(q-shuffle) algebra is proposed, alongside its anticipated properties.
