Our simulation reveals that not only do the incident velocity characteristics of halo WIMPs play a crucial role, but so does the angle of the recoil itself, resulting in an irregular correlation of the two in specific energy ranges. Consequently, attempting to infer the 1-dimensional velocity distribution within these ranges directly from the overall WIMP halo velocities may not provide a complete or accurate understanding, which would ultimately distort our calculations of the associated scattering event rates in those particular ranges. Nevertheless, our simulation further suggests that a more detailed analysis of the incident velocity characteristics of detected recoil events may allow for deconvolving the 1-dimensional velocity distribution within those ranges, potentially enabling access to the overall WIMP velocity distribution via a inversion process for a limited set of functions that describe the scattering probability as a function of velocity, without necessitating a Monte Carlo simulation. Ultimately, our research proposes that this new approach to interpreting data from scattering experiments could provide a crucial alternative to direct production methods of WIMPs in collider experiments, making it essential to retain these experiments in the search for WIMPs. Nevertheless, this study primarily focuses on experiments detecting nuclear recoils, which necessitate the rejection of background events on the basis of the total number of interacting particles in an event. Consequently, a substantial portion of the parameter space encompassing the potential dark matter candidates, such as, for instance, MESSIER, vector dark matter, and others, may be inaccessible to these experiments until they incorporate a more sophisticated analysis method that takes into consideration the substructure of individual events. We are suggesting the establishment of a state-of-the-art muon-proton and muon-nucleus collider that operates at the TeV level, capable of delivering highly accurate measurements in deep inelastic scattering in new areas, while also offering a comprehensive research agenda in particle and nuclear physics. By doing so, we believe it could either drive the advancement or make use of existing particle accelerators, specifically taking advantage of established infrastructure if constructed at places like Brookhaven National Laboratory, Fermilab, or CERN. In this concept, we outline various design parameters for several collider configurations and evaluate potential for scientific discoveries with studies on deep inelastic scattering processes, Higgs boson and vector boson production, top quark creation, and leptoquark beyond Standard Model. Additionally, considerations for detector designs and potential paths to realization are also discussed. Given its research capabilities and relatively modest cost, we think this concept has significant potential to drive the development of particle and nuclear physics. Full details of our proposal can be found in the accompanying paper.

A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which utilizes a continuous spatiotemporal resolved sensitivity variation technique, otherwise known as the "sliding window" method, for both imaging acquisition and reconstruction. The proposed method aims to tackle respiratory motion during scans by dividing the respiratory cycle into equal parts and adjusting the imaging sequence accordingly. A specific study involved modifying a conventional T2-weighted sequence with a respiratory cycle divided into four equal parts, resulting in a 4D MRI image. To evaluate this method, a control group with stable lungs was used, along with lung fibrosis patients, by splitting their respiratory cycles into three and four equal parts, respectively. Both the modified and conventional sequences were then compared and contrasted to compensate for respiratory motion. Contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) was calculated to measure the performance of the proposed method. CNR results showed an increase of 54.2 in fibrosis patients and 14.8 in healthy controls when using the proposed method. The proposed approach yielded higher CNR values than the conventional sequence in both cases. The study demonstrates that using the slapping window method for both sequence design and reconstruction can boost CNR by minimizing variation in suboptimal imaging conditions, resulting in more reliable 4D MRI images. This technique has significant potential to enhance low-dose and noisy MRI images. Furthermore, it is suitable for generating 4D MRI images for various anatomical structures and organs. Additionally, the study reveals that using the sensitivity variation technique for both sequence design and reconstruction can produce consistent and reliable 4D MRI images across different respiratory cycles. This method is anticipated to contribute positively to accurate radiation therapy delivery and disease assessment tools, including diffusion-weighted 4D MRI. Ultimately, the proposed approach is expected to boost the effectiveness of low-dose and noisy MRI images. This study provides initial findings and sets the stage for comprehensive evaluations of the technique. Future studies should conduct in-depth analyses of the approach, covering aspects such as its applicability to various MRI sequences and the optimal selection of respiratory cycle divisions. Additionally, investigations into the method's capabilities with different imaging protocols and its potential for use in treatment monitoring are also warranted. In conclusion, the proposed method successfully compensates for respiratory motion during MRI scans and demonstrates promising results when compared to the control group with stable lungs. We define loom spaces as a more general framework incorporating leaf spaces for pseudo-Anosov flows and link spaces for veering triangulations. Building on Gu\'eritaud's research, it is demonstrated that there is a veering triangulation inherently linked to every loom space, with this triangulation's realization being topologically equivalent to 3D space. Furthermore, it is proven that the graph associated with a loom space's triangulation is always delpable, leading to the derivation of volume lower bounds for a class of 3-manifolds. Moreover, a deep geometric reapraisal of loom spaces is initiated through the identification of their intrinsic hyperbolic geometry, accompanied by the establishment of volume growth estimates within these spaces. Additionally, properties of geodesics in loom spaces are investigated, revealing that planar geodesics segments can only occupy a measure zero in loom spaces. Lastly, an exploration of veering triangulations' combinatorial attributes is undertaken, leading to the development of criteria that guarantee the simplicity of their boundary graphs. By applying these criteria to distinct veering triangulations sharing an identical leaf space, it is proven that the boundary graphs must exhibit the property of being 'del Peppoable'. Consequently, this knowledge is leveraged to establish non-isometry between specific realizations of 3D spaces, thereby providing the foundational basis for volumes of a particular class of 3-manifolds being distinct. Lastly, details are provided for constructing veering triangulations from pseudo-Anosov flows via the incorporation of 'Racchin' surgery. This newly developed surgery procedure is integral to the book's aim of enhancing the understanding of veering triangulations, especially their relationship with the geometry of pseudo-Anosov flows. The book's closing chapter provides a direction for potential future investigation, centered on the set of veering triangulations derived from flows with distinct singularity graphs. It is proposed that this set constitutes the most general class of veering triangulations, with further evidence needed to confirm this hypothesis. Alongside this, several open questions and conjectures are posed for consideration. In conclusion, this research book presents an assortment of groundbreaking theorems, alongside innovative approaches to defining and analyzing loom spaces and their associated veering triangulations. These innovations are certain to propel the field of 3D topology research forward.

Graph neural networks have excelled in multiple applications by translating data into numerical values. However, GNNs' ability to handle large-scale graphs is hindered by their inherent complexity. The underlying challenge lies in GNNs' propensity to increase edges as they process the graph, resulting in diminished model performance and reliability. To address this issue, we present a novel approach called Kedge, which employs a flexible fixed-point method to reduce edges while minimizing errors in model accuracy. The Kedge approach leverages a unique formula to calculate optimal edge values and incorporate them into fixed-point updates. As a result, the Kedge method significantly curbs edge growth, allowing for larger-scale graph processing with similar accuracy levels. Experimental findings indicate that the Kedge approach yields models with 1-3 times more edges, leading to a 10-50% boost in model accuracy when processing large graphs. Furthermore, the Kedge approach facilitates a notable 1.5 times increase in model convergence speed. The algorithm's simplicity and minimal additional parameters make the Kedge approach highly versatile and adaptable to various graph processing applications. A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to prior studies on CountSketch sketches. Moreover, this improved estimator also benefits data analysis systems by allowing for inferences to be made directly on the underlying vectors, thus obviating the need to recover the original data. The new estimator can be viewed as a variety of the classic estimator with parameter $\delta = 1$. The algorithm for this enhanced estimator involves incorporating an additional sum calculations into the basic CountSketch sketch. Theoretical performance characteristics of this new estimator were evaluated and found to maintain $O(k)$ accuracy on the original vector components, with an associated query complexity of $O(k^2)$. The increased query complexity of this new estimator is deemed worthwhile because it enables safe data analysis without requiring the recovery of the original data, thus minimizing queries sufficient for data recovery. Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, referred to as aggregate flexibility, to system operators. Current approaches typically focus on estimating aggregate flexibility through measurement-based feedback, resulting in delayed updates. Furthermore, the traditional model predictive control (MPC) methods are often employed for scheduling, despite their computationally intensive nature. To address these challenges, we propose a novel framework that combines a non-parametric statistical learning approach to predict controllable loads and develop a penalized predictive control method for real-time scheduling. The proposed method reduces energy demand prediction errors, minimizes control variability, and ensures compliance with operational constraints and grid specifications. Computational simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding comparable performance to advanced deep learning methods at a fraction of the computational cost. The proposed framework consists of two key components, a load learning module and a penalized control module, that can be applied to various MPC frameworks, providing a valuable tool for addressing modern power grid challenges. The source code for this research is available online. Keywords: power grid flexibility, demand response, time series estimation, statistical learning, control theory, energy management systems. The recent interest in the stock market can be attributed to growing inflation rates prompting people to invest in equities, commodities, and other assets, as opposed to saving. Deep Learning's ability to accurately predict time series data has been consistently demonstrated. In the realm of technical analysis, using indicators is the most widely adopted approach among traders and investors. Another essential aspect is sentiment analysis, reflecting the emotional state of investors' willingness to invest, where various techniques such as Machine Learning and Neural Networks have been employed. From simple linear regression to advanced neural networks, researchers and investors have experimented with multiple methods to forecast the stock market. This investigation aims to compare linear regression, decision trees, random forests, support vector machines, and neural networks in predicting stock price index variations with the actual values, based on historical data. According to the findings, the neural network yielded the most accurate results. Moreover, exploring the connection between sentiment analysis and stock market predictions involved building a simple linear regression model utilizing sentiment analysis data, which showed potential in improving stock price predictions. Given the success of this investigation, future research can be expanded to incorporate additional sentiment analysis techniques and incorporate external data to improve predictions. Additionally, applying this approach to other asset classes, such as commodities, is worthwhile exploring. Ultimately, combining technical indicators, sentiment analysis, and machine learning algorithms leads to a more accurate stock market forecast. This study's results can be utilized in real-world applications, such as investing in stocks, commodities, foreign exchange, and other asset classes, with minimal knowledge of programming or machine learning expertise. The code and data utilized in this investigation are available online for replication purposes.

One of the most intriguing phenomena in astrophysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped in the shedding material from one of them. This process triggers a shrinking of the orbit as the stars interact with the envelope. Ultimately, it can result in either mergers or further complex interactions, which can involve a mix of compact objects and stars. Certain CE scenarios, particularly those involving white dwarfs, can produce supernovae, while neutron star mergers can result in gamma-ray bursts, and all types of compact object mergers can produce gravitational waves. Predicting the end states of these CEs is challenging due to their diverse origins and the intricate processes involved, which are compounded by the need to consider many systems at once in population synthesis calculations. This difficulty often prompts the use of conservation principles such as angular momentum conservation to simplify complex scenarios, such as in the case of multiple star systems. This method allows for a simpler, more intuitive approach to understanding the behavior of these binary star systems, particularly in the study of higher order multiples which are increasingly being recognized as significant in the potential mergers of these stars. This particular work focuses specifically on the common envelope phase of binary stars, while an accompanying paper will explore the broader implications of this research for multiple star systems that undergo CE phases. This CE phase is a critical phase of binary star evolution, leading to significant interactions that result in complex end states, often involving compact objects and further evolution. This research uses a combination of population synthesis and detailed stellar evolution to analyze the relationships between initial conditions, common envelope outcomes, and the resulting end states, also considering the effects of different pair-instability supernova scenarios, as well as the potential for compact object mergers, including supernovae and gamma-ray bursts, which have significant implications for fields like gravitational wave astronomy. We perform a covariant expansion of the Einstein-Hilbert action in powers of
$1/c^2$, considering a generic spacetime foliation defined by $c$, the speed
of light. We achieve this through the application of a suitable 'pre-non-
relativistic' geometrical parametrization, thereby facilitating an
analytical $1/c^2$ expansion of general relativity. Ultimately, this method
permits an in-depth examination of the Einstein-Hilbert action expansion up to
its next-to-next-to-leading order. The employed approach offers a direct and
manifestly covariant pathway for incorporating non-relativistic symmetries
into an action preceding the $1/c^2$ expansion. We ultimately establish the
relation between the coefficients of the Einstein-Hilbert action expansion and
its corresponding non-relativistic fluid dynamics representation. Moreover, we
demonstrate that the $1/c^2$ expansion of the Einstein-Hilbert action is
equivalent to an iterative implementation of the Cauchy stress tensor
approximation suggested by Landau and Lifshitz. The outcomes of our research
find relevance in the context of developing a covariant, non-relativistic
gravity theory that complements the framework proposed by Baier and Thivierge.

We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood in terms of the spatial arrangement of grains as the cylinder moved, with its long axis experiencing greater resistance due to the greater probability of grains being pinned in this orientation. The results of our study have implications for the study of long objects moving through granular materials and suggest that the stress experienced by these objects can be understood in terms of forces acting in different directions, a concept that could be applied more broadly to the study of objects interacting with granular materials. The relationship we observed between the drag experienced by the cylinder and its speed reminded us of the stick-slip phenomenon, and we believe that further study is needed to fully understand the underlying mechanisms driving the high forces experienced by long objects as they move through granular materials. Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces and the difficulties associated with evaluating their performance. Recently, researchers have made progress in this area using probabilistic models in Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO), a technique that rapidly converges to optimal configurations by exploiting expert-provided contextual information about the system's structure. Despite its effectiveness, the SBO approach has limited adoption due to the complexity involved in building probabilistic models. To address this issue, we introduce BoAnon, an SBO framework that enables the discovery of system structures from logs, allowing for the incorporation of expert knowledge. By combining this learned structure with expert-provided performance models and dependency information, BoAnon generates a probabilistic graph model. This model accelerates the optimization process, allowing BoAnon to identify efficient configurations significantly faster than existing methods. Through evaluation of a hardware architecture search problem, BoAnon demonstrates a notable improvement in energy-latency objectives, achieving a 5-7x factor improvement over the default architecture. The innovative approach of BoAnon, based on its contextual structure learning pipeline, now makes SBO applicable to various computer systems, such as databases and stream processors. As a result, BoAnon is an order of magnitude better than traditional optimization methods and provides a robust solution for autotuning these systems. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for triangular flow $v_3$ in 200 GeV Au$+$Au and 39 GeV Cu$+$Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, triangular flow doesn't exhibit a clear relationship with initial anisotropic geometry. Instead, $v_3$ and $v_3/v_2$ display similar transverse momentum dependencies in both collisions types, suggesting a comparable behavior of high-transverse-momentum particles in search of a potential universal baseline. Additionally, triangular flow's centrality dependence in 200 GeV Au$+$Au collisions demonstrates an intriguing discrepancy that may be attributed to differences in charge-dependent potentials. Furthermore, our findings suggest that triangular flow could serve as an implicit detector for charge-dependent potential in heavy ion collisions. Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, enabling seamless machine readability and interconnectivity.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to data of poor quality, significantly affecting tasks such as data integration, search, and interlinking.  Existing quality assessment techniques for Linked Data, although limited, suffer from decreased effectiveness with rising data sizes and become unmanageable for single-machine operations.  To address these challenges, our proposed DistQualityAssessment is an open-source, cluster-enabled implementation designed for comprehensive quality evaluation of large-scale RDF datasets, leveraging the processing capabilities of Apache Spark to distribute quality metrics computation.  This innovative, distributed in-memory approach allows for flexible metric extension via a provided quality assessment pattern and, through seamless integration with the SANSA framework, has been successfully applied in at least three external use cases, showcasing its superiority over existing methodologies.  A comprehensive evaluation of our system, involving extensive benchmarking and real-world deployments, confirms its superiority over single-machine counterparts while highlighting potential for further optimization.  Alongside its software repository, DistQualityAssessment is now openly accessible via a user-friendly web interface at https://distqualityassessment.bigdata.eu/.  In conjunction with this release, we are excited to announce the creation of the QALD-5 evaluation dataset in conjunction with the 5th Challenge on Evaluating and Reconciling Knowledge Entries, taking place as part of the 13th Extended Semantic Web Conference.  This dataset, centered on Linked Data quality assessment, comprises twenty quality-related subtasks and may be downloaded from the OAEI 2016 evaluation campaign site. When working with data generated by random processes, an appropriate model is often employed for subsequent statistical analysis, but the standard method of maximum likelihood estimation is vulnerable to model imperfections and data contamination. As alternative methods without assumptions about a specific model typically lose efficiency, this paper introduces a robust procedure for estimating parameters in discrete data sets based on a well-known distance measure. Specifically, this method defines and evaluates minimum density power divergence estimators for independent increments and Markov processes, proving its consistency and providing distributional results in the context of dependent stochastic processes, ultimately showing the method's advantages in comparison to traditional maximum likelihood estimation for common processes like Poisson processes, Brownian motion with a drift and autoregressive models. The benefits of minimum density power divergence estimators are illustrated through simulations and real-world applications. The method is made accessible to users through a set of developed R functions as part of an associated project, where the functions are shown to be efficient and user-friendly through the conducted experiments. The paper also addresses potential concerns and challenges related to the method, but it is evident that minimum density power divergence estimators offer a viable alternative to maximum likelihood estimation, especially when dealing with real-world data sets that are highly non-stationary and contaminated with significant errors. The most notable feature of this method is its robust nature, which makes it particularly useful for parameter estimation in the analysis of dependent data sets in comparison to independent data sets. The associated project exhibits the method's effectiveness across various random processes, but there is a need for a systematic comparison with other robust methods on data sets that are completely non-parametric. The development of this method is part of a broader project that aims to provide tools and techniques for statistical analysis of random processes through functional data analysis methods, where further research is required to fully achieve this goal. The results presented in this paper are part of the project's initial achievements, but there is a lot more to be done to achieve its ultimate objectives. The associated project shows the method's potential as a starting point and potential results like the one obtained for Gaussian process estimations could be critical steps towards the broader project's goals. The method's potential as the starting point also raises questions about its applicability to other types of random processes. The findings from Gemini's GMOS-IFU data, acquired at a spatial resolution of 110-280 parsecs, reveal temperature variations between 8000 to >30000 Kelvin. We discovered temperature ranges in these galaxies are significantly influenced by gas outflows producing shocks, particularly in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348, while photoionization processes fit the results for Mrk 607. The orientation of these shocks in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348 appears to be perpendicular to the axis of ionization, suggesting the potential for shock ionization to be observed more easily when obscured by a dusty torus. This implies that narrow ionization cones can coexist with wider shock patterns. Consequently, this may facilitate the feeding of black holes, driving the high-brightness nuclear activity. This study's results also highlight the significance of ionization feedback in regulating gas flows, which could lead to further research into potential limitations on black hole growth due to this feedback. The creation of realistic traffic scenarios through automation is the primary focus.
Currently used approaches insert virtual characters into the environment using predefined rules but struggle to capture the intricate nature of actual traffic conditions, ultimately resulting in a gap between artificially generated scenes and real ones. As a consequence, these simulation tools lack the required level of accuracy necessary to train self-driving vehicles. To mitigate this limitation, we propose SceneGen, a traffic scenario model that utilizes neural networks to disregard predefined rules and guidelines, allowing for the creation of a diverse range of realistic scenes. SceneGen is particularly adept at producing complex scenarios that involve multiple characters and their interactions. Through multiple evaluation methods, including visual assessment and the testing of trained models on real-world data, we demonstrate SceneGen's capacity to create highly accurate and varied scenes. Ultimately, our results indicate that SceneGen is capable of bridging the gap between artificially generated scenes and real ones, ultimately holding significant potential to enhance the development of self-driving vehicles. These measures exhibit different behavior at high and low temperatures. We demonstrate that they correspond to periodic measures found by Kelley on a Cayley tree. Moreover, we establish the relationship between Kelley's measures and the group's index-2 normal subgroups, revealing their one-to-one correspondence. This relationship enables us to classify Kelley's measures solely based on the group structure. We also examine the cyclic extension of the Ising model and discuss how it relates to Kelley's measures. Additionally, we derive an exact expression for the free energy of the Ising model on a Cayley tree using the group representation. This expression reveals an integral representation that can be evaluated through the use of Kelley's measures. We propose that this integral representation may be applied to derive high-temperature series for the free energy of the Ising model on a Cayley tree. We provide an alternative derivation for some high-temperature series currently missing from the literature. We verify that this procedure yields the same free energy as the cyclic extension, which can be expressed as an integral of the free energy of the original Ising model multiplied by a sum of positive weights that depend on the cyclic shift. We also demonstrate that this expression for free energy encompasses all known high-temperature series for the cyclic Ising model. We propose that this method may be extended to additional spin models, such as the Potts model. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of monotonicity and boundedness, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small complex systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce bounds on numerical approximations, making it possible to utilize this iteration as a part of numerical integration of ODEs and ultimately PDEs. By combining high-order preservation-based spatial discretizations with the proposed iterative method, it is possible to achieve both high accuracy and robust boundedness. The benefits of this approach are demonstrated through numerous numerical examples applied to different types of PDEs, including those with discontinuous solutions, systems with different frequency components and stiff systems. The results show that the proposed iterative method provides a viable alternative to exact solvers, enabling larger systems to be integrated efficiently. Furthermore, it allows for the integration of systems with distinct time scales that would otherwise face significant challenges. The proposed method also facilitates a closer examination of high-order preservation schemes than has been previously possible, revealing its potential to unlock further enhancements in spatial accuracy. Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this - firstly, annotating distant objects can be difficult because lidar sensors typically only return a limited number of data points at such great distances, with almost 50% of objects more than 50m away from the sensor containing zero data points. Secondly, the commonly used metrics for evaluating three-dimensional detection tasks apply the same tolerance thresholds to near and far objects, which isn't aligned with either human vision or the disparities seen in stereo images. As a result, the task of far-field three-dimensional detection has not been given the attention it deserves. For instance, it has long been believed that high-resolution RGB sensors are key to detecting distant objects, but a more in-depth analysis shows that lidar-based approaches outperform RGB counterparts on the existing leaderboards. To better assess this task, we created a new evaluation protocol and a far-field validation dataset based on the well-annotated scenes from the nuScenes dataset. We compared a variety of three-dimensional detection methods with this protocol and the results verify the challenges it poses. We've found that both efficient multi-scale methods, such as FCN-ISR, and end-to-end approaches, such as PVRCNN, outperform the standard baseline by a significant margin on this dataset. However, when validated on the created dataset, these methods still only achieve an IoU threshold of around 5%, which indicates that detecting far-field objects remains an unresolved issue for the community. To tackle this, we propose an innovative approach based on an end-to-end connection network that processes raw point clouds, prioritizing distant objects over closer ones by introducing a non-linear distance weighting function. When tested against conventional multi-scale methods on the created dataset, our method shows a substantial improvement of around 24% in terms of IoU threshold at 5%. When compared to the best baseline on the full nuScenes validation set, our method only trails behind by around 3%, indicating that it is nearly on par with the state-of-the-art methods. Chemical reactions can be comprehensively understood through a primary analytical tool called the potential energy surface (PES) which analyzes reactions by identifying key molecular structures, mapping their energies, and detailing the reaction pathways. Nevertheless, this surface-analysis method is often hindered because of the complexity of molecular systems. A newly developed algorithm called HiRAMS quickly generates PES data by utilizing a restricted set of molecular structures and their energy readings. This algorithm works within a specific framework called the high-density mode transition reaction pathway (HiRAMS) and is specifically designed to identify the highest-energy pathways in molecules by comparing areas of high and low energy. To validate its performance, HiRAMS was tested on three different molecules—N$_2$O, CH$_3$OH, and CH$_3$CHNH—and showed that it could accurately predict reaction pathways and energy barriers without prior knowledge of the molecular structure. This implies that HiRAMS has the potential to be a groundbreaking method for generating reaction pathways in complex molecules that have not been fully characterized. Furthermore, it highlights the significance of investigating reaction pathways in big molecular systems composed of many atoms. By utilizing HiRAMS's high-density mode transition reaction pathway framework, there's a possibility of understanding intricate chemical reactions that involve the rotation of molecular structures and the breaking of chemical bonds. This could lead to a deeper comprehension of how certain functional groups within large molecules facilitate or hinder chemical reactions. In conclusion, HiRAMS's capability to predict accurate reaction pathways in complex molecules sets a high standard that future algorithms must match if they are to be useful in modeling big molecular systems effectively. This achievement also paves the way for investigating reaction pathways in big molecular systems that consist of many atoms and could potentially lead to a more in-depth understanding of chemical reactions in these types of molecules. This understanding is crucial for designing novel catalysts and improving the efficiency of chemical reactions. Lastly, HiRAMS's success highlights its potential as a potential tool for modeling big molecular systems composed of many atoms and could serve as a benchmark for future algorithms that aim to model such complex systems. This could lead to a deeper comprehension of how certain functional groups within large molecules facilitate or hinder chemical reactions, ultimately contributing to designing novel catalysts and enhancing the efficiency of chemical reactions. Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs during testing. The trained network provides an optimal displacement field to map preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface, demonstrated by multiple experiments showing its applicability and efficiency with real-world data. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, conventional methods fail to account for regions in the image that contain significant scene flow activity, given their primary focus on range rather than motion. This paper reinterprets scene flow estimation as a direct approach, focused on identifying points with substantial radial velocity. A novel algorithm, directly computing radial velocity, is introduced and demonstrated to be an essential component in conventional implicit scene flow representation. The implied radial velocity function is directly represented as a distance-based point cloud classification system, thereby circumventing the necessity for gradient computation. This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields. Additionally, we calculated the thermal entropy and free energy of spin-polarized strange quark matter. Our findings show that an increase in temperature leads to a rise in entropy and free energy. However, an enhanced magnetic field initially causes the entropy and free energy to decrease before eventually increasing at higher temperatures. This research paves the way for a comprehensive understanding of the interplay between spin polarization, magnetic field, and temperature in quark stars, allowing for implications for beaming radiation observed in transient quark stars. Moreover, our model could help explain the prolonged emissions from these stars, in addition to solving the mushy hadron-quark phase issue inherent in quark stars by introducing spin-polarized quark phases. Lastly, we developed a maximum mass limit for spin-polarized stars, which in the present model is approximately $2.041M_{\odot}$. The characteristics of spin-polarized stars can be distinguished from their normal quark star counterparts via specific oscillation frequencies, particularly in the high-frequency range. The unique characteristics of spin-polarized stars provide plausible explanations for several astrophysical phenomena, including giant magnetic fields, transient emissions, and binary millisecond radio pulsars. The discovery of such stars would have substantial theoretical and observational consequences. Nonetheless, the stability of spin-polarized stars relies on the spin polarization energy being outweighed by their magnetic energy, suggesting that only stars encased in extremely strong magnetic fields can maintain spin polarization. The influence of neutrinos on the equation of state is another significant factor that needs consideration in this context. The neutrino-driven bulk viscous dissipation process, present in quark stars, may counteract the magnetic field holding the spin-polarized phase together, potentially destabilizing the star. Nonetheless, this neutrino effect alone might not be sufficient to overcome the strong magnetic field holding the spin-polarized phase together, allowing the possibility of stable spin-polarized stars to exist. A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure. Finally, this research concludes by outlining potential applications and avenues for further exploration in the field of graph theory.

In contrast, our study leverages a unique dataset that includes situation descriptions and optimal actions, enabling the application of neural common sense to enhance the team's performance. Notably, our method is particularly effective in situations that are substantially different from the training data. Furthermore, human feedback can improve the performance even further. In doing so, we have developed a dataset that enables the study of optimal actions in soccer situations and is available for public access. High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations of the wave equation solver are feasible. Despite these developments, the challenge of the large storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations remains, and two possible workaround strategies for reducing this demand are proposed, including extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data rather than wavefields. Ultimately, both methods, WRI and ESI, lead to similar improvements in reflectivity images, and an example case verifies this finding.  The proposed strategies for wavefield storage reduction prove effective in the example case discussed. Lastly, it is demonstrated that both methods, WRI and ESI, are equivalent to weighted FWI when considering the classical FWI under the assumption of an infinite number of frequency-domain wavefield storage. 

This work is an extension of an earlier paper titled "On Full Waveform Inversion in the Frequency Domain" presented at the 80th EAGE Conference.

We have presented the results from the AstroSat analysis of the high-mass X-ray binary X-ray pulsar IGR J19294+1816 during its Type-I outburst in October 2019. Timing and spectral data from the decline phase of the outburst revealed the spin period to be 12.485 seconds, with significant spectral features. A Quasi Periodic Oscillation was observed at a frequency of 0.032 Hz and an RMS amplitude of 18%. Our joint spectral analysis detected Cyclotron Resonant Scattering and an Iron emission line at 42.7 keV and 6.4 keV respectively, further highlighting the complex nature of this intermediate spin pulsar's behavior during its 2019 outburst. Comparison with historical data from Swift and Rossi X-ray Satellite revealed that the 2019 outburst exhibited the longest known spin period, offering valuable insights into the pulsar's behavior and evolution. Moreover, the detection of significant spectral features and the Opaque Absorption in this intermediate spin pulsar's spectrum during its decline phase suggests that IGR J19294+1816's behavior might be influenced by its binary partner's gravitational field. Additionally, the significant variation in the pulsar's spin period during this outburst may indicate a change in the binary system's behavior at its Light Curve Maximum. The findings from this analysis provide a deeper understanding of IGR J19294+1816's complex behavior and its binary partner's influence, further highlighting the significance of this intermediate spin pulsar in the study of High Mass X-ray Binaries. The surge in telework needs has highlighted the potential benefits of fully
automating and controlling experiments remotely. This work presents the technical
advancements of creating a two-dimensional LDV measurement system using a single-
point LDV system via a remotely controllable and automated setup. The document's
aim is to expedite the development of similar setups for this kind of application,
which is highly versatile and can be applied to various scenarios including both
air-based acoustic signal-driven samples and mechanically induced samples. The
document outlines the design of the automated system, which comprises an externally
controlled vibration generator, a computer-run program in LabVIEW, and a LDV
system connected to a computer. It discusses in detail how the automated system
executes a controlled cross-sectional analysis of a running liquid sample using a
mechanically induced frequency of 20 Hz, which yields notable amplitude measurements
of 0.45 $\pm$ 0.05 cm. Furthermore, a theoretical model describing both the AC
vibration signal applied to the sample and the associated anti-node response peak
has been validated through experimental data. The developed system has diverse
applications in analyzing sample responses, encompassing acoustic signal-induced
peaks, mechanical stimulation-induced peaks, and potential uses in both two-
dimensional LDV measurements and beyond. The created system is now an integral
component of a novel acoustic-leveraging approach aimed at enhancing near-field
acoustical levitation. The document also outlines the theoretical model and the
associated discussions for this new approach, which includes the analysis of both
the system and the proposed method. The documentation of this project is now
available online to facilitate the development of similar LDV measurement systems

The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. In experiments, our findings suggest that certain evaluation tasks prove more manageable for certain sophisticated architectures to grasp than others and, interestingly, that RNN-based architectures outperform Transformer models in these evaluation tasks despite underperforming them in standard text generation metrics. This suggests that, although the models' generated text may appear superior, their underlying understanding of dialogue language may be flawed. Moreover, our analysis highlights potential weaknesses in these models, such as their inability to anticipate critical dialogue information and their tendency to confuse semantically distinct dialogue parts. This work aims to contribute to the advancement of more sophisticated models that can accurately encode dialogue language understandings by evaluating and comparing the performance of various encoder architectures in these evaluation tasks. This represents a crucial step towards developing models capable of anticipating and responding appropriately to unseen dialogue utterances. Deep learning methods for  LiDAR-based place recognition have gained significant interest recently, however, the majority of existing approaches have focused solely on local feature extraction using 3D point clouds. This research introduces a novel, LiDAR-based place recognition system that leverages a deep learning network to learn invariance to camera images and driving conditions. By combining the network with a pattern matching module, this system is able to accurately identify recurring 3D environments from LiDAR data even in dynamic scenes, resulting in a highly robust place recognition system. Extensive testing on the autonomous driving platform, Baidu's Apollo, showed that this system performed 13.9% better than previous methods according to the mean absolute error benchmark, and successfully located places correctly in 85.3% of instances after being trained on just 10% of the data. This suggests that this system's ability to generalize place information from visual data to LiDAR data is quite strong. Furthermore, the results demonstrated that the system's LiDAR-based place recognition performance correlates highly with the visual recognition method, indicating a level of semantic consistency between the two approaches. Additionally, analysis of the system's performance under varying levels of noise and occlusion showed that it is relatively robust, and that the primary source of error is typically associated with locations that have been visited only once. This implies that the system would benefit from techniques that focus on recurring locations initially, and could lead to further improvements through the integration of additional sensors, such as GPS, to help recognize places more accurately. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech incorporates contextual acoustic features into each sentence, enabling a more detailed understanding of semantic relationships. Additionally, cross-sentence coarse-grained semantic features aid in the development of a natural prosody. Through augmenting masked acoustic features with contextual elements during training, MaskedSpeech outperformed baseline systems in expressiveness and naturalness. Evaluations revealed substantial improvements in perceived naturalness and the degree of human liking. Further analysis of speech intensity and pitch further confirmed the system's successes. Regularly, context-aware designs face challenges related to increased dimensions of cross-sentence features. This issue was addressed in MaskedSpeech by regularly decreasing the masking strategy's acoustic feature extraction dimension during training, leading to improved stability and performance. Comparative metrics highlighted the superiority of MaskedSpeech over baseline systems, the exception being a fully parallel system that surpassed it marginally in naturalness. However, this exceptional system came at a significant computational cost due to the enormous context vector size. Overall, the proposed masking strategy and the suggested acoustic feature augmentation technique resulted in the best overall performance. The context-aware design, along with the suggested masking strategy and feature extraction dimensions adjusted during training, facilitated seamless application across multiple domains. We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes a Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state. Additionally, we establish the conditions under which the spectrum possesses the required stability properties. For a specific model, we demonstrate both numerically and analytically the effects of varying parameters on the spectrum, thereby gaining insight into the stability of corresponding solitary waves. Furthermore, we bridge the gap between locally and globally stable solitary waves through a perturbation approach. We conclude by examining the implications of our spectral stability framework on the stability of solitary waves in another model. This work stems from previous research conducted by Berman and Segal in 1993. Berman and Segal's results were limited to an specific model and did not encompass a broader category of scenarios. Our study not only subsumes their findings but also expands upon them by addressing a more extensive spectrum. Moreover, our analysis facilitates a deeper comprehension of the relationships between various waves and their stabilities. Ultimately, our discoveries are expected to inspire further research within this field of mathematical physics. Q-ball studies in a single symmetry theory are common, yet the field can be more expansive, allowing for the examination of theories featuring multiple symmetries in a more general context. In this paper, we explore this broader scenario, analyzing both the standard and advanced limits within this theoretical framework and identifying essential conditions for Q-ball stability. Our findings reveal that, in order for Q-ball stability to be achieved, the difference between the lightest Q-ball charge and the global symmetry charge must be greater than the number of generated solitons. Additionally, we identify core and scalar Q-ball configurations, with core Q-balls representing a previously unexamined solution with potential stability, given specific conditions are met. Our research also establishes an established lower limit for the lightest Q-ball mass, effectively serving as a mass minimum for theories featuring multiple symmetries. A distinct relationship between the global symmetry charge and lightest Q-ball charge was another significant discovery made in this study. This relationship, applicable to both fundamental and composite Q-ball scenarios, could have implications for understanding the nature of Q-balls. Lastly, our exploration of this expanded theoretical framework also reveals potential avenues for investigating both supersymmetric theories and high-energy physics scenarios. By doing so, this research opens up new directions for investigating Q-ball phenomena within multi-symmetry theories.

Notably, in cases where K/Q is a Galois extension with a Galois group isomorphic to A4, S4 or A5, we determine essential and sufficient criteria for the ring of integers in K to be freely generated over its associated order within the rational group algebra constructed from the Galois group G. Our analysis covers base fields with any characteristic not equal to two. For characteristics two and zero, we employ a mix of local and global techniques to reach our results, while in characteristic one, we employ a purely local approach. Additionally, we establish the freeness or non-freeness of specific additive Galois modules generated by Q(xyz)(sqrt(-3)), Q(xyz)(sqrt(15)), and Q(xyz)(sqrt(5)). Our findings may be applied to examine the arithmetic properties of certain construction variables in random number generators. Leveraging our methods, we also identify new fields that fall within the scope of Cohen-Lemmerman's classification. the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of
semantic change in English vocabulary over the course of 5 decades. Our
results show that contextualized methods may inaccurately predict significant
change in words with little to no actual semantic evolution, or whose
status remains unclear. These difficult cases are scrutinized, along with
suggested categorizations, and further analysis of reasons for the spurious
change predictions is conducted. Moreover, our results reveal that around 14%
of the tested vocabulary still faces uncertainty in its diachronic evolution. 

This research is significant because it highlights the challenges faced by
contextualized methods in distinguishing between words with significant,
no semantic change, or uncertain evolution. It also introduces an ensemble
method that outperforms earlier contextualized approaches and provides multiple
perspectives on difficult cases, thus offering implications for enhancing the
precision of diachronic semantic analysis.

studied words and presents previously unexamined close readings of words like
anti, each, new, only, pure, same, similar, small, strange, true, and very.

is part of a larger effort to advance the analysis of diachronic semantic
shifts. The studied words demonstrate varied patterns of evolution, with some
undergoing significant change, some experiencing little to no change, and some
with uncertain status.

This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear model that links radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the minimum required radio luminosity was calculated for each AGN, and then radio luminosity was modeled as a function of the other variables. Of note is that a minimum required radio luminosity exists below which AGNs cease to function, likely due to radio-loud phase transition occurring at a specific spin rate. A threshold exists at a certain mass, above which radio-loud phase transitions no longer occur. between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging

the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to accurately map the migration
patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop a detailed
framework that explains how symmetric and asymmetric nucleus movements contribute to the formation of distinct
retinal regions. Our results demonstrate that localized variations in the rates of synchronous and asynchronous
nuclear movements can lead to substantial retinal expansion, facilitating the substantial increase in retinal cell
production seen during early development. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the increased expression of genes
involved in cell cycle regulation could be responsible for the enhanced retinal growth observed during this period.

neural tissues. Consequently, this research offers a comprehensive framework that can be utilized to investigate the
underlying mechanisms governing the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM and may offer insights into neural tissue
patterning and the underlying causes of neuroepithelial disruptions associated with specific neurological disorders.

Real-world code patterns, which are often non-negative, systematically structured and non-Gaussian, can impede reconstruction performance due to their non-ideal coherence properties. This research addresses this challenge by developing optimized code patterns that minimize the coherence of the sensing matrix and signal representation matrix combination, taking into consideration their inherent structural properties, specifically non-negativity, block-diagonal structure, and circular shifting, which are particularly beneficial for certain compressed sensing architectures, facilitating accurate and seamless reconstruction of compressed images. This code pattern design approach can be applied to both still and moving images, making it suitable for various compressed sensing and demosaicing scenarios. Experimental evaluations validate the proposed code pattern framework, showcasing notable enhancements in reconstruction accuracy and adaptability to diverse compressed sensing and demosaicing scenarios. Moreover, the method is found to outperform alternative code pattern design methods in terms of PSNR values. We've developed a comprehensive hydrodynamic theory that applies to polar active fluids in the presence of randomly distributed inclusions, and our model demonstrates the possibility of overcoming these obstructions to maintain a non-zero overall speed. Contrary to previous assumptions, the dynamics of this specific class of active matter cannot be accurately captured using simplified hydrodynamic models when the spatial environment is two-dimensional up to five-dimensional space; however, we were able to derive precise, dimension-dependent scaling parameters for these dimensions. Our model predicts that, regardless of dimension, the polar active fluid's ability to move freely is obstructed to the square root of its overall speed. Additionally, we found that this speed is influenced by an inherent time constant and the polar particles' interaction dynamics. Our research demonstrates that even small changes to these interactions can significantly impact the polar active fluid's motion and, ultimately, its ability to navigate through the surroundings. We also established that, in the absence of inclusions, our model relates to established theories of polar active fluids. Our findings have important implications for the study of active matter and could be verified through experimental and simulation techniques. Notably, our model predicts that, below a certain temperature threshold, the polar active fluid's motion will switch from its present, freed-by-blockages phenotype to a stuck state as the temperature drops further. This phenomenon originates from the polar particles' competition for directionality due to their local spin's inability to turn quickly enough in low-temperature conditions. This research advances the understanding of active matter by identifying various phase states and predicting unique phenomenological behaviors resulting from the interplay between activity, symmetry, and spatial environment. These findings also pave the way for analyzing a broader range of active matter systems using coarsened hydrodynamics. Our findings emphasize the importance of implementing secure email protocols to prevent the spread of malware and suggest potential avenues for collaborating with institutions to enhance email security. electron interaction fragments a continuous Fermi surface into disjoint regions.

segments, and demonstrate that it is close to a van Hove singularity, 
reaching it by adjusting a material parameter affecting its dispersion. 
We assert that, in the broader family of cuprate materials, 
the onset of pseudogap is attainable solely through inducing this exceptional

transition distinguished by heightened heat capacity and a nematic susceptibility, 
both consistent with empirical observations. 
Furthermore, we propose that the exceptional van Hove singularity 
may be indirectly created in hole-doped cuprates by suppressing a 
different van Hove singularity at the anti-Mott point,

This paper details a specialized apparatus built for use in Aberdeen Tunnel's laboratory in Hong Kong. The laboratory is uniquely situated to study spallation neutrons produced by cosmic-ray muons with 611 meters of water equivalent in depth. The apparatus consists of six layers of horizontal plastic-scintillator detectors that pinpoint the direction and location of incoming muons. Between these layers, a neutron sensor filled with heavy water and a scintillator containing gadolinium are placed to detect the thermalized spallation neutrons. Once cosmic-ray muons are identified, the neutron sensor's readout is delayed by nearly two seconds to coincide with the expected arrival time of the muon's thermalized neutrons. Simulations indicate this apparatus can detect up to 50 times more spallation neutrons containing polonium-210 than previously measured methods. Initial data analysis shows the apparatus's ability to obtain accurate rates of spallation neutron counts for several months without calibration. Furthermore, early results indicate the contamination of $^{210}$Po in spallation neutrons can be as high as 41% ($\pm$11%), significantly exceeding previously estimated levels. In addition, the contamination of $^{210}$Po in spallation neutrons contains a notable lead-time component, suggesting the possibility of lead contamination being a source of polonium contamination. In order to minimize contamination from external $^{210}$Po, it is recommended that future research utilize an on-site uranium source with a high specific activity in the experiment design. In addition, the apparatus can monitor the contamination of polonium in both water and air samples when accompanied by appropriate measurement protocols. The apparatus described in this paper can be modified to enhance its capabilities and is poised to contribute to various multidisciplinary research projects. The implementation of this system has significant potential to inspire educational and industrial partnerships that can advance its scientific reach and technological potential. The apparatus is currently operational at the Aberdeen Tunnel's laboratory; however, its optimal performance relies on continuous maintenance to counteract the effects of deteriorating detector efficiency with time. Nevertheless, the apparatus's fundamental design allows it to be adapted for use in any deep underground laboratory setting with accessible muon beams. The innovative approach outlined in this paper may spark the development of novel ideas for the detection of rare nuclear processes. The knowledge gained from designing and building this apparatus can be applied to various other projects that require the extension of existing infrastructure and the integration of custom-built scientific instruments. The experience gained from building this apparatus has highlighted the importance of maintaining open communication between physicists, engineers

Ground-based observations of planetary movements are crucial in validating the findings of space-based missions like Kepler and TESS. Although these missions show that planets are widespread, the success of these missions relies heavily on the use of transit photometry and ground-based radial velocity surveys to determine the physical properties of these celestial bodies. The TESS telescope is capable of identifying planets around bright nearby stars, which are ideal candidates for follow-up observations. We propose the TESS-Keck Survey to investigate various properties of these exoplanets. Utilizing 100 nights on the Keck/HIRES, the survey's primary objectives include analyzing how planetary compositions are linked to the characteristics of their host stars, understanding the diversity of planetary system architectures based on the planets' dynamical configurations, and pinpointing suitable targets for study with the JWST. We introduce a fully automated algorithm for selecting targets, which identified 103 planets across 86 planetary systems in the final TKS dataset. The stars hosting these planets are generally inactive, solar-like, and in the main sequence stage, with temperatures ranging from 4500 K to 6000 K and diverse metallicities. The TKS dataset comprises 71 small planets with radii smaller than four times that of Earth, as well as systems featuring multiple transiting candidates, short orbital periods, and planets situated near or within their host stars' habitable zones. The target selection strategy described can be adapted to facilitate the comparison of observational data with theoretical models of planetary population, and is openly available at https://github.com/ashleychontos/sort-a-survey, suitable for any survey that requires striking a balance between diverse scientific goals within a given telescope allocation. The initial TKS analysis reveals several significant discoveries, including three small, rocky worlds with large cavities around their hosts in the TESS Sectors 1 and 4, suitable targets for the JWST, additional members in the TESS-Rest four-planet systems, and several members of the recently identified planetary systems such as TOI-0505 b, TOI-0532 b, and HD 221830 ab. The study highlights the significance of ground-based observations in validating the findings of space-based missions like TESS, and is set to contribute significantly to the ongoing efforts to characterize the thousands of exoplanets discovered to date. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations. The ground state was determined by the imaginary time propagation of a given initial state and assessed through its overlap with expected values derived from the coherent state. The accuracy of this method was validated by comparing its results to those of a first-principles operator-evaluation method for multiple scenarios. The quantum harmonic oscillator provides a useful theoretical framework that helps understand the behavior of more complex quantum systems in various states. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts rotation rates in small asteroids by exerting torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation axis of these asteroids gradually precesses. Unfortunately, optical observations are not sufficient to fully understand the YORP effect on asteroiuds with extremely slow rotations or those located near the Sun. A study involving radio astronomical measurements of rotational periods was conducted and it was discovered that the YORP effect led to an increase in rotation speed in the asteroid 2015 HC116. Not only did this asteroid's rotation acceleration match theoretical YORP predictions, but it was also confirmed that the YORP effect dominated over gas torque under close approaches to the Sun. As a result, 2015 HC116's rotation acceleration and overall status were re-evaluated, revealing that its rotation acceleration was sufficient to explain the recent abrupt slowdown detected in optical data. Furthermore, it was found that this slowdown could be attributed to the effects of close approaches to the Sun rather than any sudden changes in asteroid shape. Additionally, a prediction was made that 2015 HC116 will eventually spin out of control and break apart, with this potential event set to occur in the year 2044. A closer analysis of this asteroid's rotation and its near-Sun environment also led to the development of radio-frequency multi-band strategies that could be employed to monitor the YORP effect on other asteroids. In doing so, it is possible to anticipate potential disruptions caused by close approaches to the Sun up to 12 months in advance. Although the YORP effect on 2015 HC116 was found to be consistent with theoretical predictions, this discovery also highlights the need to re-assess previous YORP studies in order to better understand how solar radiation impacts asteroid rotations. In turn, improved radio-frequency multi-band observations will play a crucial role in further investigating the YORP effect and its impact on the rotation of near-Earth asteroids. In the context of this research, detailed radio-frequency observations were conducted on three additional asteroids: 2003 HS16, 2016 GH53, and 2019 AM10. Although no significant YORP effect was detected on these asteroids, their data did provide valuable insights into their rotational characteristics and shapes as well as minor alterations to their orbits. In addition, a brief analysis was conducted of potential YORP-related slowdowns observed in optical data for the asteroids

The youth are increasingly relying on Instagram as a source of information, with political figures leveraging the platform to disseminate opinions and agendas. We examined online discussions on Instagram in relation to politics from a network perspective, focusing on communities of co-commenters. Our analysis revealed salient co-interactions - instances of user engagement occurring more frequently than chance would suggest - to be crucial in driving online discussions and information dissemination. We based our study on 10 weeks of data surrounding key elections in Brazil and Italy, observing users who commented on posts from politicians and celebrities. We found communities centered on politics to be more active in discussions, with members producing longer comments containing more emojis, hashtags, and negative language compared to communities focusing on other topics. Additionally, we observed a diverse range of topics over time, with some topics receiving fleeting attention while others centered on fundamental issues continued to be actively discussed. Communities involved in politics displayed dynamic characteristics, with some users consistently contributing to discussions and retaining their status as top commenters. Our research offers an Instagram-based model applicable to analyzing online discussions on other platforms, with a special focus on activating latent topics that capture short-term trends and long-term underlying themes. By combining topic modeling and community detection, we revealed distinct topics, co they could be used to inform content distribution across existing social media groups, ensuring relevance and encouraging engagement from users who already share common interests. This approach has the potential to enhance user experience, promote meaningful discussions, and reduce the spread of misinformation. We made our implementation publicly available to facilitate the analysis of online discussions on Instagram, offering a flexible framework that can be adapted for analyzing conversations on other platforms. By utilizing this system, we identified prominent topics rising in importance over time, co they could be used to trigger discussion on underlying issues that require attention. Our study demonstrated the value of focusing on co-interactions as primary building blocks for analyzing online discussions, with potential to give insight into the underlying social dynamics driving online communities. By activating latent topics from these interactions, we can capture both fleeting trends and fundamental themes. We believed this approach to be particularly relevant to Instagram, given its temporal-based commenting system, large user base, and extensive content library. Nevertheless, we acknowledged that succeeding in activating these issues would also require significant resources and existing awareness of the underlying problems in question.
