Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the application of such methods.  This paper explores a new direction in research, where a single label can be utilized to generate multiple conditions simultaneously.  First, an approach was tested that uses an additional network to recombine the generated conditions;  however, this method was found to be impractical due to the difficulty in optimizing the weights.  Instead, the paper investigates the possibility of training generative adversarial networks that operate directly on the multi-condition aspect.  Various experiments were conducted using multiple conditions, demonstrated the ability of the network to generate multiple conditions from a single label.  Further research is still needed to overcome the challenges associated with conditional GANs operating directly on multi-condition aspects.  An annotation-efficient framework for generative models is proposed, where a single label can control multiple conditions, streamlining the annotation process.  This approach simplifies the annotation process by generating additional conditions without the need for extra labels, effectively prioritizing the most important conditions and making the most of the annotation effort.  Several experiments were conducted to evaluate the proposed approach, comparing it to a method that uses an additional network to generate multiple conditions;  however, this method was found to be impractical due to the difficulty in optimizing the weights.  The proposed approach was also found to generate more accurate results but was challenged by the difficulty of optimizing the weights for different conditions.  The paper also explores the application of this approach to two tasks:  cross-domain data generation and the production of multiple views from a single image.  While promising results were obtained for the latter, the former was found to be more challenging to achieve.  The source code and annotations used in this research are available online for review and replication.  This research offers a starting point for the development of annotation-efficient generative models, addressing an significant issue impeding the broader adoption of conditional GANs.  This approach has the potential to unlock more extensive use of conditional GANs, making them more practical for a wider range of applications.  This new direction in research is expected to give rise to multiple new research paths, fueling significant progress in the field of generative models.  Several potential research avenues were identified, offering the potential to resolve challenges and give rise to new capabilities, thus paving the way for numerous potential future directions. This study investigates the property of energy dissipation associated with the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation, introducing an upper bound that decreases over time, aligns with the original energy at time zero and as time approaches infinity. The upper bound can be perceived as a nonlocal-in-time modified energy, which includes both the original energy and a cumulative component stemming from the memory effect of the time-fractional derivative. Specifically, it demonstrates that the original energy actually declines as time passes in a localized area near the starting point. Although the theory mainly focuses on the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation, it can be applied to other time-fractional phase-field models like the Cahn-Hilliard equation.

In discrete time, first-lag BDF and second-lag BDF methods are analyzed for local and global stability in relation to the modified energy. It is found that the first-lag BDF method maintains the decay feature of the original energy and the linearised time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation. Moreover, the second-lag BDF method has the advantage of preserving global stability and the original energy can be used as an energy method for analyzing its linearised version.

Numerical illustrations are provided to verify the theoretical findings and compare the stability of first-lag BDF, second-lag BDF and Crank-Nicolson methods. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms. Specifically, it yields an abstract expression of the energy-momentum relationship as a kind of "Einstein relation". Moreover, our approach facilitates an abstract derivation of the Bogoliubov inequality, along with a computational cost estimate for approximating physical properties from abstract algebraic ones. Finally, this framework enables us to define a functor that maps physical systems to their associated C*-algebras of observables. This functor essentially encodes the physical properties of a system within its algebraic structure. Consequently, this leads to an abstract classification of physical systems based on the algebraic properties of their associated C*-algebras. This classification process amounts to identifying subgroups of automorphism groups that act on these algebras. Consequently, this results in physical systems being associated with crossed products of Abelian subalgebras, reflecting the structure of local symmetries within the system. This abstract classification approach to understanding physical systems based on their algebraic properties of their associated C*-algebras is known as "Algebraic Physics". However, its foundations have historically been introduced in an ad hoc manner. This research seeks to establish these foundations in a unified manner, aiming to provide a direct mathematical relationship between physical states and the abstract collections of physical observables within a C*-algebra. This relationship is captured through an abstract adjoint relationship, thereby providing a comprehensive foundation for Algebraic Physics. Consequently, this research offers an opportunity to directly address pressing issues affecting the development and application of these theories. The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would be insufficient to account for high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth.  In addition, we discovered that the model's shortcomings could be mitigated by incorporating the presence of relativistic electrons that bracket the radio galaxy category.  Finally, hadronic collisions between high and low energy particles could result in gamma-rays, but only if the particles collide within the narrowest of jets designated as "unidirectional".  In contrast, more broad jet patterns fail to account for gamma-rays due to inadequate absorption of low-energy photons, allowing the gamma-rays to emerge in the energy band.  In conclusion, the model's application to radio galaxies and Sgr A* could offer insights into the mechanisms governing high energy radiation phenomena.  In doing so, it highlights the significance of hadronic processes and supports future multi-wavelength observations aimed at understanding gamma-ray emissions from these sources.  In addition, it underscores the necessity of accounting for absorption from low-energy photons in order to accurately account for gamma-rays in the energy band.  Finally, it emphasizes the value of relational physics in predicting the outcomes of hadronic interactions that occur in high energy environments.  In doing so, it sets the stage for the application of this model to hadronic processes occurring within neutron star mergers that involve high energy particle collisions that give rise to high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth. By leveraging these methods, our approach can efficiently handle large portfolios and accurately compute moments of interest. We primarily focus on the long-only strategy and develop an adaptable method for this type of investment. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the limited expertise of some healthcare providers.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds without expert labeling.  Initially, a data augmentation technique is applied to improve the robustness of models despite having limited access to abnormal cases.  Later, a fusion approach is explored that combines multiple feature extractors and models to enhance performance in the presence of limited training data.  Experimental evaluations using two publicly available datasets show that model-based training yields superior results compared to direct training from unlabelled data.  Furthermore, techniques like frequency amplitude manipulation and ratio feature extraction lead to significant improvements when applied to data augmentation.  Across all experiments, models that utilize unlabelled data for training outperform those that do not, indicating that cardiac auscultation can be analyzed effectively without expert labeling.  At the optimal configuration, a deep neural network achieved a high F1 score of 0.81 on the larger dataset, representing a significant improvement over previous methods.  The findings provide a solid foundation for further research aimed at fully automating cardiac auscultation analysis.  The code for this study is available at https://github.com/ashishp90/Cardiac-Auscultation-Unsupervised.  The paper's data and experiments can be replicated based on the code provided.  New methods developed through this research have been successfully patented (AU 20211035, filed 21/04/2021).  The associated challenges necessitate continued exploration into cardiac auscultation analysis.  Potential extensions to this research could involve developing low-latency models that efficiently process cardiac auscultation sounds in real-time.  Furthermore, investigating the applicability of this analysis to diverse heart conditions and cross-dataset evaluations present interesting research directions.  The developed code can serve as a foundation for other point-of-care auscultation analysis applications, requiring the adaptation of models to account for factors like varying recording devices and environmental conditions.  Ultimately, achieving a fully automated, high-performance cardiac auscultation analysis will have a significant impact on heart condition diagnosis.  The study's advances in deep neural networks and data augmentation techniques contribute significantly to this goal. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. The paper's findings and code contributions aim to spur substantial healthcare advancements via federated learning techniques. We tackle current, striking discrepancies in flavor anomalies observed within the $K$ and $B$ meson systems, specifically focusing on CP-violating Kaon decay and lepton-flavor universality violation in $B$ meson decays, with the introduction of heavy flavorful vector bosons at an energy scale of $\sim 1\,\mathrm{TeV}$. If these vector bosons are substantially heavier, around $\sim 1\,\mathrm{TeV}$ or above, a problem arises, as we then encounter difficulty in resolving the $\epsilon'/\epsilon$ anomaly consistently with the $K^0$-$\overline{K^0}$ mixing constraints. However, the proposed framework is compatible with the given data within the one-sigma confidence threshold for each anomaly, with the parameter space to be examined by experiments such as NA62 and KOTO and through direct searches at the Large Hadron Collider. The proposed vector bosons also leave observable signatures in $B$ decays, specifically in $B^+\to K^+K^-$ and $B^0\to K^0\overline{K^0}$ decay channels. Consequently, precise measurements of these channels have the potential to uncover the vector bosons' energy range, thereby shedding light on the underlying physics driving the flavor anomalies observed to date. The proposed framework also addresses the $J/\psi K^0$ resonance reported by the LHCb collaboration, interpreting it as the manifestation of a different resonance, specifically $\tau\nu J/\psi K^0$, observed in $\tau$ lepton decays with a mass estimated at $\sim 4.5\,\mathrm{GeV}$. The new vector bosons' energy range also influences the $B_s$ system; it offers the opportunity for us to predict the $B_s\to K^+K^-$ decay rate at zero momentum, which can be examined in depth by upcoming $B$ factories such as the Belle II detector. The proposed framework is further supported by the fact that the new vector bosons' introduction resolves the $R_{D}$ anomaly observed in $B$ decays, a result that is consistent with the given data within the one-sigma confidence threshold. Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand the scope of identification in a few-shot learning scenario. We enhance prototypical networks with a hierarchical loss function and a technique for aggregating prototypes according to the structure of a predetermined musical instrument taxonomy. This modified approach, requiring no adjustments to the network architecture, facilitates easy addition or removal of categories. Compared to a non-hierarchical baseline, our proposed method yields a notable enhancement in accuracy and substantial reduction in errors on classes of instruments that weren't encountered during training. This advancement is attributed to the ability to exploit shared knowledge between similar instruments, thereby minimizing over-reliance on distinct features. Resulting models with our proposed technique are substantially more effective in complex tasks requiring the identification of numerous instruments, as evident from results on the MISC dataset containing 677 classes and the Extended MISC dataset with 833 classes. Moreover, our approach allows a notable expansion of the number of classes that can be learned with a small dataset consisting of just five shots per class. System evaluators must not only assess model performance on each question but also evaluate the accuracy of the answers generated by the models, which is often difficult because the models' outputs are not accompanied by justification. Consequently, a new metric known as the best-performing model's accuracy becomes a crucial evaluation criterion. Interestingly, models perform better when evaluating the accuracy of answers that require reasoning about relationships between paragraphs rather than those that do not. Nonetheless, there is still significant room for improvement in models in this domain as their average accuracy of about 30% is remarkably low. Models that generate answers that require reasoning about relationships between paragraphs typically perform at a level of around 20% accuracy or less. Moreover, when evaluating the models' performance on each question rather than each answer, their performance increases to about 50% but still, there is considerable scope for improvement in this domain. Moreover, models tend to perform better when evaluating the accuracy of answers that have been proven true rather than those that have been disproven, which indicates that the models tend to reject false statements rather than accepting false information, which is demonstrated by the fact that models accept false information in about 1 out of 100 cases. Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By analyzing the PTA signal, the parameters of these binaries can be inferred. However, calculating the PTA signal across all relevant orbital periods proves computationally expensive. By comparing various methods to calculate the PTA signal, this study finds that employing an analytic approach yields the most efficient computation, allowing for a significant reduction in computational costs. The optimal implementation of this method is demonstrated to possess a linear relationship with the number of PTA probes considered, despite previous studies suggesting a quadratic relationship was likely. The most efficient method is further utilized in a statistical analysis to predict the minimum detectable binary mass as a function of its semi-major axis and eccentricity. The results of this analysis are presented in a form that can be utilized in future PTA experiments to estimate the detectability of such binaries based on their expected signal-to-noise ratio. The detection thresholds for a significant number of current and future PTA experiments are calculated and the findings are presented in the form of detection contours within parameter space defined by the binary's mass and orbital characteristics. It is found that future experiments will be capable of detecting a substantial number of such binaries with significant signal-to-noise ratios once sufficient data has been collected. The most demanding challenge for such detections will likely be mitigating noise through pulsar timing data processing. The most efficient method for computing PTA signals, based on highly elliptical supermassive black hole binary orbits, is publicly available under an open-source license as a part of the GWecc package for Python. The GWecc package can be utilized to calculate PTA signals, predict detectable binary locations, and produce plots for such detections. The package is readily downloadable from the PyPI repository and is compatible with the most current versions of PAUL and EPM pulsar timing data sets. The development of the GWecc package is hosted by the GitHub platform along with the accompanying paper, which is published in the Classical and Quantum Gravity journal. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. Many languages possess specific guidelines for abbreviating words, which often result in unique challenges for machine translation systems. For example, the inability to accurately abbreviate words with different prefixes in the same sentence leads to machine learning models producing subpar results. To enhance the capabilities of machine translation systems in the face of acronym-related difficulties, we propose a novel task known as Controlled Abbreviation Machine Translation. This task necessitates machines to translate text from one language to another while adhering to specific abbreviation rules governing the source text and adhering to target language abbreviations. We have introduced a new evaluation metric called Max-Span, which assesses machine translation systems' ability to grasp the extent of abbreviations within a sentence. To further complicate the task, we have incorporated a constraint that machine translation systems must follow the same prefix pattern as the original text. Our research is grounded in the context of the WikiAns dataset, which comprises paraphrased sentences with controlled abbreviations, to demonstrate that our approach can learn to anticipate and maintain the same prefix patterns across different languages, thereby outperforming the current state-of-the-art machine translation systems. Our findings have shown that our proposed method can effectively anticipate and maintain the same prefix patterns across different languages, ultimately resulting in a 10% absolute improvement in Max-Span score compared to state-of-the-art machine translation systems. Moreover, our approach has achieved a 5% absolute improvement in BLEU score on the WikiAns validation set, ultimately resulting in a 10% absolute improvement in Max-Span score. We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. In our study, we also investigate the impact of light-based association and initial magnetization when a precise condition is met. Furthermore, we explored two scenarios: one in which the dark state condition is met imperfectly, either generally known as the adiabatic case, or not at all. In the adiabatic case, we derived an inelastic non-rigid pendulum model, which enables discussion on magnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum" as well as the emergence of large amplitude oscillations in molecule-atom pair entanglements. In the non-adiabatic case, we obtained a more complex physics involving molecule-atom pair entanglements and leading to magnetic instability only at very high magnetization levels. Both scenarios occur when spin-exchange collisions are much slower than optical association, resulting in the dominance of pair states over molecule-molecule interactions. In contrast, when spin-exchange collisions are comparable to optical association times, we found evidence of multiple stable and unstable phases during both the adiabatic and non-adiabatic cases. In the adiabatic case, we found evidence of magnetic instability only at very high magnetization levels, whereas in the non-adiabatic case, we found evidence of magnetic instability at any magnetization level whenever the molecule-atom pair state frequency difference is smaller than the molecule-molecule pair frequency. In both cases, when spin-exchange collisions are comparable to optical association times, multiple stable and unstable phases arise, leading to complex atom-molecule pair state dynamics involving molecule-atom pair entanglements. In such situations, spin-exchange collisions result in the emergence of two frequency scales, significantly influencing the physics by shaping the atom-molecule pair state energy landscape. In this context, the usual three-body recombination equivalent description is insufficient, and a full-scale analysis is required to understand the complex atom-molecule pair dynamics arising from the interplay between one-body, two-body, and three-body interactions, prominent in this scenario. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects. This design represents a significant evolution in DNA data storage, addressing previous limitations and showcasing an architecture suitable for diverse storage applications. The developed system has been put into practice through the actual storage of downloadable web pages on a DNA substrate. The retrieved data demonstrated extreme sequence instability, with errors reaching up to 15.9%. This prompted us to carry out an in-depth error analysis, which led us to employ error-correcting codes and recovery data to enhance the system's reliability. Consequently, we were able to accurately recover nearly 99% of the stored data through resequencing the entire dataset. This breakthrough implies that, with the use of error-correcting codes and targeted design of indexing systems, DNA storage can support multiple writes. Moreover, the ability to locate specific data objects with minimal scope can result in as much as a 140x reduction in sequencing costs, thereby making DNA storage a viable option for massive data archives. The versatility of this DNA-storage architecture makes it suitable for various storage applications and lays the groundwork for us to investigate novel DNA-storage protocols that can operate with existing sequencing technologies. The open-source DNA-storage software we've developed is available online at https://github.com/Chenxiaozhong/DNAStorage. The sequence data used in this study have been deposited into the Sequence Read Archive under accession numbers SRP010574 and SRP010575. The DNA storage test data are available at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/0AC1tYw1w8h1zdGlrc

Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines. Lastly, it highlights potential applications arising from the unique properties of nodal lines, such as their sensitivity to external fields and inherent fermion doubling, which could enable precise Hall conductivity measurements. This framework is expected to facilitate a deeper comprehension of topological nodal lines and their implications for artificial and real materials. A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention guided network (MAG-Net) that uses MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model is trained on the Figshare dataset containing images of three tumor types, meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumors, and outperforms existing models through numerous trials while requiring the fewest parameters.  Experimental results show MAG-Net's high accuracy in classifying and segmenting brain tumors, demonstrating its potential as a reliable tool for tumor diagnosis and analysis.  Furthermore, MAG-Net focuses on radiologically distinct features associated with brain tumors and produced readable and practical segmentations for real-world applications. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, and geometric details from images. Moreover, this method enables the creation of generative models, such as neural textures, that can efficiently generate highly detailed images with realistic shadows, even with minimal training data, surpassing current state-of-the-art approaches according to various evaluation metrics. The proposed method and resulting models are available at https://github.com/daunson/pbr-diff-learn for downloading models and demo videos, as well as an interactive demo accessible at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H6i4g6tZ4uo. By providing a more accurate, faster, and free method for computing scene visibility, we hope this approach will provide a useful tool for researchers and developers working on image-based learning problems. System videos can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H6i4g6tZ4uo and model results at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6Q6s6Q6tZ4u.

A popular technique, widely used for enhancing video playback on television and recording, is interlacing. This technique doubles the perceived frame rate without boosting the bandwidth, yet generates undesirable effects like visual distortion and flicker during playback. Present methods fail to balance real-time processing with satisfactory quality. They either prioritize real-time processing over visual clarity or improve quality at the expense of processing speed. This research proposes a groundbreaking approach utilizing deep convolutional neural networks, capable of delivering both high-quality results and real-time performance. Diverging from traditional super-resolution models that assume pixel invariance, our approach incorporates spatial locking for dividing the image into distinct sections, processing each independently to minimize computational demands. This system runs on a single GPU, achieving real-time processing speeds through the use of a shared architecture. Comparative tests confirm that it outperforms existing methods in both accuracy and processing speed. Furthermore, our approach successfully mitigates interlacing-related visual distortions and delivers a seamless viewing experience. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. The model incorporating new direct measurements from an ADCP probe enhances its performance, and it is particularly effective in predicting flow velocities at deeper water depths. The developed methods demonstrate potential for enhancing flood risk management, particularly in data-poor rivers. Nevertheless, more research is needed to address limitations such as flow turbulence and incorporate multiple flow velocity measurement types. Ultimately, this work has the potential to contribute to the development of efficient and adaptive flow velocity prediction models, critical components of autonomous river monitoring systems. The associated code, data, and model files are available online for further investigation and application in this context. The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Open-World Softmax, this proposed method is called, outperforms state-of-the-art uncertainty modeling techniques in both synthetic and real-world scenarios. Additionally, EBOS achieves comparable performance to conventional, non-open-world methods, such as multi-task training and label noise, without requiring additional data or perturbations. The proposed approach can be used to enhance the calibration of machine learning models. The code for this paper is available at: https://github.com/strmlb/EBOS.git

Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. Consequently, this implies bulge growth is the primary driver of the mass-star formation rate relation's shape. Furthermore, this model suggests the mass-star formation rate relation's slope at the low mass end is shaped by the interplay between star formation in bulges and disks. Lastly, a description of the projected NUV$-r$ color map of local star-forming galaxies is provided, offering a tool that researchers can utilize when selecting sample sets based on specific NUV$-r$ colors across various stellar mass ranges. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. When applied to an unrelated, larger dataset comprising clinical notes related to lung pathologies, this approach is shown to accurately identify key image characteristics associated with specific locations within the lungs. Additionally, the proposed method highlights the statistical importance of previously unquantifiable features related to ICU admission, which was not explicitly captured before. Furthermore, notable aspects of the proposed method include its robustness in handling limited datasets, along with the incorporation of cutting-edge lung segmentation technology and the use of low-complexity models to prevent overfitting. Experimental results demonstrate the method's effectiveness in extracting important features from datasets with ICU admission labels and highlight the potential for applying this approach to other imaging modalities and diseases. This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor, built with a Field Programmable Gate Array. Although content-addressable memories have been successfully implemented on FPGAs, our design uniquely captures Caxton C. Foster's pioneering ideas on parallel processing, incorporating the concepts of simultaneous parallel writes and the merging of output values – features commonly omitted in typical CAM applications like network routing. The resulting system allows a host computer to interface with the CAPP over USB/UART using a simple serial communication protocol, which has been effectively demonstrated with a Python-based driver. The experiment showed that the CAPP can learn new contents without being reset, thus exhibiting the ability to blend the old and new information in a controlled manner. The achievable high search speeds, ranging from 100 MHz to over 200 MHz, serve as a key advantage of the CAPP. Furthermore, the integration of an external clock signal enables the CAPP to operate in synchronization with other system components. The system's flexibility and performance make it suitable for various machine learning tasks and could also serve as a building block for larger-scale content-addressable networks. We've conducted an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching. We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that mass asymmetry, resulting from absorbed and irregular matter, is accountable for their diminished star-formation activity by channeling it towards their core. Furthermore, three observed features - quiescent, lopsided disks, and massive cores - can be explained by considering both galaxy growth dynamics and the absorption of absorbed structure during the merging of major galaxy collisions. This leads to several galaxy-collision predictions, including increased far-IR radiation and a rise in black-hole mass following the merger. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that leverages static code analysis for weak supervision. Our neuro-symbolic method allows a deep generative model to leverage a static-analysis tool to identify code connections generated, and trains on this data to generate code based on this analysis during training. When tested on the task of creating full Java functions within existing classes, our results reveal our approach outperforms state-of-the-art models that use function code segments as input. Furthermore, we find that our approach produces more connected and efficient code, reducing unnecessary type casts and method calls. We have made our method and data available at https://github.com/alleghenyhealthnetwork/CodeConnect. We hope this initiative encourages the development of other generative code models that integrate static analysis for improved performance. We have also included an example of a new Java function generated using our approach in the supplement. The primary contribution of this work lies in demonstrating the potential for deep generative code models to produce connected code, and we believe this is a crucial aspect of advancing code generation beyond the current focus on individual code elements.

We examine the dispersion relations of relativistic fluid modes in various configurations, including pure viscositic modes in both 3D and 1D, and in situations where there are non-dispersive waves and coupled modes. Our primary goal is to determine how these modes behave under different approximations, such as when temperatures are high and thermal masses are significant, and whether they match expected linear or exponential behavior. Our findings will be verified by comparing them with existing studies and relativistic linear response theory. Moreover, we outline the parameters required for simulating a relativistic linear response model that incorporates dissipation and goes beyond the first-order gradient expansion. This model would allow researchers to investigate the properties of diverse systems, including those with time-dependent backgrounds and multiple fluid components, and could potentially be applied to problems like jet quenching and convection in fluids. As a preliminary step, we simulate a first-order model with a single fluid and demonstrate that it is consistent with our viscositic mode calculations. This model could also be used to drive fluids out of equilibrium and generate initial conditions for simulations that follow. Ultimately, this framework has the potential to be an essential tool for developing a theoretical understanding of relativistic fluid dynamics and its applications. As such, it should be considered a key component for any code that seeks to model the microscopic properties of relativistic fluids in diverse systems. As a result, this code could be employed to investigate a wide range of theoretical and experimental phenomena associated with relativistic fluids. As part of this project, we have developed an open-source code called 'KyotoCode', which takes the parameters of a given system and solves the full set of Boltzmann equations for the distribution functions. This code can then derive the relativistic linear response model, which includes dissipation and goes beyond the first-order gradient expansion. It can also simulate the full set of first-order relativistic linear response equations, as well as the Israel-Stewart model and other first-order models. This code can be used to calculate the thermodynamic fields, derive the equations of motion for fluid fields, solve the full set of first-order fluid dynamics equations, and generate initial conditions for simulations that follow. It can be applied to multiple fluid components and has a graphical user interface that allows users to select the parameters of a given system and visualize the results. It can be found at https://github.com/HirotadaNishimura/KyotoCode. It is also available on GitHub at https://github.com/HirotadaNishimura/Kyoto

Real-time anomaly detection in continuous data streams presents difficulties for conventional and advanced methods due to shifting concepts and ongoing learning requirements. Existing approaches, such as using hash functions or nearest neighbors with fixed memory, can struggle to accommodate frequent fluctuations, remove smooth outliers, and adapt to deep neural network architectures. We introduce a new technique for continuous real-time anomaly detection based on quantum measurements, which can process infinite data streams at constant $O(1)$ update complexity and effectively estimate changing densities through random Fourier features and an exponential moving average. This approach was thoroughly evaluated by comparing it to 12 prominent algorithms for real-time anomaly detection on 12 diverse data streams. The study involved experimenting with different cleanup frequencies, hidden layers in neural networks, and the drift rates of stationary data streams, resulting in consistent performance improvements of our algorithm in terms of precision and recall. The code is openly accessible on GitHub under the name QuantumAnomaly.

Hence, our analysis yields substantial insight into the $b\to s\tau\tau$ sector from $b\to s\ell\ell$ transitions, offering various predictions for low-dipole mass scenarios that could be verified or refuted with impending data from LHCb and future $B$ factories. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the stellar parameters using stellar oscillations and surface metallicity, and also analyzed the core and outer rotation rates using two independent methods. Both approaches yielded consistent results, indicating the star's core rotates approximately 40-50% faster than its outer layers. This discovery may indicate the presence of an angular momentum redistribution mechanism that operates within stars of intermediate mass, or it could suggest that the star in question has experienced some form of engagement with a massive companion that caused its core to spin rapidly. Further research is necessary to better understand the conditions under which stars with complex internal rotation patterns emerge. These findings also highlight the importance of discovering more low-energy giants similar to KIC 9267654 that exhibit significant internal rotation differences, which will provide us with a broader understanding of this phenomenon. Additionally, to solve the mystery of this star, we recommend constructing rotation profiles for a range of additional low-energy giants and examining possible combinations of core and outer layers that could result in stars with complex internal rotation patterns. This study is a part of a larger project known as the CoRoT and Kepler Surface Gravity Mode Global Oscillation Study (GOS). It aims to use global oscillations data from these satellites to gain insight into the internal rotation curves of low to intermediate mass stars that have evolved into giants. It also seeks to use this new information to test angular momentum conservation principles through direct observations of internal rotation rates within these stars. It is anticipated that this research will yield at least three well-studied low-energy giants with distinct internal rotation patterns that require further analysis. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and uses a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. Moreover, the ability of the system to process multi-domain, multi-category and selective visual information for efficient learning achieves notable performance improvements. The system's effectiveness in learning from only a limited number of labeled samples demonstrating a significant reduction of up to 11% in error rates compared to traditional batch learning methods. The code of the proposed system has been made available online at the address specified in the paper. This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and investigate the well-posedness of this transport equation within $H^{3}(S)$ for a limited period of time. Additionally, we find that introducing a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ also leads to the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time. This implies that non-local flow causes instability leading to the formation of shocks, consistent with the idea proposed by Helmholtz. This lower bound is influenced by the non-local flow's strength, represented by the term $|H|^{2}$, as well as the decay rate determined by $\Lambda^{\alpha}$, and is comparable to the upper bound derived through the method of characteristics. The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in pairs is minimized to less than 10-fold.
This robust approach to control exchange interaction strong or weak as desired opens up a vast parameter space for exchange interaction in silicon.

The research offers a wide range of exchange interaction patterns, including the capability to create robust, high-density arrays of exchange interaction in silicon, enabling numerous potential applications. 
This breakthrough also paves the way for the study of quantum valley Hall effect and valley exchange boson phases in silicon. 
Ultimately, this finding has the potential to enable the development of quantum technologies that rely on valley exchange interaction, independent of the need to control valley valley coupling.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the system, including its probabilistic inference capabilities and stable dynamic behavior. Furthermore, we established a novel generalization framework for extracting abstract system features from specific realizations. Through rigorous testing on the matrix product state class, our findings demonstrate that the extracted high-level descriptors can be utilized to predict an entire system type based on a single, randomly selected system parameter – a capability that would be exceptionally challenging, if not impossible, to achieve through traditional numerical methods. Our research offers a groundbreaking perspective on the capabilities of graph neural networks as tools for analytical understanding of complex systems and their underlying dynamics. It also paves the way for investigating other fundamental algorithms and exploring the scientific implications of this work. The speed at which massive spectroscopic surveys collect data directly corresponds to the number of optical fibers used in each observation. This paper assesses the effectiveness and efficiency of a method to coordinate astrobots in the SDSS-V by running numerous simulated and real-world tests. We demonstrate that our approach establishes a complete coordination framework based on the specific features and configurations of astrobots, their objectives, and operating parameters. To optimize the algorithm, a method involving cooperative artificial forces is used to create safe, coherent trajectories for the astrobots, leading to faster convergence and reduced oscillatory movements. The algorithm's performance is evaluated with random and catalog-based target distributions, proving its capability to handle any potential collisions during the coordination process. Once the initial conditions are met, the algorithm achieves full convergence. Implementing efficient target assignment strategies results in reduced convergence times and fewer oscillations, and in rare cases of incompleteness, adjusting astrobots' parameters resolves the issue. Ultimately, our method fulfills the requirements for high-speed observational operations and can handle the large numbers of targets anticipated in future surveys. Moreover, this algorithm will serve as the foundation for other coordination frameworks across the SDSS-V by addressing the same challenges and sharing the same performance metrics. Despite being tailored for the SDSS-V, our algorithm's fundamental principles can be applied to any similar large-scale survey systems.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size. Furthermore, the algorithm outperforms the existing benchmark in terms of computational time. Additionally, we apply the proposed method to a real-world dataset, gaining new insights into the New York City taxi dataset. The new algorithm is named NYC (French for new child), representing novelty and the potential for a fully developed future model. The implementation of the algorithm is available online. Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-700 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 kiloparsecs of our targets. Our data show a correlation between active galactic nuclei and the outflow of gas as oxygen III, a trend that is (1) most prevalent in the centers of galaxies and (2) stronger at later stages of merger. For example, during late stages of merger we measured an outflow 1.5 times as powerful as during early stages of merger. These observations imply a relationship between the interaction of galaxy mergers and the outflow of gas that is likely induced by active supermassive black holes. This outflow in turn may block or delay the gas that is in progress of being consumed to form new stars, a process we observed in our targets as a decrease in star formation as merger progresses. A potential side effect of this interaction is the enhancement of [OIII] outflow that contains abundant ions that are absorbed by cooler gas clouds, a process that contributes to the widening of the Tully-Fisher relation as well as the rise in the mass of bulge that occurs during major merger events. More extensive surveys with similar IFU observations are required to validate our early yet promising findings. Finally, our data also include broad hydrogen alpha lines as wide as 4530 kilometers per second, a feature that is likely the result of gas flows that are occurring at speeds greater than 211 kilometers per second. However, a majority of these lines contain unknown origins and several contain evidence of multiple gas flows within a single target galaxy merger. How these gas flows contribute to the formation of bulges, tails, and streams that result from merger events yet to be cleared remains a topic worthy of additional research. Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a camera installed on the vehicle
or mounted separately, suffer from limitations of field of view and real-time data
availability. Researchers have been exploring the potential of using machine learning to
identify weather conditions from images captured by a camera installed on the vehicle's
dashboard. However, existing datasets like CrossDiseaseShot and Real Weather Dataset
contain limited examples of rainy conditions. To address this gap, we present the
RFS Dataset, created from images that describe various weather conditions collected
while driving at city speeds. The dataset comprises over 100,000 labeled images
featuring three categories of weather conditions: light rain, heavy rain, and rain with
hail. The experimental application of a method called Correlation Alignment was
successfully used to improve the accuracy of a model trained on the dataset, with
results showing significant improvements of 11.43% in classification precision and
35.27% in mean average precision when compared to baseline models. The increased
performance was attributed to the better handling of data with similar labels, thus
highlighting the potential of the RFS Dataset to contribute positively to the field.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present paper outlines a simple single-column two-fluid model featuring ascending and descending fluid components with the exclusion of additional sub-filter variation modelling. Upon incorporation into a fully integrated atmospheric model, a multi-fluid scheme for long-wave radiation proved necessary for maintaining equilibrium. The model was then employed in testing the method's ability to replicate diurnal cycles of temperature and humidity with varying levels of success. Adjusting model parameters in response to this feedback proved beneficial; nevertheless, further significant improvements are required before it is capable of simulating the observed fluctuations accurately using a convection-driven relaxation procedure. Nevertheless, this preliminary research indicates that incorporating multi-fluid models could enhance our understanding of the interactions between atmospheric convection and radiation and ultimately facilitate better simulations of tropical convection. These findings also suggest that resolving sub-filter variations modelling requires a more sophisticated approach. The ability to simulate accurate diurnal cycles relies heavily on the choice of model parameters and the method used for determining them. The proposed model highlights several key features that could be integrated into more complex multi-fluid models of atmospheric convection. The challenge of developing a suitable multi-fluid model of atmospheric convection remains an open research question. The proposed approach to using this type of model also raises questions about the potential applications of this kind of model. The theoretical model described in this paper represents a starting point for exploring multi-fluid models of atmospheric convection. A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to significant consequences, such as cutting off field divergence and limiting energy growth. The Newman-Penrose formalism can be applied to investigate the behavior of charged black holes undergoing this polarization. The process leads to a change in the polarized electrodynamics field's geometry, specifically in the shadow radius, which provides insights into understanding thermodynamic phase transitions in black holes. Utilizing the Misner-Sharp formalism, we found that the evolution of shadow radius during this phase transition can indicate critical points. Additionally, shadow radius analysis offers a new approach to detecting phase transitions in black holes. The method involves monitoring shadow radius changes in a diagram plotting adiabatic mass gain against energy gain. The method's feasibility is demonstrated through a review of the electron-positron plasma environment found in black hole binaries. The method could potentially be used to explain the variability of black hole shadow images. The method is relevant to the upcoming Generation III telescopes, such as the Extremely Large Telescope, which will have a significant impact on the field. The new approach is expected to significantly contribute to the effective use of these telescopes in the study of black holes and their shadows. The method's effectiveness is showcased through an analysis of an electron-positron plasma environment observed in the GW170608 binary black hole merger, where the evolution of shadow radius is monitored over time. Furthermore, we establish that the model's transient state probability ratio converges to a non-trivial value, and this value converges to a fraction that normalizes the tree's size. Moreover, we establish that the model's coverage rate at its critical point undergoes a phase transition as well, resulting in a proportionate increase in the tree's size. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the probability distributions produced by a larger network. Traditionally, this approach relies on having access to the original network, but in real-world scenarios this is often not the case due to practical constraints such as distributed training setups or third-party license restrictions. This paper addresses this challenge by proposing a new framework that allows a knowledge-distilled model to be trained using only labeled data and the output from the original network, which is no longer required during training. We demonstrate this approach's viability by evaluating a compressed ResNet-50 model trained on the ImageNet dataset, achieving a top-1 error rate of 25.38% on the validation set. This represents a 0.26% reduction in error compared to a model trained using traditional distillation methods and allows for a significant increase in latency of up to 127x on mobile devices without sacrificing accuracy. The benefits of this approach can be applied beyond knowledge distillation, making it suitable for a range of other deep learning applications. Code is available at: https://github.com/kuangchiyan/DistillWithoutTeacher.

A strong geodetic subset of a graph~$G$ comprises a selection of vertices~$S$, which allows for the coverage of the remaining vertices in~$G$, by establishing unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$. The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, with at most~$k$ elements, which is strong geodetic. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for all graphs. In contrast, determining if a graph has a strong geodetic subset of size~1 is NP-complete in general, although it becomes tractable for specific types of graphs, such as complete graphs, stars, and series-parallel graphs. A graph~$G$ is strong geodetic if it contains a subset of vertices~$S$, which covers the remaining vertices in the graph, based on unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$. The ultimate goal of imitation learning is to develop efficient policies using nearly optimal expert examples. Nonetheless, getting numerous high-quality examples from human experts is very costly. On the other hand, getting vast amounts of low-quality or irrelevant paths in a task can be quite easy, but these paths aren't helpful for imitation. Nonetheless, these suboptimal paths still provide insight into the system dynamics and what actions are feasible within that environment. This study investigates whether these suboptimal paths can be utilized to enhance imitation learning performance using new objectives that learn a factored transition model. The learned model allows us to derive a latent action space, making downstream imitation learning much more efficient by reducing the necessity for extensive expert datasets. This is achieved by leveraging additional non-expert data. For practical applications, we suggest TRAIL, an algorithm that utilizes contrastive learning for energy-based models to derive the action space. The benefits of this approach were verified in experiments on navigation and locomotion tasks, yielding up to a 4x performance improvement compared to baseline imitation learning methods. The source code for this study is available at https://github.com-googlecloud/ml-pipelines-samples/tree/main/imitation-learning.

In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. Expert medical analysts, for instance, primarily utilize organ edges when performing manual segmentations. Influenced by these observations, this study proposes Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), an easily integrable module that complements standard encoder-decoder networks, capable of processing edge and texture information simultaneously. By prioritizing edge extraction and incorporating an auxiliary supervision, the EG-CNN module refines its output and merges it with original network predictions. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. Furthermore, we identified potential issues with the correctness of MongoDB's transactional protocols in its distributed deployment, specifically with lock acquisition and conflict resolution. Our findings suggest that MongoDB's transaction protocol may not provide strict serial isolation in its distributed deployment, and we demonstrate the implications of this on database consistency. Our analysis also highlights the potential risks of data inflation and lost updates in MongoDB's distributed deployment. To mitigate these risks, we propose a simple modification to MongoDB's transaction protocol. Our evaluation of this modification indicates that it has minimal performance impact. In our work, we have made our implementations and findings publicly available to facilitate further discussion and improvement of MongoDB's transactional protocols. Our approach can be applied to the analysis of other distributed storage systems. Our findings have significant implications for the use of MongoDB in high-concurrency applications that rely on data consistency, and require lock acquisition and conflict resolution to be reevaluated. Our proposed modification to MongoDB's transaction protocol provides a starting point for addressing these issues. Our analysis and proposed modification are not limited to MongoDB, and can be applied to other distributed storage systems that employ transactional protocols. Our approach focuses on the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transactional protocols, specifically with regard to strict serial isolation, and our findings have implications for the lock acquisition and conflict resolution techniques employed by these protocols. Our work has identified the need for a more thorough evaluation of the consistency guarantees provided by distributed storage systems, particularly those that claim to support transactional protocols. Our approach has an open-source license, and we invite experts in the field to collaborate with us and contribute their knowledge to enhance our analysis and findings. Using the elementary symmetric function basis, we re-express the chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck paths with a bounce number of three via a combinatorial interpretation related to the inverse of the Kostka matrix from Egecioglu-Remmel (1990). This analysis shows the positivity of specific coefficients and confirms $e$-positivity for an expanded class of these functions, beyond a particular instance explored in Cho-Huh (2019). Moreover, this study establishes a connection between the expanded functions and Schur functions, revealing that they can be expressed as a sum of Schur functions via the $M$-basis, in line with recent findings from Huh (2015) and Cho-Huh (2019). Further analysis extends the results of Huh (2015) and Cho-Huh (2019) by establishing the connection between the expanded functions and Dyck paths with increasing bounce numbers. Lastly, this study introduces and proves a combinatorial interpretation related to the Poset of Dyck paths with a bounce number of four, utilizing the results to confirm the $e$-positivity of associated functions.

The success of medical image analysis using machine learning largely relies on high-quality datasets.  However, when these datasets contain biases, the models can learn them, compromising their ability to generalize and produce reliable results.  While research exists on developing unbiased models, the problem lies in identifying and mitigating the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  In an effort to address this issue, we first establish a metric to quantify data intrinsic bias and propose a new framework for detecting biases in medical image datasets.  Our proposed framework, comprising of two primary components, specifically aims to identify and reduce the inherent biases found in medical image datasets.  Initially, a discriminator model is trained to recognize the differences between images and their corresponding labels.  Once trained, this model is used to assign a bias score to each image based on its ability to guess the label without accessing the actual label.  Images with the highest bias scores are considered representative of the inherent biases present in the dataset.  A data augmentation technique is subsequently employed to generate new images representing the inherent biases found in the dataset.  A resulting dataset comprised of both the original and generated images is created to evaluate the performance of models trained on this dataset.  Our proposed framework is applied to two specific medical image analysis tasks: cardiac phase analysis and detecting strokes in MRI images.  Our experimental results demonstrate the capability of our proposed framework to identify biases representative of specific classes and produce notable reductions in the biases of models trained on the resulting datasets.  A data quality metric was also introduced to evaluate the diversity of datasets before and after bias reduction, further highlighting the effectiveness of our proposed framework.  Our proposed framework is made publicly accessible through the following repository https://github.com/ivanovnikita/Medical-Bias-Framework.  In conclusion, our study presents an original framework for identifying and mitigating the inherent biases present in medical image datasets, paving the way for developing more reliable and generalizable machine learning models in medical image analysis.  Additionally, our framework is characterized by its simplicity, making it easily integrable into existing datasets.  While our study successfully demonstrated the capabilities of our framework on two specific medical image analysis tasks, it is versatile enough to be applied across a broad spectrum of medical image analysis scenarios.  In order to foster further advancements in this area, we are willing to share our framework with the community through an openly accessible repository.  Future research is anticipated to be enriched by our introduced framework, which is compliant with widely established benchmark standards, facilitating comparison and replication of results.
