Research on intricate systems from the human brain to social connections has uncovered a higher-level structure that can be characterized through aggregates of interconnected triangles. To uncover these concealed geometric patterns, researchers are using topological methods and advanced graph theory to study dynamic processes and the spatial distribution of resources among interlinked nodes. This study leverages a recently developed model for triangle-based network assembly, where the connection of two existing links generates a new link, and it simulates a sandpile-like dynamics to analyze the distribution of node degrees within the network as it ages. The results show that nodes at the edges of the network tend to accumulate more connections and experience more disturbances due to their position in the robust structure of interconnected triangles. The findings are further supported by numerical simulations and imply that older nodes tend to occupy positions of higher stress and are more prone to failure, which provides insights into understanding the functioning and potential vulnerabilities of complex networks characterized by intricate geometric patterns. Moreover, the degree distribution at which breakdown occurs can be anticipated by analyzing the network's assembly process and its underlying geometry. Lastly, older nodes with a greater degree tend to exhibit distinct behavioral characteristics in line with recent research findings. The proposed model and theoretical analysis pave the way for exploring more intricate geometric patterns in complex networks and revealing the hidden structures that govern and are interwoven with dynamic processes within these systems. The methodology employed here can be applied to any network in which the connection of two existing links generates a new link, such as laser-induced molecular structures or certain types of self-assembled polymeric aggregates, and it offers a novel framework for investigating degree-dependent dynamics and the coexistence of robust structures and vulnerable nodes in complex networks. The model developed in this study is available online for public use. The research introduced here is a preliminary step toward a new theory that aims to investigate complex networks with concealed geometric patterns, where the connections between nodes are influenced by the spatial relationships among the interconnected nodes, such as molecular structures, polymeric chains, or granular media, and the interplay between robust structures and vulnerable nodes holds the key to understanding the functioning and behavioral characteristics of these systems. The proposed model for assembling triangle-based networks and its dynamics provides significant new insights that could be applied to a broad spectrum of intricate systems characterized by intricate geometric patterns and offers a unique opportunity for further research and theoretical and numerical analysis. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but it indicates that any enhancements in solar wind energy flux are short-lived and cannot effectively propagate to the solar surface from greater distances. As a result, we propose that particle flux fluctuations observed at the inner edge of the solar system are likely driven by changes in the solar magnetic field that affect the behavior of particles across short distances of up to a few solar radii. Furthermore, we discovered that the relationship between energy flux and the potential temperature of solar protons is an example of a relationship that could be described by a quadratic function. Additionally, we observed that the conditions of solar wind varied significantly between the approaches, indicating that particle flux enhancements observed at the inner edge of the solar system are likely the result of local changes in the solar magnetic field that affect a small portion of the solar surface, often lasting only a few days. Lastly, we found that any solar wind energy flux that cannot effectively counteract gravity's pull and reach the solar surface instead gets redirected back into space. As a result of this study, we are now in a position to model the behavior of solar particle flux more accurately, which is essential for better protecting both people and spacecraft from the harmful effects of solar particle events. Moreover, this model can be utilized to analyze the limitations of current spacecraft designs in avoiding the full impact of solar particle events. Consequently, this study paves the way for enhancing the understanding of solar particle flux behavior and developing the capabilities to forecast and mitigate the consequences of solar particle events. Thanks to speech-emotion recognition technology, computers can engage with people on a more emotional level. Nonetheless, the accuracy of speech-emotion recognition in real-world situations remains an area of improvement. A major limitation of existing methods is their inability to adapt models to new domains seamlessly. In response, researchers have developed innovative domain adaptation techniques that transfer knowledge across domains, yielding significant improvements. While these advancements are promising, there is still room for growth in adapting models to real-time, live data scenarios. A deep reinforcement learning-based strategy is presented here to fine-tune a pre-trained model in a real-world setting, resulting in a 13% increase in accuracy. The experimental results demonstrate the new approach's effectiveness when compared to conventional domain adaptation methods, revealing a 11% difference. Furthermore, the proposed system excels in detecting various emotions in multiple domains, showcasing a 77% accuracy rate. The innovative solution mitigates the challenges of speech-emotion recognition in real-world scenarios, providing a reliable foundation for developing more sophisticated systems. Additionally, the system's capacity to function across multiple domains paves the way for numerous practical applications, including emotional analysis in public forums and human-computer interaction systems that adapt to an individual's emotions. Although the proposed system achieves a high level of accuracy in a limited set of scenarios, it may still struggle with recognizing emotions in scenarios with background noise or where the emotional intensity is not as the model was trained. Future iterations of the system could be further improved by incorporating more diverse data and techniques that prioritize interpreting the emotional intensity of each utterance. Our X-ray diffraction data does not exhibit a phase transition under pressure but lattice changes suggest a series of structural adaptations as the pressure increases.  Initially, BFTO displays a quasi-tetragonal symmetry but transforms into an orthorhombic structure beyond 8 GPa.  Our Raman spectroscopy analysis reveals local structure alterations at 5.5 GPa, contradicting crystallographic changes, and our Nuclear forward scattering measurements disclose the onset of magnetic order in BFTO above 5K under high pressure conditions, with enhanced magnetic order at 2K under 4.5GPa pressure.  Conversely, elevated pressure above 5.5GPa leads to magnetic order disappearance at all temperatures examined.  Furthermore, our dielectric constant measurements disclose a rise in dielectric constants up to 5.5GPa followed by a decrease at higher pressures and the emergence of an unexpected dielectric behavior above 5.5GPa, attributed to unique structural attributes of BFTO. Additionally, pressure-induced magnetic order in BFTO may offer a pathway to discovering other materials exhibiting induced magnetism as a result of applied pressure. Hybrid methods tackling continuous shortest path problems start by local optimization
of discrete shortest paths. The discrete version is defined on a grid of node points,
while the continuous version represents a domain without gaps. Depending on the
discrete method employed, local optimality in the continuous case may not guarantee
the fewest crossings. A new algorithm is presented to calculate discrete shortest paths
on a grid for flight planning, where the goal is to find the most efficient crossing
of terrain features while minimizing altitude changes and avoiding obstacles. The
discrete method is based on the Euclidean shortest path and accounts for graph
density. The continuous method uses the ray algorithm as a starting point and is
improved to handle dense graphs. Results show that the new methods outperform existing
approaches. The study also examines the impact of graph density and method on
efficiency and accuracy. Further research is needed to apply the methods to real-world
data and to improve handling of dense graphs. The algorithms are available online. 
Key words: Euclidean shortest path, graph density, hybrid optimization, planning
flights.

path planning, addressing complex terrain with altitudes. The method starts with a
local optimization technique on a grid of elevation points, developing two approaches.

general graph theory approach. Both discrete methods are combined with a continuous
optimization technique, the ray algorithm, to account for elevation contours.

Researchers studying strong shock waves in an expanding universe have found similar results using both approximate analytical and exact numerical methods to solve self-similar equations. When the adiabatic index lies between one and approximately 1.16, these solutions consistently occupy all space without gaps, showing close alignment with each other. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure drops to zero at a finite distance from the origin, and in both scenarios, a spherical void forms. All matter becomes concentrated in a thin layer behind the shock wave's front. This layer's structure, however, changes depending on the index, especially where the inner edge meets a sudden and infinite density at approximately 1.4 in both models, even though the pressure at this edge remains consistently zero. Any additional features forming in this process, such as subshocks or oscillations, are determined by how the index behaves at extremely small distances, considered negligible in the analyzed scenarios. Consequently, early theories assuming pressure maintains a direct proportionality with density and a second power of time, particularly for moderate indices, may be challenged only when analyzing very brief periods of time. Both models also produce similar equations governing the evolution of shock fronts in expanding universes, even when based on incorrect assumptions, leading to concerns about the validity of these assumptions in those instances. It's also found that high-density layers within shock waves can dissipate over millions of years. Therefore, recording the history of shock waves requires studying the large-scale structure of the universe. It's further suggested that analyzing the distribution of matter in the universe can lead to an understanding of its early history. It's finally proposed that analyzing shock waves can provide valuable insights into the fundamental laws of physics. Both analytical and numerical approaches to studying these shock waves have similar results, using both methods producing solutions that consistently show alignment with each other in all aspects considered. Any potential differences found through these two methods have no significant impact on the overall understanding of shock waves in an expanding universe. It's also found that regardless of the method chosen, any subshocks or oscillations that form behind the shock front wave have the same structure and behave in the same way. It's further noted that while both methods can model the same phenomena, they have distinct advantages and are better suited to different situations. It's also suggested that combining aspects of both methods could lead to better models of these shock waves. It's finally proposed that regardless of the method chosen, both models produce similar equations governing the evolution of shock fronts in expanding universes, even when based on different laws of physics

A persistent issue in signal processing has been resolved by our research, where we extract dynamic information from acoustic emissions resulting from adhesive tape peeling under steady force. Through phase space reconstruction, our findings reveal the deterministic chaotic nature of these dynamics by confirming the existence of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent at specific traction velocities. The outcomes demonstrate that deterministic chaos can be present across multiple scales, providing evidence that chaotic signals often considered random in nature actually arise from the interaction of multiple underlying processes. Furthermore, our research indicates that these processes' frequencies are separated by substantial gaps, leaving little room for the intermediate processes to manifest as distinct frequencies in the signal. As a result, our study challenges the common assumption that the interaction of multiple processes with vastly different frequencies is a prerequisite for chaotic behavior. Instead, we show that significant gaps in frequency are not necessary to produce chaotic signals, rendering this condition insufficient. Additionally, our research challenges the common assumption that chaotic behavior is characterized by the separation of frequencies over time, known as the Diophantine property. Our findings indicate that systems operating according to strange attractors can generate signals free of chaotic behavior. Consequently, our research suggests that the common distinction between chaotic and random signals is outdated and needs revision for a deeper understanding of the underlying dynamics. Ultimately, our study implies that higher-level processes with frequencies close to the system's edge frequency can give rise to chaotic behavior, providing a framework for revising current theories governing the analysis of chaotic signals. As such, our research is a significant step towards unlocking the mysteries of chaotic behavior in signals characterized by the absence of apparent periodic components. In epitaxial InAs/Al structures, our experimental analysis reveals the stochastic behavior of planar Josephson junctions and SQUIDs as temperature varies, exhibiting a crossover between macroscopic quantum tunneling and phase diffusion. The threshold temperature for this phase transition, T*, can be manipulated by adjusting a gate. The observed switching probability distributions are in line with minimal capacitance and moderate resistance, causing the switching current to be only a small portion of the critical current. Furthermore, synchronization between two JJs can cause a disparity in the switching current when comparing measurements of a single JJ versus that same JJ within a symmetric SQUID loop, where T* can be fine-tuned through applied magnetic flux. Additionally, initial data suggests that the threshold temperature T* might be connected to the macroscopic quantum state splitting energy by capacitance and resistance in these devices. A theoretical model, incorporating quantum fluctuations and capacitance-induced potentials, supports these findings and predicts that T* should be around 1 K for our devices, aligning with our empirical measurements. Nevertheless, there remains a discrepancy between the predicted and measured switching current values. A parallel investigation into the threshold temperature T* in magnetic flux-driven switching within the same device family has led to groundbreaking findings, including the discovery that the interplay between magnetic flux, capacitance, resistance, and quantum effects can result in the creation of multiple macroscopic quantum states that can be modulated by applied magnetic flux. This groundbreaking research paves the way for the development of highly sensitive magnetic field detectors capable of operating at relatively high temperatures. Moreover, this study opens up possibilities for the study of macroscopic quantum phenomena, including quantum tunneling, phase diffusion, and switching, and could facilitate the creation of precise current and magnetic field standards based on Josephson junction technology. Ultimately, resolving the remaining theoretical discrepancies will be crucial for fully realizing the potential of these devices. Still, even in their current state, they have already demonstrated switching current stability and capacitance-based threshold temperature control, paving the way for significant advancements. As such, further investigation is warranted to unlock the full potential of planar Josephson devices. The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed to understand the implications of introducing non-abelian aether-like terms that violate Lorentz symmetry, specifically within thermal quantum field theory. By incorporating temperature effects and spatial compactification via Thermofield Dynamics, corrections to the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law and non-abelian Casimir energy and pressure are calculated for both zero and finite temperatures. Additionally, thermofield dynamical behavior is used to obtain corrections to the non-abelian Casimir energy and pressure. By applying variational techniques, we develop a limiting model for a set of functionals subject to linear differential constraints. This framework models the energy of a heterogeneous material with a high-contrast composite structure at a microscopic scale, comprising a periodically perforated matrix filled with a dissimilar substance. Our key finding involves analyzing the $\Gamma$-convergence as the material periodicity diminishes, demonstrating that the limit functional comprises two components: the stored energy within the matrix, and the stored energy within the fillings. To overcome the coercivity issue inherent in variational methods, we employ different approaches, including establishing a direct continuous inclusion for the material operators. Ultimately, our results yield insights into the structural properties of materials with high-contrast inclusions. 

Keywords: Variational techniques, differential constraints, $\Gamma$-convergence, material science, high-contrast composites, periodic homogenization.

We undertook a statistical investigation into tidal features surrounding early-type galaxies of massive proportions, utilizing data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program. Our analysis revealed that roughly 28 percent of 2649 galaxies, selected due to their mass greater than $10^{11}M_{\odot}$ and within a redshift range of 0.05-0.15, exhibited distinct tidal features exceeding one percent flux fraction. Observations indicated an exponential decline in the number of galaxies as tidal features became more pronounced. Additionally, within our defined stellar mass scope, we observed tidal features increase in frequency by two-fold when shifting from $10^{11}M_{\odot}$ to $10^{12}M_{\odot}$. A thorough analysis including pair-counts to estimate the merging rate of massive early-type galaxies revealed that tidal features persist for a duration of approximately 3 billion years. This outcome was found to align with findings from prior studies. A substantial proportion, approximately 17 percent, of tidal features observed in our data set exhibited pairs of components. This outcome suggests that gravitational interactions play a significant role in the development of tidal features surrounding massive early-type galaxies. Consequently, viscous gravitational processes caused by these interactions lead to a lifetime of tidal features of roughly one galaxy collision timescale. Ultimately, our research implies that galaxy collisions play a crucial role in maintaining tidal features, ultimately fueling their persistence. A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities in a way that prioritizes current generations over future ones. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize intergenerational mobility, opportunity allocation should benefit both current and future generations. Additionally, we demonstrate that our model's benefits for the current generation come at no cost to the next, and the opposite is true for a different model of mobility. Finally, we discuss how our model applies to real-world scenarios and modifies assumptions to accommodate varying mobility patterns. The result is a clearer understanding of the relationship between education, mobility, and wealth distribution. The proposed model also provides theoretical support for intergenerational mobility-driven economic policies. The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation for significant progress in numerous sectors, including semiconductors, communications, biology, defense, and national security. However, accurately modeling these laser systems using CPA and NLO is a complex task due to their interconnected linear and nonlinear processes, and the high variability in available modeling frameworks. The absence of a unified software platform for CPA-NLO modeling restricts further development and potential implementation of these systems in data-driven approaches such as inverse design. We introduce a modular software model that encompasses various amplifier configurations and nonlinear techniques to provide time and frequency-resolved electromagnetic field data and essential physical properties, enabling characteristics of energy, fluence, and spectral distribution. To showcase its capabilities, we apply our software to the LCLS-II photo-injector laser, an example of a complex CPA-NLO system requiring high power and precise control. The generated models can be accessed through a visualization tool, enabling efficient discussion and collaboration among researchers and potential users. The software framework is openly available online.

A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system. Specifically, if the source phase is randomly altered to a limited degree, we discovered that the proposed attack can bypass the system's security, resulting in the entanglement-breaking channel without being detected by the users. Our findings suggest that randomizing the source phase to a limited degree may not be sufficient to safeguard phase-encoding QKD systems using weak coherent states. Furthermore, with only moderate growth in system cost, we propose a potential solution to mitigate this attack by significantly increasing the variation in the source phase. Our research provides valuable insights into optimizing the phase source in practical phase-encoded QKD implementations.

To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) must shift from traditional resource allocation methods. By integrating computation capabilities into Base Stations, we can optimize resource usage and efficiently manage resources near the edge of the network. Leveraging techniques such as time-series forecasting and control theory, we can develop methods for optimizing resource management and ensuring system performance guarantees. In this research, we utilize neural networks and LSTM models to evaluate and compare their effectiveness in predicting edge computing resource demands at Base Stations. By combining these predictions with optimal control theory, we can assess and optimize resource allocation across the network. Our results show that there is potential for significant energy savings (up to 50%) achieved through proactive resource allocation strategies. Furthermore, our findings indicate that LSTM-based models can provide more accurate predictions of resource demands compared to baseline methods. However, larger training datasets are required to realize this level of performance. Consequently, future research should focus on developing more flexible and efficient edge learning methods that can effectively utilize small-scale datasets. The potential for integrating other predictive models alongside neural networks in such networks is also worth exploring. The approaches considered in this research provide a foundation for advancing the design and operation of critical edge computing systems, with applications extending beyond MNs. These approaches could also be applied to other time-critical and resource-constrained systems that rely on proactive decision-making to optimize performance and ensure guarantees. Ultimately, this research paves the way for a broader investigation of machine learning methods in such systems and encourages the community to contribute to this field of study. A more recent model proposes the viscous ring-instability to account for ring structures in protoplanetary disks. It suggests that particles may reduce the disk's conductivity, inhibiting the growth of instability. Using GPU-based simulations of interacting gas and dust, this study investigates this model's validity. As the disk evolves, ring structures become unstable, breaking into smaller whirlpools, and subsequently forming stable dust formations. These structures provide ideal environments for the growth of planetary building blocks through gravitational collapse and the streaming instability. Observational data on exoplanets supports this process and creates favorable conditions for planetary system formation. The findings of this study demonstrate the viability of the viscous ring-instability model and provide a possible explanation for the existence of small, rocky planets in our galaxy. Moreover, this theory could pave the way for a deeper understanding of planetary system evolution and the multiple pathways to planetary formation. The study also highlights the importance of dust formations in protoplanetary disks, identifying potential targets for future investigation using observational data on exoplanets and forthcoming telescopes such as the ELT and TMT. In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices is maintained. DR-DSGD outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms, including EXTRA, PDSGD, and DR-FEDGD, across multiple datasets, networks sizes and settings. DR-DSGD also effectively handles shifts in data distribution, showing only a minor decrease in performance, of less than $5\%$, on real-world distribution shifts encountered in the CMU MindCloud dataset. DR-DSGD also achieves a notable reduction of up to $50$ percent in communication costs when dealing with large-scale datasets and network sizes. DR-DSGD is shown to be an efficient and reliable solution for robust deep learning tasks in real-world scenarios. The implementation of DR-DSGD is now available under an open-source license. We have examined the methods used to estimate pressure within the hard-disk model by conducting a thorough evaluation of various correlations and analyzing fluctuations for different system sizes. Our findings were consistent across distinct ensemble selections and demonstrated a clear connection with the combinatorial factors associated with pressure calculations. Based on our analysis, we propose a theoretical framework that explains why certain pressure estimators should exhibit sublinear relationships with the size of the system. Consequently, our discoveries yield valuable implications that can inform policymakers in their assessment of highly energetic configurations within self-interacting particle systems. Our study ultimately underscores the value of critically assessing pressure estimation techniques in such settings. Our results have also been verified through extensive computer simulations. We demonstrate that a particular class of pressure estimators can be categorized as minimally correlated and show how these estimators behave in high-energy configurations. Our theoretical framework can be applied to a broader class of interacting particle systems that have a similar harmonic potential relationship. We find that in these systems, the harmonic potential relationship can be altered by changing the interaction potential. We propose that this change effectively creates a new dimension in parameter space that can be independently adjusted. We find that in the hard-disk model, the dimension corresponding to the harmonic relationship can be directly modified by changing the density of the system. We demonstrate that at high densities, the hard-disk model can be accurately described by a model that has a harmonic potential relationship that is twice as steep. We demonstrate that this model can be solved analytically and that the resulting equation describes a potential liquid-vapor coexistence curve that has a critical point. We show that this model is equivalent to a well-known statistical physics model and that the corresponding universal class can be directly obtained from the hard-disk model by adjusting its harmonic relationship parameter. We demonstrate that in these systems, different components can have distinct coexistence curves and that these curves can map directly onto each other along specific critical lines. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Throughout its operation, Forsage has consistently adapted its structure to avoid detection by regulators, ultimately flourishing into a $700 million dollar blockchain-based pyramid scheme. Our research into Forsage is an important starting point for investigating other hidden transaction networks. The techniques we use to analyze Forsage can be applied to other complex financial systems, providing unique insights that might not be captured through traditional economic methods. We examine the methods used to model light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that represent atoms as localized oscillators. The conventional approach places these models in the velocity gauge, describing the electric field as a derivative of the vector potential. An alternative exists in the dipole gauge, where the electric field is directly correlated with the vector potential. To compare the gauges, we develop a finite-difference TB model corresponding to a tight-binding Maxwell gauge. The conversion between the velocity and dipole gauges is achieved through a simple transformation of parameters. The velocity-gauge model exhibits greater similarity to its classical counterpart, especially in terms of response to constant fields, with no notable differences found in quantum calculations. The dipole gauge, on the other hand, displays increased convergence with respect to mesh size and shows less field localisation, a phenomenon that can be attributed to the absence of fictitious mass in this gauge. The choice of gauge ultimately depends on the nature of the system being modeled - the velocity gauge is more appropriate for systems with high oscillator strength and intense field regimes, whereas the dipole gauge is preferred for delocalized states and smaller field strengths. The proposed finite-difference TB model corresponding to the Maxwell gauge can serve as a reference point for evaluating other models describing light-matter interactions. The findings related to the gauges are demonstrated through numerical examples involving hydrogen molecules and van der Waals molecules. In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems using the principle of minimization, serve as quantum codes to prevent information loss, and accurately describe phenomena exhibiting power-law behaviors. A key finding reveals that networks comprising a single type of tensor and possessing erasure correction capabilities can't simultaneously possess certain desirable traits - those that facilitate the efficient calculation of physical properties through a local process and those necessary for an accurate representation of power-law behaviors in data. This contradiction motivates the creation of network guidelines that utilize diverse types of tensors, allowing these networks to successfully capture the characteristics of power-law behaviors while adhering to the principle of efficient calculation. A concrete example of such a network has also been developed - one that closely resembles the holographic HaPPY pentagon code under the assumption that specific system parameters can be set to a particular small range. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this type of network can be used to model systems experiencing changes over time by introducing additional tensor types that account for changes in time, and that these networks can be transformed into approximate simulations using standard tensor network decompositions. As a result, we can apply established protocols to achieve quantum teleportation and corrective actions far more efficiently than previously possible. This breakthrough could play a crucial role in developing scalable quantum storage devices capable of retaining information for extended periods of time. Additionally, we uncover a previously unknown relationship that may find applications in various fields beyond quantum information theory. Lastly, we outline potential pathways for developing new quantum codes using the principles learned from these networks. These insights could lead the way in creating new, accountable quantum simulation models and developing quantum error correction systems with minimal interference. Ultimately, this research paves the way for a deeper understanding of quantum systems through realistic, accountable simulations, making it a crucial step towards developing reliable quantum technology. Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and

Multi-layer Perceptron frequently surpasses more advanced deep learning models

due caution is required as they perform differently across various process stages
and it's also advisable to establish results with strong baselines like simple
Multi-layer Perceptron. The underlying code and data are publicly accessible

Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical combinations of radiative electron beam flux spectra consisting of two electron beam models: a high-flux simulation with a high energy cutoff and a lower-flux simulation with a lower energy cutoff. This two-component approach effectively explains the Balmer line broadening, the optical color temperature, the Balmer jump strength, and the far-ultraviolet continuum in the peak phases of this flare. This finding is supported by high-resolution observations of this AD Leo flare and its implications for electron beam energy loss, energy distribution, and the energy flux of energy release during white-light flares. We study the behavior and evolution of Boolean networks with sparse connections that interact with themselves using Glauber dynamics, where the dynamics occurs simultaneously for all elements in the network. Equilibrium is evaluated by modifying and applying a method for systems that update in parallel. Similarly, dynamic behavior can be assessed using an advanced version of the method for systems that update at different times. Nonetheless, applying this technique to networks that interact with themselves is challenging because it causes the network to rely heavily on past events, making it difficult to model the network's behavior over extended periods of time. However, it has been proven possible to transform the network into an equivalent bipartite network with double the variables, allowing for analysis of systems that interact with themselves using traditional methods. This breakthrough enables a deeper examination of how systems behave during transitional and extended periods of time. Lastly, we investigate networks that interact with multiple components and are utilized in gene regulation systems by transforming these systems into equivalent bipartite networks that interact through pairs of elements. It is shown that these types of systems, where the flow of information is bidirectional, have the capacity to develop multiple equilibrium states that can vary in stability. Moreover, we propose a concept called the 'information half-life' that represents the time it takes for the network to forget older events and is influenced by the network's structure and its components. It is also proven that half-lives can be highly extensive in networks that interact with themselves repeatedly. Finally, we examine networks that interact with multiple components and propose that their behavior be controlled through an external influence that is connected to an 'input half-life' that is distinct from the internal half-life of the system. It is hoped that this research will contribute to a deeper understanding and better analysis of dynamic systems that interact with themselves. It also provides a foundation for investigating systems that interact with multiple components and could lead to improved management of systems that depend on internal and external elements. It is possible that this approach may also be applied to systems that use different update dynamics and could potentially be expanded to include systems that interact through continuous changes. It is clear that this research lays the groundwork for analyzing systems with complex internal and external connections and can be used to study various biological networks that interact with themselves and other components. It is possible that this approach may be applied to different types of dynamics and could be employed to investigate various technological and social networks that interact with multiple elements. It is clear that this research provides a foundation for investigating systems that depend on internal and external elements and could lead to improved management of these systems.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis from a surprisingly low 20.4% to an impressive 83.8% which is a major breakthrough. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing. None of our researchers have any personal gains from this code or model.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
We recognize current time representation approaches' shortcomings and suggest a
cycle-aware time-encoding framework for time characteristics that is universally
applicable and provides a more comprehensive time representation. Our unified
framework focuses on processing time-sensitive data within temporal knowledge graph
embeddings. Experimental results show that our proposed solutions equal or outperform
state-of-the-art models using semantic matching on multiple evaluation metrics. The
code for our approach is available at https://github.com/hubutu/Time-LowFER.

Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been enhanced to detect complex RPA eigenenergies in the complex energy plane. By applying this method, the RPA poles that characterize excited states such as $^{16}$O's electric dipole giant resonance were located within the complex energy plane with great success. Contrary to traditional views, research has revealed that the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, which has historically been understood as a solitary and broad resonance, actually consists of multiple poles with distinct widths, origins, residual interaction responses, and distinct densities of fluctuation components within the RPA framework. Moreover, a clear separation between a primary, narrow resonance known as the $\gamma$-resonance and a broader, more complex collective mode just above it was discovered. The findings of this research demonstrate the importance of exploring excited states within the complex energy plane and highlight the need for a more detailed understanding of the many complex features that underlie simple apparent phenomena in nuclear physics. Additionally, it is suggested that a hard dipole giant resonance may be reached in $^{16}$O or $^{40}$Ca configurations if excitations above 20 MeV in $^{16}$O are considered. Some theoretical issues related to the RPA and its extensions also have implications for the study of complex systems elsewhere.

Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training data can't distinguish genuine text from fabricated text. Current training methods fail to achieve a balance between generating plausible text and competing with the discriminator's severe penalties. To address this issue, we've developed a training framework that treats the generation process as a Markovian process, allowing the generator and discriminator to update parameters sequentially. This approach enables us to train the generator and discriminator efficiently, achieving superior performance on various text generation tasks. Our method achieves a significant improvement over the baseline generator, attaining an outstanding RoCNLE score of 41.50 on the Chnex4 dataset, surpassing the state-of-the-art score of 41.24. Moreover, our method is versatile, compatible with various generator architectures, including the standard Transformer, the multi-Head attention encoder, and the rapid Transformer. Our process also facilitates a notable reduction in training time and parameters compared to the baseline generator. The code for this project is available on the Gitee platform. The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is introduced which accounts for the transport of microorganisms through both space and time, and makes predictions about the dispersal patterns of genetic material. These predictions are compared to measurements of bacterial genes found in meteorites, and suggest that life could have been carried from one planetary system to another, with evidence of this interstellar panspermia potentially dating back over 7,000 years. Furthermore, the model predicts that the number of bacterial genes discovered in meteorites will continue to increase as more are studied, and hints at the possibility that the Earth may have been the source of microbial life for several interstellar voyages. The model is applied specifically to a group of 33 bacterial genes found in the Sinton Planitiba meteorite, and the results suggest that these genetic materials originated in a planetary system with conditions similar to those of the Earth, and traveled through interstellar space for a considerable distance before becoming incorporated into the meteorite. The theoretical framework presented here could be utilized in the analysis of any genetic material discovered in meteorites or other celestial objects, and may provide valuable insights into the long-standing mysteries surrounding the origins of life on Earth. The most promising direction suggested by this study is that life on Earth originated as a result of being seeded with genetic material carried by interstellar panspermia, a theory supported by additional research into the distribution of nucleotides found in meteorites. The findings presented here raise further questions about the extent to which life on Earth was influenced by the arrival of extraterrestrial microbial life forms. The results also highlight the need for a thorough examination of the Earth's biological heritage in order to better understand the possibilities and limitations of interstellar panspermia. The challenge remains of identifying plausible routes by which microbial life could travel through interstellar space, but the potential for discovering new life on planets that have already been studied, such as Mars, may provide a way to test the theory of interstellar panspermia. The proposed concept of induced spontaneous symmetry breaking is explored through a theoretical scenario. This scenario posits that spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs at the highest energy level, causing a cascade of symmetry violations at lower energy levels resulting from subtle mixings between them. A simple model has been devised to illustrate this idea using scalar portals, where the significant difference in energy scales, such as the Planck and electroweak scales, arises from the multiplication of several small factors related to the mixing coefficients. The formation of dark matter fields is also examined in this framework, where it is possible for these fields to emerge from matter fields located on one or more intermediate energy levels between the highest and lowest. The quantity that measures their fraction is dubbed the darken factor, and it could be calculated for each specific scenario. The most straightforward way to create dark matter fields is found to require the most elaborate symmetry structure, making the model quite plausible. The induced nature of spontaneous symmetry breaking also provides a justification for the axion dark matter scenario. The axion, in this case, would be a purely consequence of the darken factor, unrelated to the underlying physics that causes the symmetry breaking. The model suggests that the axion's frequency within the dark matter distribution could be modified, potentially leading to the existence of axion-like particles with different properties. The framework introduced here could offer a unifying explanation for various phenomena, including the matter-antimatter asymmetry and the existence of dark matter and axion-like particles. The model's potential to be tested by present and future experiments using light dark matter is also examined. The simplest way to discover light dark matter fields is found to rely on experiments involving nucleon targets rather than leptonic experiments. Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal without requiring knowledge of the underlying resource selection process.  Given that capture-recapture data contain information about resource selection and population density, we hypothesized that it would be possible to estimate resource selection and population density parameters directly from data involving animal encounters and observations.  By reparameterizing and combining model components, we derived a statistical framework that simultaneously estimates these two sets of important ecological variables from capture-recapture data, which includes information about encounter rates, detection probabilities, and spatial organization.  This new framework also allows for the incorporation of biological and environmental factors that influence resource selection and density.  We further developed an efficient Bayesian computational method for numerical solutions to these complex statistical models.  Through simulation and real-world examples, we showed that our method yields unbiased estimates for a wide range of biological and environmental variables of interest.  A notable feature of these new models is that they can utilize existing capture-recapture data, such as data from camera traps or genetic analysis, which can significantly simplify future data collection efforts and provide valuable ecological insights.  We anticipate that these models will significantly contribute to enhanced understanding and management of animal populations.  We provide a publicly accessible software implementation of these new spatial capture-recapture models as part of the R package, **SCRC**, which can be obtained from the R repository CRAN.  We also include the R code for the examples discussed in this analysis as part of the package documentation available on the R project website.  We recommend reviewing the user guide included with the package for information on how to utilize the models and associated capture-recapture data.  We are continuing to develop and refine these models in an effort to address additional capture-recapture analysis challenges.  We invite wildlife researchers to collaborate with us and contribute their expertise and research problems to further improve the capture-recapture models and associated resource selection models.  We are particularly interested in receiving suggestions for enhancing biological interpretation and model validation.  We are also interested in participating in the development of new methods for analyzing capture-recapture data, which can be discussed with one of the paper's corresponding authors. In designing minimum power networks, we are given an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ along with associated edge costs. The objective is to select an edge subset $F \subseteq E$ satisfying a specific minimum power criterion. Specifically, for the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem, F must contain exactly k disjoint st-paths. Notably, a k-approximation algorithm has been previously developed for this problem; however, whether such an algorithm exists with an approximation ratio sublinear in k even under the scenario of unit costs had yet to be determined. We present a new $4\sqrt{2k}$-approximation algorithm applicable to general cost settings. Moreover, under unit cost conditions, we derive an $8k$-approximation algorithm. These results represent significant advancements over prior work. Additionally, we demonstrate the existence of Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths instances for which any solution requires an edge subset of approximately $\sqrt{k}$ times larger than k in terms of power consumption. This leads to the conclusion that an $O(k^{\varepsilon})$-approximation algorithm must be employed for some $\varepsilon > 0$ when dealing with unit cost settings. Further still, we present a $8k$-approximation algorithm for the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem within the context of undirected multigraphs, a previously unaddressed scenario. Lastly, we explore the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem within directed graphs and provide $O(k^2)$-approximation algorithms for specific subcases. Our methods introduce a novel local-lifting approach, which we believe may be applicable to other graph design and approximation algorithms. Our research for the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem paves the way for further investigation into its underlying theory and related graph design and approximation algorithms.

Evaluating defensive strategies in team sports can be complicated due to the limited availability of data from individual game events. Previous researchers developed methods for assessing football teams' defensive prowess by predicting the likelihood of gaining possession of the ball and being attacked, based on the location of all players involved. These existing approaches, however, underestimate the complexity of the problem by assuming a static game scenario and ignoring the influence of time on player positioning. Moreover, none of these researches applied their methods to real-world data sets. This study introduces novel evaluation metrics for both offensive and defensive team performance, takes into account the temporal aspects of player positioning, and proposes the use of deep learning models to predict game events from raw data. Furthermore, we present an analysis of the influence of different factors on the likelihood of gaining possession of the ball and being attacked, revealing several common misconceptions held by football fans. Our approach to player positioning representation was tested against alternative methods, showing that temporal aspects of player positions should be considered to accurately predict game events. Finally, we successfully predicted game events on real-world data sets from the English Premier League and German Bundesliga, outperforming the state-of-the-art methods in multiple metrics. We proposed introducing a standard normalization to mitigate these issues, alongside a comprehensive set of criteria for evaluating the effectiveness of polarization measurement methods. By normalizing the scores, the methods that previously underperformed significantly improved in accuracy, with some of them rivaling the best performers. Our research lays the groundwork for conducting rigorous evaluations of polarization measurement methods and enhancing their reliability. However, despite achieving better results with the methods we tested, our findings are not exhaustive in this regard. Consequently, further explorations of the properties of polarized groups that influence the performance of these methods are still warranted. Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with known conditions, or identifying an operator based on its conditions or a portion of its conditions is all considered an inverse problem for differential operators. These problems have been explored in various contexts, including the study of differential operators in vector spaces and the analysis of partial differential equations. Theoretical investigations of the compatibility conditions for the Cauchy stress operator, which arises in the context of continuum mechanics, reveal a deep connection between this operator and the de Rham complex. By utilizing this connection and the established properties of the de Rham complex, we are able to devise an algorithm to compute compatibility conditions and a method to determine the underlying operator for a given differential form, thus solving the inverse problem. These methods can be applied to simplify non-linear elasticity equations in the presence of boundary conditions that involve stress, resulting in a more manageable form that retains the original meaning of stress. Similarly, they allow us to convert boundary conditions for partial differential equations derived from the de Rham complex into more manageable form. The utility of these methods is further illustrated through a simulation involving non-linear elasticity. The simulation demonstrates the ability to accurately solve the elasticity problem by employing a combination of the Newton-Raphson method and a nested iteration scheme. The nested iteration scheme is based on our analysis, which demonstrates that when the linearized elasticity operator is invertible, so too is the full linearized operator, with an analysis showing its inverse to be bounded. The efficiency of these methods is demonstrated through their application to a range of continuum mechanics systems, involving both linear and non-linear operators, structures of varying complexity, and different types of boundary conditions. The methods are also open to further improvement, with numerous optimization opportunities identified. The methods for computing compatibility conditions, determining operators, and simplifying partial differential equations have been implemented in the DifferentialOperator package, which is now available on MathSource. The implementation of this package has an associated size of less than 10 kilobytes. We introduce HyperPrompt, an innovative architecture that utilizes HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning for self-attention in Transformers through prompt-based generation. In this setup, hyper-prompts can be optimized end-to-end by a HyperNetwork. By employing hyper-prompts as global task memories, HyperPrompt enables networks to learn task-specific features while facilitating flexible information sharing among multiple tasks. Notably, HyperPrompt offers a balance of high performance and efficient use of resources - it achieves exceptional performance with significantly fewer additional task-conditioning parameters compared to other methods, amounting to $0.14\%$ of the parameters required, ultimately showcasing great computational efficiency. Through thorough experimentation on diverse models and benchmarks, such as the GLUE and SuperGLUE tasks for Natural Language Understanding, HyperPrompt has consistently outperformed prominent multi-task learning approaches like Prompt-Tuning, HyperFormer++ and T5. The robust performance of HyperPrompt can be attributed to its ability to achieve both rich task-specific mapping and efficient resource allocation. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a network's total size, particularly in distributed systems with concurrent node communication. We develop a new algorithm capable of accurately determining the network's size, even in the presence of a small number of malicious nodes. The algorithm is designed for focus on discovering the network's size in an incomplete graph and can handle up to $O(k^n)$ malicious nodes, where $n$ represents the total number of nodes and $k$ is the number of node connections. This algorithm operates under a binary communication model and utilizes a single message exchange round. We demonstrate its effectiveness through a simulation involving $10^5$ random trials. Additionally, we examine an application of the algorithm in a specific context involving binary communication and present a novel approach to enhance its performance. This algorithm offers improved efficiency and can be utilized as a foundation for more complex algorithms tackling additional challenges. We outline its design versatility and intend it as a foundational component for developing more intricate algorithms handling additional complexities. We intend this work as a starting point for exploring alternatives and would appreciate feedback on its concepts and theoretical contributions.

Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Our results demonstrate notable anomalous Nernst coefficients in these materials with values up to 0.15 $\mu$W/$(\Omega \cdot K)$ along with discussions on their thermodynamic and scattering mechanisms. Moreover, a significant enhancement of the anomalous Nernst coefficient relative to the anomalous Hall coefficient in these materials is observed and attributed to their specific electronic structures. This study advances our understanding and potential manipulation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic materials. Moreover, it highlights the value of combining experimental measurements to enhance accuracy in quantifying physical phenomena. Lastly, it emphasizes the significance of comparing the anomalous Nernst and Hall effects in magnetic materials.

This research demonstrates the potential for machine learning to enhance the analysis of large datasets in material science research. It facilitates the generation of accurate structural models and associated characteristic data from diverse simulation datasets, thereby offering a novel approach to modeling complex materials.

This work revisits linear gyrokinetic theory for geodesic acoustic modes and develops a general dispersion relation applicable to various ion distribution functions. A specific bi-Maxwellian ion distribution is analyzed to determine the impact of temperature anisotropy on mode frequency and growth rate, which shows significant increases due to anisotropy, heavily influenced by the electron-to-ion temperature ratio. Additionally, a significant reduction in mode growth is found when considering the effects of anisotropy, and this could help explain the relative rarity of GAM observations in anisotropically heated plasmas. A linearized global model also leads to a mode frequency ratio equation that relates local modes to modes that undergo an anisotropic transition. Numerical calculations demonstrate the potential for an anisotropy-induced mode gap in experiments like TJ-II or Alcator C-Mod. The proposed model can be tested by investigating GAMs in anisotropically heated global modes. The ion flux fluctuations associated with these modes provide a potential diagnostic tool, involving a non-linear relationship between anisotropy and beam heating. A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems. This approach relies on the unique properties of quantum systems under adiabatic evolution. However, one major issue needs to be addressed: quantum annealing is vulnerable to phase quenching and magnetic fluctuations caused by poorly calibrated annealing schedules. This problem is especially detrimental in quantum annealing systems that employ anti-ferromagnetic interactions, which can lead to quenching-induced ground states becoming trapped in low-energy states, thus bypassing the necessary adiabatic condition. A key insight from this research indicates that this specific type of quenching can actually be harnessed to perform 'quantum heating' - essentially the inverse process of quantum annealing. This concept of quantum heating was demonstrated using a quantum-sparse Hamiltonian and was found to result in the system entering a highly excited state. This outcome could potentially be applied to improve the performance of quantum annealing, allowing the calculation of combinatorial optimization problems while simultaneously minimizing the number of quantum trials required. A previously unexplored quantum trial schedule was developed to achieve this improvement. This new schedule, which incorporates a quenching-induced driving force, can accelerate the completion of tasks by as much as 220 times. The benefits of this approach were observed in large-scale systems, specifically when solving the exact cover by ones 3-SAT problem, a randomly generated instance of which was solved successfully using just one quantum trial. This breakthrough indicates that certain quantum annealing algorithms have the ability to efficiently solve complex, disordered problems on par with their classical counterparts. Consequently, this research represents a significant advancement in the development of quantum annealing technology. This progress could potentially pave the way for the widespread adoption of quantum-inspired quantum computing in fields such as finance, logistics, and medicine.

This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. Throughout nearly his entire directorate, van Rhijn struggled to secure additional funding due to severe challenges including the 1930s Depression, the Second World War and its aftermath, his personal health issues during the 1940s, the lab's distant location, and a governmentally favored infrastructure in Leiden. Lastly, the circumstances that led to Adriaan Blaauw accepting the position of director in 1957, setting in motion the revitalization of the lab, are analyzed in the latter half of this study. In addition, various key events from 1957 to 1968 are examined in a series of concluding remarks that highlight the early stages of the Netherlands Foundation for Radio Astronomy at the lab under Blaauw's direction. These periods of development, struggle, and transformation shaped the lab's ultimate growth into the prestigious research institution the Netherlands Institute for Radio Astronomy (ASTRON) is today. Consequently, this study aims to provide a comprehensive account of the earliest stages of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory, encompassing its most pivotal period of transformation, to offer fresh insights into the broader evolution of Dutch astronomy. Consequently, this study of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory's earliest stages of development, encompassing its most critical period of transformation, is poised to contribute fresh perspectives on the broader development of Dutch astronomy. In doing so, it is hoped that this study will stimulate further inquiry into the intricate relationships between the advancements of astronomy in the Netherlands and the broader cultural, social, and economic developments that have shaped the country since the late 19th century. In this vein, it is also considered that a deeper examination of the laboratory's development could provide valuable lessons for the current and future initiatives aimed at promoting publicly funded scientific research across the Netherlands. This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. We demonstrate that this method not only converges to an optimal solution, but also facilitates structural optimization. The proposed method also significantly reduces training time and decreases the memory usage per machine. A distinguishing aspect of this framework is the presence of holomorphic currents that serve as the basis for the higher-spin symmetry properties. A notable consequence of this framework is the presence of a holomorphic current with an exponential formulation, which can be utilized to construct multi-surface correlation functions that exhibit a higher-spin symmetry property. A key example of this type of correlation function is one that involves the primary field of the Liouville conformal field theory, commonly denoted as $X(z)$. Correlation functions of this type exhibit a higher-spin symmetry property and can be represented by a mathematical formula that includes the boundary contribution of a chiral boson with a high spin value. This formulation can be derived from the parent Toda conformal field theory using a specific symmetry property known as the'spin-step' rule. A key aspect of this rule is that the spin value of a given boundary contribution is determined by the difference between the spin values of the parent and decayed conformal field theories. A notable consequence of this rule is that it makes it possible to derive the mathematical formula for multi-surface Liouville primary field correlation functions, which exhibit a higher-spin symmetry property. These correlation functions can be represented by a mathematical formula that includes the boundary contribution of a chiral boson with an excessively high spin value, exceeding even the maximum possible value of two in conformal field theory. A key aspect of this type of correlation function is that it can be utilized to derive the mathematical formula for multi-surface Liouville primary field correlation functions in the comprehensive expansion of the $M_{2,2}$ Toda conformal field theory. A notable consequence of this derivation is the discovery of a previously unknown higher-spin symmetry property associated with the $X(z)$ field, which is inherent to the $M_{2,2}$ Toda conformal field theory. Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through scalar field scattering yields results that support the first law of thermodynamics for non-extremal black holes, confirming that the singularity in such black holes is hidden by an event horizon. The validity of this theory for near-extremal and extremal black holes is confirmed by analyzing their minimum function values after the scattering process. The findings show that neither near-extremal nor extremal black holes can become overcharged due to such processes. The outcome of scattering when a certain relationship between the electric potential and scalar field is met is that the extremal black hole retains its extreme properties. In contrast, when this relationship is not met, the scattering causes the extremal black hole to transform into a near-extremal black hole with a different mass and charge configuration. The horizon of the near-extremal black hole formed by this process contains a naked singularity, thus providing evidence that naked singularities can exist in a region of general relativity space. The conditions under which the singularity-naked hole formation occur can be understood through the potential-scalar field diagram. The extent of the singularity-naked hole formation in the universe would be minimized if the universe follows the predictions made by the authors in regards to the scattering process. The predictions state that overcharged near-extremal black holes would quickly emit energy through scalar field emission, resulting in a singularity-hidden horizon. The extent of this emission would be sufficiently brief that the universe would not have the opportunity to observe the singularity-naked hole formation. The possibility of observing singularity-naked holes in the universe through gravitational wave signatures is analyzed by the authors in their work. The study reveals that the chances of detecting such singularities through gravitational wave signals in the universe are extremely low. The reason for this is that the vast majority of the matter in the universe does not have the right conditions to produce such singularities that could be detected through gravitational waves. In addition, even if such singularities are produced, the universe would likely not have the opportunity to observe them before they are covered by a horizon due to the emission of energy through scalar field emission. The validity of the cosmic censorship conjecture is thus confirmed by the analysis of the authors. The study also confirms that the entropy of near-extremal Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes follows the formula proposed by Hawking by analyzing the scattering process. In this paper, we offer a groundbreaking reimagining of set theory through a
paracomplete and paraconsistent four-valued logic system. Unlike classical logic,
this approach accommodates propositions that may be neither entirely true nor
entirely false, as well as propositions that can simultaneously embody both
truths. In contrast to the proposed system, traditional attempts at updating logic
through paraconsistent and paracomplete principles fall short. Our reimagined set
theory is then utilized in developing a novel model for the axiom of choice, one
that deviates from the expected outcomes of classical logic while remaining
consistent within the new four-valued logic framework. Moreover, we demonstrate
that this model results in the axiom of choice being logically equivalent to the
law of excluded middle. Finally, we explore potential applications of our four-valued
logic system to other mathematical frameworks. Specifically, we suggest its
feasibility in models of real numbers and set theories featuring urelements,
alongside speculative ideas for its adaptability in models of infinite sets and
sets of sets. Ultimately, this work aims to initiate a discussion on the
paracomplete and paraconsistent logic system within the broader context of set
theory. It also presents novel solutions to mathematical challenges, most notably
the axiom of choice, while identifying numerous areas for further exploration. 
This research is part of an ongoing project to develop the BZFC system and
investigate its implications within the context of set theory. It is an extended
version of an article that first appeared in the 13th Scilat Conference proceedings. 
It has since undergone significant revisions to align with the interests of a
broader audience. 
Keywords: paraconsistent logic, paracomplete logic, four-valued logic, set theory,
Axiom of Choice, Real Numbers, urelements, infinite sets, sets of sets.
