Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. Ultimately, this work demonstrates the feasibility of developing a BCI that can reliably decode and respond to walking states and provide closed-loop control over prosthetic devices for paralysis rehabilitation. Leveraging this approach could also enable the development of more advanced prosthetic technologies that consider the intricate aspects of human gait. In the future, combining this BCI system with current prosthetic technologies may enable greater control and mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Additionally, this study's findings could lead to a deeper understanding of the underlying neurophysiological mechanisms governing human gait and the integration of walking state information into closed-loop prosthetic systems. In order to achieve this, further research is needed with subjects who have spinal cord injuries and are using prosthetic devices, in conjunction with ECoG-based BCI systems. In order to take this approach a step further, the researchers suggest conducting training sessions with these subjects, utilizing their individual ECoG recordings, in order to provide more natural and adaptable prosthetic support that complements their unique gait patterns. In order to accomplish this, studies should explore developing hybrid approaches that combine BCI feedback with other sensory feedback methods, in order to create a more integrated prosthetic system that is capable of processing multiple sources of feedback, in order to provide a more natural walking experience for individuals with spinal cord injuries. In order to achieve this, future research should investigate the effectiveness of this approach in real-world settings, in order to move closer to developing a reliable and practical BCI-based prosthetic device for safe control. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. Alongside its superior performance, DECENNT offers a more comprehensive understanding of complex dynamic systems and their relationships. The code for DECENNT is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/yikc5/DECENNT. The project website can be found at https://www.yikc5.com/DECENNT. The model's datasets and training settings are detailed in Section 4 of the accompanying technical paper. https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.00123. DECENNT has been successfully applied to multiple research projects, involving the study of neural networks, sleep stage classification, prediction of emergent language, and modeling of brain networks. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. To facilitate accurate phylogeny reconstruction, various stochastic processes have been developed to generate random phylogenetic trees or networks, which can be used to validate results or inform Bayesian analysis. Notwithstanding the creation of numerous network generation tools, a shortage of discourse and comparison among these tools persists. To address this disparity, we undertake a comparative analysis of a range of phylogenetic network generators by evaluating and contrasting the topological characteristics of the generated networks as a function of the number of reticulations present. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between network topology and the number of reticulations required for lateral gene transfer events. Moreover, we examine the impact of varying tree sizes and the number of reticulations on the generated networks. A corresponding study is also conducted on the topological characteristics of phylogenetic trees derived from networks, in addition to evaluating the network reconstruction capabilities of different methods on these artificially generated networks. The comprehensive study of multiple phylogenetic network generators in relation to reticulate evolutionary history has significant implications for an accurate understanding of the evolutionary processes underlying genome data. The data and methods employed in this research are freely accessible online. The research presented herein is part of a broader project aimed at developing new phylogenetic network generators that can effectively capture the complexity of genome evolution. We examine topological and localization transitions within one-dimensional systems
under spatially random mutations in their Brillouin zone. This phenomenon, known as the
topological Anderson insulating phase, can be induced by altering a one-dimensional
photonic, electronic, or mechanical system's topology through a random process. By means
of exact calculations and theoretical frameworks, we find that topological transitions in
Anderson systems are characterized by unique symmetry protection and display both
gapped and delocalized states. The topological Anderson insulating phase can be created
by mutation-generated point defects or by varying a model parameter and has an
underlying topological invariance. We demonstrate that topological protection in
Anderson systems can be unveiled through boundary state analysis and that the topological
Anderson phase can be distinguished from its conventional counterparts via the
analyzed matrices of a system. Furthermore, we examine the applicability of established
theories to describe topological transitions in Anderson systems. Lastly, we propose a
method for experimental identification of the topological Anderson phase in microwave
cavity arrays. The study of topological transitions in Anderson systems provides new
insights into the physics of disorder-induced topological transitions and may lead to
the discovery of topological phases in other systems. The most notable discovery made
in this study is the creation of a topological Anderson insulating phase in one-dimensional
systems capable of conducting both gapped and delocalized states. The most notable
feature of this phase is its robustness against backscattering mediated by mutations. The
study of this phase may enable researchers to develop efficient methods for managing
point defects in topological systems. The generated models and theoretical frameworks
may also be applied to systems influenced by hybridization, coupling, and drive. The study
of the topological Anderson phase can be experimented upon using microwave cavity
arrays, making it feasible to design and execute actual experiments. The discovered
phase' topological characteristics can be utilized in the development of robust quantum
devices, enabling reliable operation even when faced with unpredictable mutations. The
study of this phase may also enable the creation of efficient algorithms for calculating
topological invariants and the identification of topological phases in systems
complicated by hybridization, coupling, and drive. The study of the topological Anderson
phase may also enable the development of effective methods for managing both intrinsic
and extrinsic disorders in topological systems. The research may also lead to the
discovery of additional topological phases in one-dimensional systems

This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section calculation for complex parameters, supplemented by higher-order corrections. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson. The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons are carried out up to the NNLO QCD level. The study also considers two-loop electroweak effects and SUSY QCD corrections at the NLO level, with corrections for squark effects dependent on the phases of the complex parameters demonstrated. The analysis highlights the importance of incorporating correct on-shell properties for the external Higgs bosons through finite wave function normalisation factors, obtained from the $\texttt{FeynHiggs}$ code. The results have been incorporated into an extension of the $\texttt{SusHi}$ code, referred to as $\texttt{SusHiMi}$. The new code allows for precise predictions of major production and decay processes of neutral Higgs bosons at the LHC and future colliders, with implications for the ongoing and future experiments at the LHC, the proposed LHC Upgrade Phase II and III, the LHC at 100 TeV and future colliders like CLIC, CEPC, FCC, CCP and ILC, with a focus primarily on the LHC but with extensions to these other experiments also considered. A new quasi-score linearity test has been developed for assessing linearity in continuous and count-based network autoregressive models. The test's asymptotic distribution is analyzed under various scenarios, including fixed and increasing network dimensions, null linearity, and local identifiability. Key findings indicate that the test's distribution converges to the chi-square distribution with specific degrees of freedom, consistent with previous results for a score-based test. Notably, when network dimensions remain constant, the test's asymptotic distribution is equivalent to a chi-square distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the number of identifiable parameters. However, when network dimensions increase at a rate comparable to the square root of the number of observed time points, the test's asymptotic distribution is equivalent to a beta prime distribution with known parameters, providing a degree of freedom that can be used for finite sample size calculations. When network dimensions increase at a rate faster than the square root of the number of observed time points, the test's asymptotic distribution is no longer identical to the beta prime distribution, instead converging to the chi-square distribution due to the dominant effect of model identifiability. A data-driven approach has been established for determining the critical value of the test based on the network dimension's rate of increase relative to the number of observed time points. Through simulation studies and an analysis of real-world data, the effectiveness of the proposed approach has been validated. Furthermore, the results highlight potential issues with traditional approaches that fail to account for the network dimension's rate of increase, prioritizing the identification of parameters over the network structure in such cases. The established approach provides a degree of freedom that can be used for calculating critical values, allowing for a more accurate assessment of linearity in network autoregressive models. The methodology developed herein is applicable to a broad range of time series models that integrate network autoregressive models, including seemingly unrelated regressions, ARMA models, and models that account for individual effects and time-varying coefficients. The R package 'QuasiScoreLinearityTest' is available for implementing the proposed quasi-score linearity test and associated methods. The package also enables the creation of graphical tools for visualizing linearity test results and generating step-by-step guides for conducting quasi-score linearity tests across different models. The methods and results discussed herein are presented in an approachable manner, accompanied by reproducible code to ensure ease of use and understanding. Recent breakthroughs in declarative networks and related work have demonstrated the capability of differentiating the solution mappings of continuous parametrized optimization problems. This has enabled the integration of optimization-based modeling techniques within end-to-end differentiable architectures, bypassing the necessity for explicit formulae for network gradients. By exploring this differentiability property, we provide an in-depth examination of how deep declarative networks can be constructed from first principles, focusing particularly on the optimisation problems they embody. Through concrete examples, we illustrate the flexibility this approach affords in designing network components that can model complex functions and aggregations within optimization problems, culminating in an exploration of various differentiation paths as means of deriving new functions from existing ones. The flexibility and expressiveness of deep declarative networks make them suitable as building blocks for additional modeling constructs and differentiation techniques. This work is an invitation to leverage this differentiability property in a way that is both mathematically rigorous and computationally feasible, and to explore the numerous possibilities it presents for modeling real-world challenges. This work is primarily theoretical in nature; however, we also provide the implementation details and empirical results for the networks it describes. This includes the Python code that utilizes the Jax library for tensor operations and the Cirq library for quantum-related functionalities, in addition to key model parameters and training outcomes. This research is an early exploration of the potential of deep declarative networks and does not yield superior results compared to established deep learning models in the specified tasks. Yet, it is our hope that this work will lay the groundwork for further research and advancements in this area. A cell's behavior during spreading and movement is influenced by various interrelated events that are activated by external stimuli at different scales. Due to the cell's living nature and complex response mechanisms, it is not sufficient to apply traditional material mechanics principles to it. Rather, cells comprise constituents with repeatable reactions such as contractility in single fibers and actin networks but also exhibit non-deterministic reorganization upon external stimuli. With consideration of this complexity, our goal is to develop a multi-faceted framework for modeling cellular spreading and locomotion, taking into account the movement of proteins across lipid membranes. This proposed approach simulates protein diffusion, binding, and filament reorganization, ultimately giving rise to the emergence of spreading and motility. To support this framework, we establish mathematical justifications for each component and demonstrate its applicability through numerical examples. Furthermore, we investigate how different protein properties influence spreading speeds and find that they can be classified into three distinct speed regimes. Additionally, we explore various fingerprint patterns that emerge as a result of an asymmetry in external stimuli and cellular structure. Lastly, we explore the effects of surface lipid membrane features, such as lipid raft domains, on spreading and motility behavior. This comprehensive framework has the potential to be an invaluable tool for analyzing and predicting the spreading and locomotion patterns of diverse living cells. This prediction capability could be achieved by modifying the model to incorporate various cellular pathways that influence spreading and motility behavior. This model is part of a larger cell modeling paradigm that focuses on multi-faceted component modeling, where each component model has scientific credibility and can be solved efficiently by established numerical methods. This approach is an important step towards building computationally integrated models of living cells through systems biology. The unique combination of decentralization, redundancy, and pseudo-anonymity in public blockchain platforms has made them appealing for cryptocurrency adoption. However, these same features have enabled cybercriminals to exploit vulnerabilities in blockchain technology and deceive users through social engineering to execute malicious plans. Existing methods for identifying malicious actors typically rely on transaction history from specific wallet addresses, but often neglect the underlying money trails. In contrast, we propose an innovative approach centered on money trail analysis, incorporating new features to detect suspicious activities within cryptocurrency blockchains. Specifically, we investigate the cyclic behavior present in temporal transaction graphs within a blockchain, focusing on uncovering hidden patterns. By applying our methods to the Ethereum blockchain, we reveal distinct cyclic patterns indicative of malicious activities such as gambling, phishing, and money laundering, as well as identify two specific temporal cyclic transfers. Notably, our approach is versatile and adaptable to other cryptocurrency blockchains with suitable modifications tailored to the characteristics of the underlying cryptocurrency. By leveraging our feature set, we are able to differentiate our method from existing approaches that rely on pairwise transaction analysis, and instead position our research as an extension to these methods. Furthermore, we are able to identify novel types of malicious activities that have evolved as a consequence of our analysis. Inevitably, detecting malicious activities within cryptocurrency blockchains poses significant technical challenges. Despite these difficulties, we are able to achieve exceptional performance on classification tasks related to malicious activities, achieving accuracy rates of up to 99.5% in certain scenarios, and accurately identifying malicious actors in 96% of cases. Ultimately, our approach has the potential to enhance the security and trustworthiness of cryptocurrency platforms by minimizing vulnerabilities and preventing the exploitation of their limitations. As a result, more users will feel confident in utilizing these platforms for everyday transactions. In addition, our approach can be applied to other applications centered on blockchain analysis, such as monitoring the circulation of funds and pinpointing the origin of illegal funds. In order to facilitate the adoption of our approach, we have created a publicly accessible dataset featuring 2 million transactions from the Ethereum blockchain, in addition to a comprehensive evaluation of our method that is free from hidden biases. This dataset and evaluation can serve as a foundation for the development of advanced machine learning models capable of identifying complex patterns within cryptocurrency blockchains, as well as for comparing the performance of competing approaches. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. Furthermore, we established a connection between decoding performance and learning parameters, revealing that optimal decoding results can be achieved when the decoder's reward structure is consistent with the underlying noise process. This research paves the way for developing a family of decoders tailored to specific codes, environments, and fault channels. Moreover, it suggests that deepQ learning can be used to improve decoding efficiency in scenarios involving isolated errors, ultimately facilitating the development of complex code systems. This work also explores the possibility of incorporating temporal information into decoding processes, laying the groundwork for future applications in dynamic scenarios. This innovative approach to code research, rooted in artificial intelligence, may lead to a deeper understanding of code behavior and noise generation mechanisms. As such, this study represents a significant step towards creating a family of decoders that can be optimized for various codes, environments, and fault channels, and could potentially enable the development of complex code systems. However, further research is needed to fully leverage the capabilities of this learning framework. This initial investigation into temporal decoding faces several challenges, including the limited duration of error correction cycles; despite this, the results provided offer a preliminary exploration into incorporating temporal information. This study is further significant because it lays the foundation for a new code design philosophy, centered around learning the characteristics of codes and developing adaptative decoding methods that can be applied to any code environment. This could ultimately enable the creation of complex code systems capable of correcting multiple types of faults. However, resolving the fundamental issue of decoding cyclic errors will be crucial to this goal. This study has demonstrated the capability to create rapid surface code decoders using deepQ learning, and has established a connection between decoding performance and learning parameters, revealing that the best decoding results can be achieved when the reward structure of the decoder is consistent with the underlying noise process. This research also explores the possibility of incorporating temporal information into decoding processes, representing a significant step towards creating a family of decoders that can be optimized for various codes, environments, and fault channels. Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single, non-invasive measurements on individual parts of the system. Although this typical approach requires resource-intensive quantum state manipulation, our research reveals an alternative method. We show that any quantum state can be transformed into an equivalent entangled state that maximizes precision improvement during measurement. This process involves a novel application of quantum circuit reversal, enabling the creation of optimal entangled states using only quantum circuits that focus on measurement collection. As a result, existing quantum simulation software can be leveraged to achieve this without the need for state reversal. This breakthrough has implications for the adoption of quantum metrology in real-world applications. Furthermore, the ability to create these optimal states may lead to the development of new quantum states with unique properties. The research described here has been thoroughly validated numerically and experimentally. The experiments were conducted using a system consisting of up to 20 ions trapped in a linear string and were executed on the Ion Trap Quantum Simulator at the University of Tokyo. The research was successfully demonstrated by executing the algorithm with both classical and quantum simulations. The experiment resulted in a precision improvement of approximately 10 times over the original state. The duration of the experiment was approximately 5 minutes and 30 seconds. The ability to create these optimal states could lead to the development of new quantum states with unique properties, making them useful for other applications. The research described here has the potential to contribute to the development of quantum networks by enhancing the precision of interferometry measurements in nodes with small numbers of nodes. The research could also pave the way for the creation of novel quantum states with unique properties when extended to larger-scale quantum systems. Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has seen a significant surge in interest lately. This surge particularly occurred in the realm of wireless applications, where communication constraints can significantly impact decision-making. Especially in scenarios where context dimensions are substantial. This paper addresses a decentralized, memoryless contextual linear bandit learning problem. In this problem, agents that observe the context and make decisions are physically isolated from the learner. This learner executes the learning process but remains unaware of the context. Contexts are generated randomly and a linear connection between the context and rewards exists. This paper develops a new context-compression approach. This approach involves finding a reduced-dimensional linear subspace that closely resembles the original context distribution. The paper also creates an efficient method for computing the optimal compression context. This computation involves minimizing the expected quadratic error between the original and compressed contexts. The paper primarily focuses on scenarios where the context and system dimensions are comparable. It demonstrates an upper bound of approximately $5d$ bits per context. This upper bound serves as a significant improvement over existing bounds. The paper verifies its results through numerical simulations and an upper bound of approximately $5d$ bits per context is achieved. This achievement represents a notable improvement over previous bounds, especially in scenarios where the context and system dimensions are close.

However, the global shift to fully remote working brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic was a unprecedented phenomenon. This research involves a two-phase, multi-method approach. Initially, it investigates how working from home affected Scrum practitioners through a qualitative survey. Subsequently, it proposes and empirically tests a theoretical framework using PLS-SEM with data from a sample of 200 software engineers who collaborated on Scrum projects from home. Our results demonstrate the reliability of all key constructs and the validity of all hypotheses, while also highlighting the advantages of combining home working and Scrum practices through an IPMA analysis. Notably, supporting employees' inherent needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness is crucial in the remote working context. Our findings indicate that both home working and Scrum use contribute to project success, with Scrum playing a mediating role. However, Scrum's effectiveness in this regard depends on the strength of team relationships. Our proposed model provides valuable insights for IT project managers on how to adapt Scrum to achieve optimal results in a remote working environment. This research offers a theoretical framework that can be applied to similar projects beyond the IT domain. This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal gain resulting from optimal power control in contrast to binary (on/off) power control in large interference networks, focusing on uncovering new theoretical insights. Numerical studies were conducted to verify the validity of the extremal GDoF gain predictions in various scenarios, including an overview of how the gain varies under different scheme designs. One of the key findings showed that the extremal GDoF gain can achieve a substantial boost, up to an order of $\sqrt{n}$ improvement, over traditional binary power control approaches in certain cases. It was also found that the extremal gain tends to follow an inverse relationship with the number of transmitters involved. Moreover, our results indicated that binary power control can be seen as a GDoF-equiprobable strategy, thus enabling us to derive key performance indicators (KPIs) such as throughput and error probabilities directly from GDoF results. To further demonstrate this, we provided specific expressions for the asymptotic GDoF per user of various binary power control schemes, including fully distributed, decentralized schemes. It was also shown that the extremal gain from optimal power control can be achieved through specific 'interference-coordinated' schemes, essentially resulting in a class of 'extremal networks' that require no coordination between transmitters, which in turn can be realized under an 'extremal probability distribution'. To verify the validity of our extremal gain predictions, we conducted numerical studies in various scenarios, including homogenous networks, tiered networks, and ad-hoc networks, using both analytical and simulation approaches. The results from these studies confirmed the extremal gain predictions across all scenarios considered. One of the key outcomes from these studies showed that the extremal gain from optimal power control can be as high as $\sqrt{n}$, and that this gain exhibits an inverse cubic relationship with the number of transmitters involved. It was also found that binary power control can be viewed as a GDoF-equiprobable strategy, thus enabling the derivation of key performance indicators such as throughput and error probabilities directly from GDoF results. The findings from this work are expected to provide valuable theoretical insights that can be used to guide the development of near-optimal schemes in large interference networks. The work is further expected to facilitate the study of extremal network theory by providing a deeper understanding of extremal networks and the concepts of extremal gain, equiprobability, and extremal probability distribution

A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Ultimately, the robot attained its target height of 15.5 body heights in a single hop. This study demonstrated the capability of high-fidelity terrain simulations to facilitate the development of control systems for robots interacting with granular surfaces. Additionally, it highlighted the potential of the RFT to guide the design of force control systems, albeit requiring additional tuning and the support of sophisticated feedback controllers. This work paves the way for investigating more complex locomotion methods, such as bounding and walking, on deformable terrain. Nevertheless, significant hurdles remain to be overcome before similar robots can be realized in the physical world. This project's findings are relevant to the broader field of legged locomotion research and could be applied to other robotic platforms operating in uncertain environments. This study's results are consistent with established theories governing grain interactions and highlight the limitations of current research in granular dynamics, particularly when dealing with collisions between robots and granular surfaces. This work identified several key factors contributing to ground reaction forces, including the robot's velocity, shape, and size, as well as the granular material's properties. Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, allowing for the evaluation of models' ability to understand the effects of negation on implied information. Additionally, it demands that models engage in a negotiation-style game with other models, where they must take turns adding new information to a statement, either affirming or negating existing claims to ultimately determine a final assertion. Our assessment metric, a multi-stage evaluation, assesses models' performance in understanding negated text, inferring the effects of negation, and engaging in the CONDAQA game. The current state-of-the-art models, despite achieving remarkable results on various other tasks, struggle with CONDAQA, highlighting the difficulties involved in processing negation and the significance of this work in the pursuit of more human-like language models. The dataset is available at this link https://github.com/tencent/CONDAQA for public access.

In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. The underlying dynamics of quench and annealing appear to exhibit an invertible relationship, described by a dynamic map that reverses the quantum state's flow over time and effectively inverts the annealing process. This insight, coupled with the directional nature of this mapping, allows for the annealing gap to be predicted from quench data in a backward-analyzing approach that can be utilized to develop new, dynamically motivated quantum annealing algorithms. These novel algorithms prioritize minimal annealing gap points by selecting the best quench parameters in a discrete, multi-level process that ensures the most efficient solution-finding process. When compared to established protocols, these algorithms result in the greatest possible reduction in heating, leading to a significant improvement in solution-finding efficiency. The most efficient algorithm among those examined achieves an exceptionally low level of thermal correlation at the minimal annealing gap point, resulting in solution-finding efficiency that is substantially higher than that achieved by current protocols. This advancement has implications for the development of quantum annealing algorithms capable of solving complex, intractable problems efficiently. Furthermore, the ability to model the annealing gap's behavior based on quench data may prove invaluable in better understanding the fundamental dynamics of quantum annealing. Starting from a reliable two-dimensional model with two bands derived from
$d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band, resulting in a
ground state that is also antiferromagnetic. However, when screening is more
extensive, the movement of $d$-electrons is curbed, leading to a more complex
phase diagram with additional ground states. 
Full lattice simulations validate our simplified model's calculations. 
Our analysis of a variety of related models confirms that moderate
screening can trigger a variety of phases of matter with strong interactions. 
This is further illustrated by applying this framework to a simple 
Hubbard model on a triangular lattice, where moderate screening allows for 
the emergence of magnetic ordering and charge-orbital ordering. 
This study's findings also imply that strong correlations could facilitate the 
exclusion of oxygen orbitals from specific lattice sites, providing a potential 
explanation for the high conductivity observed in high-$T_c$ materials. 
Lastly, a critical assessment is given to the two-band doped-lanthanum 
nickelate model that has been previously proposed, along with a proposed 
alternative based on a more extensive screening scenario. 
This alternative is supported by our study, which indicates that strong 
correlations may cause $d$-electrons to accumulate in response to $s$-electron 
excitation, resulting to a tendency towards charge-orbital ordering. 
This proposed picture of the physics governing infinite layered nickelates 
offers an explicit framework that can be utilized for discussions of both the 
experimental and theoretical aspects involved. 
It is hoped that this study will spark a fresh perspective on this topic. 
It is also worth noting that the most essential aspect of this study can be 
appreciated even without a thorough understanding of its technical details. 
It highlights the value of incorporating screening effects when developing 
effective Hamiltonians, as well as the potential for two-band models to 
give rise to ground states driven by strong interactions that are entirely 
distinct from those obtained from one-band models.

We use radiance data from space to study wave slopes in oceans during the day, specifically using about 300 channels between 3.6 and 4.0 $\mu$m, which takes into account solar radiation reflected off the water. This approach uses a large dataset of around 150 million observations, enabling a detailed examination of wave slope probabilities up to 20 degrees. Our method involves using probability distributions for three degrees of freedom, all of which have adjustable parameters, to model wave slope data. Our analysis focuses on near-solar angles and includes a theoretical explanation of how wind and solar radiation can influence wave behavior. Our results demonstrate that wave slope probabilities are affected by wind speed and solar intensity, particularly when near-solar angles exceed 5 degrees. This is particularly evident in the shape of wave slope probability distributions, with influences visible on skewness and kurtosis coefficients. Our research also compares wave slope probability distributions to model predictions, including interactions between wind and solar radiation and how they affect waves. We find that these interactions can alter wave slope probability distributions, potentially leading to rippling winds occurring under strong solar radiation. This could result in increased aerosol entrainment and altered cloud coverage, with further research needed to fully understand these phenomena and their effects. modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting during subsequent updates. By leveraging parallel
calculations on shared memory systems, we enhance testing speed, ensuring optimal
results can be obtained even as software systems scale up. Comprehensive
experiments utilizing various applications reveal a significant boost in testing
speed resulting from parallel processing, outperforming sequential calculations by
an average of 5-9 times. Moreover, our method achieves a 10-17% reduction in the
number of calculations required for optimal results when utilizing parallel
calculations, making it suitable for large software systems. The methodology is
suitable for detecting minimal regressive changes with lower-order singular value
decomposition, leading to potential applications in other domains involving

optimization problem that can be reformulated as a group action on high-dimensional
spaces. This is demonstrated through the minimal regressive travel sales problem,
which involves finding the fewest changes required to adapt a sales route when

be solved efficiently through the proposed method, making it worthy of further
research and extension to even more complex problems. The developed method and

The established Tai mapping between two trees $T_1$ and $T_2$ is a unique one-to-one correlation of their nodes that maintains the ancestral relationship. However, determining the maximum-weight Tai mapping between two unordered trees is a well-known NP-complete problem. We now introduce a contrasting concept - anti Tai mapping - as a binary relationship between two trees. An anti Tai mapping, defined as the subset $M$ of $V_1\times V_2$, excludes any node pairs $(x,y)$ and $(x',y')$ that would conflict with each other's ancestral relationship, implying either $x=x'$ and $y$ is a descendant of $y'$ or $x$ is a descendant of $x'$ and $y=y'$. We demonstrate that maximizing the weight of an anti Tai mapping can be computed via a 0-1 integer programming formulation and propose a more efficient algorithm using a two-parameter LP relaxation. Moreover, we investigate the geometric interpretation of this relaxation and find that the optimal solution values for both the LP relaxation and the 0-1 integer programming have the same worst-case ratio of $\frac{1}{2}$. We also examine the connection between anti Tai mapping and Tai mapping, as well as the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping. Additionally, we present a strong lower bound for the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping problem and demonstrate its computational intractability. Finally, we conduct experiments using both artificial and real data to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithms. 

Keywords: anti Tai mapping, maximum-weight anti Tai mapping, integer programming, lower bound, experimental study, bioinformatics, phylogenetic trees, metric space.

Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional. Additionally, it provides an alternative proof for a previously established conjecture regarding the dimensionality of polynomially bounded solutions to the eigenvalue problem under these conditions. We have developed an efficient approach for condensing complex systems into their fundamental behaviors using their primary underlying features. By leveraging observed data, we pinpoint a low-dimensional structure that characterizes the systems' gradual evolution and generate an extremely simple representation of the systems' dynamics within that structure. Building on the SSMLearn algorithm, which applies implicit optimization to fit a system's underlying structure to available data and simplifies the systems' dynamics, we have created two new algorithms that achieve similar results using explicit optimization methods. These algorithms have the advantage of requiring less technical knowledge and being more computationally efficient, making them better suited for large-scale systems and systems with noisy data. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of these algorithms through numerical tests and real-world applications, including the analysis of a model predicting renal colic episodes and the analysis of a model predicting electricity demand. The results show that these algorithms can accurately model systems using a small number of dimensions, leading to more manageable and actionable insights. The models also exhibit good generalization performance when applied to new scenarios. The code for these algorithms and the associated data is available online. The algorithms we present have the potential to significantly reduce the complexity of advanced modeling tools, making them more accessible to a broader range of users. The model simplifications also have computational benefits, allowing for faster performance even with existing optimization techniques. The research also explores the relationship between the proposed models and another prominent method for analyzing complex systems, providing a theoretical comparison and illustrating the differences in practice. The work is further enhanced by the development of a user-friendly graphical user interface that provides a simple and intuitive way to create the model structures, select the model dimensions, and visualize the results. The GUI is an important step towards greater adoption of the model simplification framework by non-technical users. The research is complemented by the development of an open-source software package that is an extension of an existing software platform, offering an efficient and user-friendly solution for condensing complex systems and their dynamics. The success of this approach is evaluated through the reduction of model complexity, computational efficiency, and generalization performance. The most efficient algorithm achieves a 30 times speed increase and the model simplification results in a 15 decibel reduction in the error compared to the original model. The algorithm also demonstrates robust performance across different data sets, systems sizes, and levels of noise. This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model outputs from an untrusted client and a semi-reliable server. The goal is for the client to obtain the inference output while the server learns nothing. Although initial studies by Lehmkuhl and Chandran have shown significant advancements, there remains a considerable gap between current solutions and practical implementations. To address this issue, our proposal SIMC 2.0 maintains the foundation of Chandran's work while improving the efficiency of linear and non-linear layers within the server's protocol. Key innovations include a customized coding framework that reduces the client's computation and communication costs and a versatile layer construction method allowing composition of layers with diverse dimensions. Furthermore, SIMC 2.0 reduces the client's computation time and communication volume with the server by utilizing an alternative encryption method. Experimental results show that when utilizing Chandran's work as a baseline, our proposal SIMC 2.0 achieves a notable improvement in layer composition. Specifically, it reduces the client's computation time by approximately 150 times and communication volume by approximately 30 times across various ML models, without compromising their accuracy. Moreover, our proposal SIMC 2.0 facilitates complex layer construction, such as the MatConvNet module, where Chandran's work failed to accomplish. Consequently, the efficient SIMC 2.0 protocol makes secure ML inference more feasible for widespread adoption. Additionally, our proposal SIMC 2.0 serves as an early implementation of a secure multi-party computation protocol, paving the way for further research and broader applicability. Our research includes a sensitive radio telescope observation of nearby spiral galaxy M101 and its surrounding region, conducted using the FAST. This allowed us to identify an enlarged and irregularly shaped HI disk around M101. Inside the optical disk of M101, the HI velocity field appears ordered, whereas there is a significant disturbance in the outer disk. In addition, three previously undetected HI clouds have been discovered near the southern edge of the M101 disk. These HI clouds have estimated masses of 1.3$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$, 2.4$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$, and 2.0$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$ respectively. The HI clouds in M101 rotate in sync with its main HI disk. In contrast to a similar nearby galaxy, NGC 5477, which also shares a disk, these HI clouds in M101 have no visual counterparts. Also, a newly found HI tail in M101 supports evidence that the galaxy is interacting with its dwarf companion, NGC 5474. This interaction may be the origin of the extra-planar gas and HI tail observed in M101. Its disk disturbance is a result of an interaction that triggered its central activity. Meanwhile, a previously known HI tail in M101 has expanded to a longer tail with additional HI tail found within it. This suggests recent galaxy interactions may still be responsible for its current state. In addition, four new HI bridges have been discovered connecting M101 to its companion NGC 5474, made up of elevated HI densities. These findings were made possible by the FAST's high sensitivity and wide field-of-view, allowing for a large HI structure surrounding M101 to be thoroughly detected and analyzed. This led to the identification of a massive interacting galaxy-at-center (IArA) system. More radio telescope observations of M101 and its surrounding region are suggested to monitor its interaction status as it interacts closely with the approaching M101.1-2 galaxy network. This could provide insight into the effects of interaction on a galaxy's molecular gas and its potential to trigger its central activity. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy. Astronomical environments, particularly in comets, are rich in molecular cations whose exceptional brightness under UV to visible light can facilitate the understanding of local plasma environments and the composition of cometary neutral gas. Although molecular cations generally exhibit stronger UV to visible light emission than their neutral counterparts, comprehensive spectral data for cometary environment molecular cions are limited. This study presents newly identified or modified molecular cations from the 1999 Jupiter-family comet Taylor, as well as new spectral series and a revised set of rotational temperature and total cation population assessments for specific species. The findings from the CFHT 12.9-meter telescope and the IUE satellite reveal various additional cometary molecular cations, enhancing the existing database by more than five times and highlighting the significance of precise total cation population measurements. The new data also reveals significantly broader electron emission spectra widths in the CFHT data, suggesting possible interactions between high-speed cometary particles and their surrounding gas as a contributing factor. Furthermore, the new spectral series and more accurate total cation population assessments from the JAXA/DAYA satellite during the flyby of the 2010 comet Hartley 2 provide support for these findings. In this study, we introduce a direct procedure for dividing any element of a global domain (either a number domain or a global function domain) into the sum of the minimal-length squared components. This technique works seamlessly across domains with algebraic or valuation properties. It offers an uncomplicated method for creating new expressions of partial positivity or complete positivity for elements within a domain. Furthermore, it enables the effortless extension of many existing techniques tailored to integer domains to their counterpart domains. Lastly, it enables the creation of novel expressions of partial or complete positivity within domains that were previously inaccessible. For instance, it enables the creation of totally positive elements below any desired level of minimality in the domain of rational numbers, a feat previously unachievable. It also enables the creation of expressions of complete positivity in the field of rational functions over any finite set of variables, a feat previously unachievable. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. Three-dimensional rotating turbulence, once believed to be dominated by stable geostrophic vortices, has recently been observed to support highly dynamic, downscale energy cascades. In a recent study, researchers employed direct numerical simulations within a triply periodic box, artificially suppressing geostrophic vortices to investigate the properties of turbulent flows. These simulations revealed an inertial wave turbulence that conforms to a specific spectrum first described analytically by Galtier in 2003. Interestingly, it was found that the same underlying mechanisms could either give rise to wave turbulence or stable geostrophic vortices depending solely on the initial conditions, thus further establishing the concept of bi-stability in rotating turbulent flows. Moreover, comparing these findings with earlier experiments and simulations yielded excellent agreement, thereby providing a comprehensive validation of the model. Furthermore, analyzing the balance of various turbulent forces revealed their respective dependencies on rotating shear and buoyancy forces, thereby providing a fundamental framework that could be applied beyond the specific parameters studied. In addition, the simulation data were found to conform to a specific anisotropic energy spectrum that could be parameterized by the ratio of the Coriolis and buoyancy forces, thereby implying that the anisotropic nature of wave turbulence could be influenced by the same forces that control the bi-stable nature of the flow. In conclusion, the discovered tripartite bi-stability of rotating turbulent flows, encompassing wave turbulence, stable geostrophic vortices, and potentially other states, was found to provide a plausible explanation for the observed relationships between turbulent energy and forcing parameters observed in numerical simulations and experimental studies. Moreover, it was proposed that this concept of bi-stability could be applied to even more complex systems, such as turbulent flows within bounded domains and turbulent shells, thereby offering a unifying framework for understanding the diverse phenomena observed in rotating turbulent flows.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  However, a more detailed cost-benefit analysis would require a more comprehensive examination of the costs of providing treatment against the associated reductions in future crime.  In addition, the research found no differences in reduced recidivism rates based on the type of mental health treatment provided.  The findings support the inclusion of mental health treatment as part of probation sentences as an effective way to lower future crime rates.  They also suggest that court systems should provide a range of mental health treatments to achieve similar results and initiate the crime reduction process.  The research relies on a large dataset but could be improved by accounting for unobserved factors that influence the decision to provide mental health treatment.  As such, it utilizes an instrumental variable approach based on the distance between the offender and the next nearest provider of the chosen treatment type.  This method assumes that defendants are unaware of all treatment options available to them and that courts make treatment decisions based on the closest available option to the offender's location. A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its minimal computational requirements. Evaluations using publicly available MRI datasets - specifically ACDC and MMWHS - demonstrate that this proposed technique outperforms existing semi-supervised models, with source code available on GitHub.

To handle increased luminosity at the Large Hadron Collider in 2021, the ATLAS collaboration will undertake a major upgrade to the LHC's detector system. This enhancement includes upgrading the Level 1 trigger based on calorimeter data to utilize finer details of the data, courtesy of the Feature EXtractors (FEX) system. Specifically, the jet FEX (jFEX) system aims to enhance jet identification and calculate global variables within an extremely tight latency constraint of under 400 nanoseconds. This will involve six distinct modules, where each module on an ATCA board contains four high-end Xilinx FPGAs to process the data at an astonishing 3.6 terabytes per second rate. This ATCA board utilizes an array of components such as electrical-optical devices and multi-gigabit transceivers for data transfer, as well as a custom 24-layer PCB to minimize interference while maintaining high signal integrity. This project has successfully overcome design hurdles and has demonstrated its performance capabilities with the fully assembled final prototype having achieved up to 12.8 gigabits per second during in-house and CERN integrated testing. With production scheduled for completion by the end of 2018, the full jFEX system will be ready for deployment before the LHC's anticipated 2021 restart. This deployment will mark the largest and most complex custom digital design to be produced by the ATLAS collaboration, with over 500 custom modules manufactured to precision standards by various companies. This achievement highlights the effectiveness of a collaboration between design experts, engineers, and production managers to overcome design hurdles and meet tight deadlines. As such, this project can serve as a model for guiding future design projects involving custom high-speed digital components within the ATLAS collaboration. Furthermore, this design will play a crucial role in enabling the ATLAS detector to take full advantage of the LHC's upgraded performance in 2021, which in turn will greatly increase its detection capabilities for various key physics phenomena. This includes enhancing the ability to detect top-quark pair production, which is expected to result in as many as 1 million top-quark pairs available for study annually. As such, the successful deployment of this system prior to the LHC's 2021 restart will be crucial to fully leveraging its upgraded capabilities. This will be instrumental in positioning ATLAS optimally for the upcoming LHC upgrades that will be delivered by the Future Circular Collider (FCC) study as it initiates its research into potential future upgrades. extends DNR. In experiments and user evaluations, ANR consistently outperformed not

plausibility in both static and dynamic scenes. The significant enhancements
achieved--including more accurate skin, shirt, and hair rendering--greatly simplify
avator-based visual storytelling. To support further research, we are releasing the
code and model variations used for face, hair, and shirt rendering in anticipation

To gain a deeper understanding of the performance and lifespan of materials, 
it's crucial to assess their internal atomic disorder. To this end, we use a unique
approach that leverages graph neural networks to create an interpretable disorder 
metric, effectively capturing local atomic configuration variability across the
solid to liquid phase spectrum. This methodical approach is tested on three
models featuring different disorder levels, including interfaces between solid 
and liquid phases, multi-crystalline microstructures, and grain boundaries, 
using elemental cobalt as a demonstration. Our study shows that our disorder 
metric can be utilized to track the progression of damage under mechanical stress 
and thermal expansion, and serves as a foundational framework for further 
exploration and industry applications. 

Furthermore, our approach enables the distinction between intrinsic barriers 
to movement within materials and those caused by defects, and could be employed 
to investigate the impact of disorder on energy dissipation and storage across 
the phase spectrum. By providing a clear visual representation of local atomic 
arrangements, our disorder metric can be inspected for areas with unpredictable 
behavior, making it an invaluable tool for informed material design. 
Additionally, our study highlights the benefits of combining this approach with
other analysis techniques, such as machine learning force field modeling, to gain 
a more comprehensive understanding of the internal workings of materials. 

Ultimately, this research paves the way for a thorough investigation of the 
interrelations between structure, performance, and durability within materials, 
enabling the development of a universal framework that can be applied across 
the full spectrum of solid-to-liquid phases. 
This study sets the stage for exploring a wide range of materials beyond 
cobalt and could serve as a foundation for various industry applications. 
More broadly, our approach to analyzing internal materials structure can 
be used in conjunction with other simulation techniques to gain a more 
comprehensive understanding of these complex substances.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\eta(\theta)$ and an unknown distribution $G$ as the mixing distribution. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. GMLE's utility in sampling problems is illustrated through simulated examples and real data analysis. The method is particularly useful when maximizing the likelihood function directly is challenging due to the presence of discrete parameters. The proposed approach provides a straightforward solution to estimate $\eta_G$ and this method's efficiency can be evaluated empirically even when the parameters $\theta$ have unknown distributions. Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in high-stakes educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 5 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing.

Given any manifold $M$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses closed range in $C^\infty(M)$. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition. A method for constructing an operator $Q$ that reverses the action of $P$ is also described, with conditions under which this is possible in terms of local boundary conditions. A key aspect of our approach involves utilizing Sobolev spaces rather than smooth functions, enabling the consideration of non-smooth solutions. This is demonstrated through a notable example concerning the Laplace operator on a manifold with irregular boundaries. The approach is purely intrinsic, operating within the framework of smooth functions and without reliance on boundary-defining functions or other machinery associated with partial differential equations. The resulting theory is applicable to any smooth manifold lacking compact components. The approach also yields a straightforward proof that every elliptic differential operator is self-adjoint. The discussion is further illustrated through concrete examples and embeddings. The paper's initial section provides an overview of the underlying concepts, covering elliptic differential operators, their symbols, and the associated Hamilton maps. The middle section explores the implications of closed range operators, the role of surface pressure, and the methods for constructing operators that reverse the action of given operators. The paper's latter section is devoted to specific applications, including Helmholtz decomposition, Reiman's theorem, the role of surface pressure in fluid dynamics, and the consideration of non-smooth solutions on surfaces with irregular boundaries. The paper also includes an appendix discussing the embedding of Sobolev spaces into smooth spaces. The paper's novel approach to elliptic differential operators offers a renewed perspective on established results while also facilitating the consideration of more intricate examples. The method for constructing operators that reverse the action of given operators also enables the consideration of more complex scenarios. The discussion on surface pressure also sheds light on its implications for fluid dynamics, while the consideration of non-smooth solutions on surfaces with irregular boundaries presents new possibilities for analyzing partial differential equations. The paper's approach to Helmholtz decomposition via the method of constructing operators that reverse the action of given operators offers a more flexible and versatile tool compared to earlier methods. The paper's conclusions can be further expanded upon, with the method for constructing operators that reverse the action of given operators having implications for the consideration of quasi-regular operators.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm addresses this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving performance while minimizing communication costs for each device. In this research, the feasibility of utilizing a buffer for federated learning is theoretically proven, and the benefits of asynchronous learning are demonstrated in terms of reduced communication overhead and increased scalability. The proposed FedBuff method is shown to converge globally under certain conditions and outperform existing methods, especially in large-scale environments. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER). Our best outcome involved a 41.6% WER decrease on the Czech ZeroEpic test set with no additional fine-tuning, achieving a score of 137 WER or a 41.6% word error rate on the Czech ZeroEpic test set without any further fine-tuning. Additionally, our approach led to a 8.4 WER reduction on the larger Czech Epic dataset with only alphabet modifications, resulting in a 3820-word-audio-file corpus having a 8.4 WER reduction. Moreover, our technique led to an 8.4 WER reduction on the larger Czech Epic dataset with nothing more than alphabet modifications, resulting in a 37.8 WER. When employing the fine-fine training style on this dataset the method produced a 29.2 WER or a 12.6 WER reduction when compared to baseline models, resulting in a 37.2 WER. All of our models and data are available for public access.

A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. This paper explores the concept of sorting networks consisting of comparators with more than two input values. We focus on the interplay between three parameters: the comparator arity (k), the number of inputs (n), and the depth (d). Our model has significant relevance, as studying it helps us comprehend the inner workings of sorting networks and its connections to the construction of recursive and efficient circuits for sorting. In particular, we aim to identify the lowest required comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with limited depth. Through our research, we found lower bounds on the comparator arity (k) for sorting networks of a specific depth. We found that when the depth is 3, the comparator arity needs to be at least n, and it decreases gradually from n to $\lceil \sqrt{2n} \rceil$ as the number of inputs increases. This discovery was made possible by constructing a new family of sorting networks with comparators of arity $\lceil \sqrt{2n} \rceil$. Additionally, we found that any sorting network with comparators of arity k can be simulated by a network with comparators of arity 2, requiring approximately $k^2$ operations to achieve the same depth. This relationship leads to the conclusion that deep sorting networks with small arity comparators can be costly in terms of the number of operations, which contradicts our earlier findings about k for small depths. As a result, we can conclude that the relationship between k and n at small depths represents a unique phenomenon driven by the fundamental limitations of deep sorting networks. Lastly, we established a lower bound of approximately $\log n$ for the required depth (d) of sorting networks with comparators of arity 2, which further research is intended to refine. The most recent improvement to our research includes a new lower bound of almost $\log n - 1$ for the depth of sorting networks with comparators of arity 2, which will be discussed in greater detail elsewhere. Throughout this research, we expressed lower bounds in terms of implications in the context of straight-line computations. Nevertheless, when necessary, this language will be adjusted to accommodate the more common notation related to circuit complexity. Ultimately, our research on sorting networks has far-reaching applications in the study of circuit complexity, particularly in analyzing lower bounds on depth-based circuit dimensions. In doing so, we are exploring fundamental questions about the intricacies of computational circuits. As a result of this research, we are confident that the findings related to sorting networks will yield valuable insights into the underlying principles governing computational circuits

The method also results in a simplified expression for the potential $m(r)$, eliminating the need to solve the first integral of the Hubble parameter. By applying a suitable choice of covariant gauge, we can directly obtain the relationship between mass and radial volume, giving rise to an equation of state $p(r)$ in a covariant form that depends on mass and radial volume. A notable feature of this approach is that it yields an expression for pressure in terms of mass and radial volume, effectively giving an equation of state $\frac{p(r)}{\rho(r)} = \frac{m(r)}{r^3} - 1$. To illustrate the methodology, we calculated the mass and pressure profiles for a non-rotating isotropic fluid sphere, matching the results predicted by the standard Schwarzschild metric.
