Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To evaluate this approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to new target domains with as little as 200 parallel sentences. Moreover, our approach yields a 0.54 F score on average when fine-tuned without domain-specific parallel data. The code and model weights are available at https://github.com/hubersat/meta-gec.

Current public datasets for re-identifying individuals are limited due to the difficulties associated with labeling them. Despite the abundance of unlabeled surveillance footage that can be easily obtained, it's unclear how to leverage this content to develop useful re-identification representations. Typically, existing methods focused on unsupervised and domain adaptation use publicly available datasets and then apply them to the target domain after removal of the labels, relying heavily on the relatively small size of the training data. This typically involves fine-tuning the method using the target domain's unlabeled training data in order to achieve good results. By building upon recent advancements in large-scale self-supervised image classification that utilize contrastive learning, we propose learning re-identification representations directly from large quantities of unlabeled surveillance video without relying on labels. By utilizing pre-trained pedestrian detection tools and applying contrastive loss at both the image and tracklet levels, we also integrate camera labels that are available free of charge for the principal component analysis step. Our large-scale evaluation of the method on an unlabeled dataset demonstrates significantly superior performance when compared to other methods that do not utilize training data from the target domain. Moreover, we observed a notable increase in accuracy with a larger dataset, thereby highlighting the method's immense potential as the dataset continues to expand in size and number of entries. The method we propose is easily adaptable to any new re-identification domain, thereby making a strong case for the use of unlabeled video in domain adaptation. The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for supervised learning scenarios. DataScope focuses on a wide range of performance metrics, including validation accuracy, fairness, and calibration, enabling users to identify and correct anomalies in the training data. The system incorporates an innovative hybrid algorithm to minimize computation time while providing precise Shapley value estimates and is seamlessly integrated with a user-friendly visualization interface called ScopeView, enabling users to explore and analyze the results easily. The effectiveness of DataScope is demonstrated through its application to three diverse real-world datasets. The system's computational efficiency, combined with its intuitive visualization features, equips data scientists with a powerful tool for diagnosing issues in machine learning models and facilitating the development of more robust and fair models. The DataScope system is currently available online at https://datascopesystem.github.io/. The code for the system can be found at https://github.com/datascopesystem/datascopesystem. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. The emergent team behaviors resulting from our method are remarkably consistent with those obtained from offline learning on high-quality data. Moreover, our technique successfully handles scenarios with distinct distributions of individual trajectories, resulting in more coherent team behavior. V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed.  V392 Persei, which rapidly shrank from 2 days, exhibited early spectral characteristics pointing towards several massive ejections interacting and causing both gamma-ray and optical illumination through shock waves.  This interaction resulted in the generation of very narrow spectral lines, along with the production of polidispersal light and massive gas movements exceeding 6000 km/s.  V392 Persei's massive evolution eventually faded in infrared images from 2020, yet its central white dwarf continue to show signs of activity, with a temperature increase detected in 2020, suggesting that the nova's energy source, an accretion disk, has not been fully eliminated.  V392 Persei, which has an exceptionally short orbital period of 7.98 hours, still exhibits regular brightening and fading, with its most recent outburst commencing in May 2022.  This paper delves into the extraordinary observations of V392 Persei, incorporating both new and previously published data, and offers several possible explanations for the nova's extraordinary behavior.  Its unusual nature makes V392 Persei an intriguing subject for further study in the field of astrophysics.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Simulation results confirm the benefits of this approach in code domain multiplexing applications. Further research potential is highlighted for applications like codebook updating and mobile terminal initiated transmissions.

Humanity has continually sought knowledge, a pursuit amplified over the past century through the vast growth of scientific literature. However, despite employing metrics such as citation counts and impact factors, it remains unclear how a discipline's knowledge amount correlates with productivity, specifically how the value of new knowledge varies with each new advancement. To address this question, researchers compiled 185 million articles spanning 19 disciplines and analyzed the citation networks between authors, essentially mapping the evolution of scientific knowledge within each area. Using both structured and unstructured entropies to analyze the resulting data, they devised the Quantitative Index of Knowledge (KQI), which measures knowledge amount as a disorder difference created by increasing order within the scientific literature. Subsequently, they discovered that the growth of new literature accelerates the growth of new knowledge, but there is an evident slowdown before this threshold. Consequently, disciplines require substantially more knowledge to achieve the same understanding, implying an eventual slowdown of new knowledge development is inevitable. Notably, this analysis may offer valuable insights to policymakers seeking to enhance funding prioritization within scientific disciplines. Moreover, it highlights the challenges faced by interdisciplinary research initiatives that struggle to effectively quantify the knowledge advancements made across multiple areas. Ultimately, this study demonstrates the potential for entropy theory to provide novel frameworks for analyzing complex literature networks in an effort to better understand the evolution of scientific knowledge. This new approach to studying scientific knowledge may also pave the way for predictive models that forecast future knowledge development based on current literature patterns. This, in turn, could enable more effective multi-disciplinary research initiatives that accurately assess their contributions to the advancement of scientific knowledge. This study is a crucial first step in developing these predictive models, as well as a framework that can be applied across multiple disciplines to provide a unified understanding of scientific knowledge evolution. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. In the complex context of an urban intersection with automated and human-driven vehicles, we explore an essential challenge: generating safe pathways for automated vehicles. Our research focuses on preventing rear-end collisions when a connected vehicle's human-driven leader approaches the yellow and red phases of the traffic light. We've developed a predictive control system that can instantly forecast the leader's braking timing and anticipate the connection vehicle's required braking distance. The accuracy of this prediction enables the automated vehicle to adjust its safety trajectory in time for the predicted braking episode. The efficacy of this approach was validated through hundreds of real-world tests, showing that even in situations with high uncertainty, the proposed method can significantly reduce the risk of collisions by up to 35%. Moreover, we found that the severity of the threat can be assessed through the difference in speeds between the leader and follower. The underlying algorithm underlying our predictive controller relies on model predictive control, and we've further optimized this algorithm to minimize the computational burden. The resulting approach can be integrated with various sensing technologies, such as lidar and camera sensors, that provide the necessary input for the system. The potential of this approach to be applied to multiple traffic scenarios is discussed in the conclusion. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
Evaluations revealed little difference between scores obtained by agents in normal and optimized versions of the games. 
As a result, countless testing scenarios and rigorous experimentation become feasible, making it significantly easier to develop and refine agents. 
We created TexGAN, a groundbreaking generative model that generates complex game levels, and successfully applied it to several critical challenges despite prior difficulties in achieving meaningful results. 
We also launched a new version of the game, called MultiWorldExpress, which introduces multiple coexisting worlds and demands agents to prioritize solving one problem over another in a fully integrated game scenario.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition tasks, where LSTMs are typically paired with convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to extract spatial and temporal features from video frames. In this paper, we examine the internal mechanics of LSTMs and propose an alternative architecture called the $micro$-LSTM module, which simplifies the structure of LSTMs by reducing the number of fully connected layers while maintaining comparable performance. We then integrate this new module into a deep neural network called the $micro$-LSTM network, which further refines the LSTM structure to minimize model complexity. This modified network achieves a significant reduction in parameter count compared to traditional LSTMs and CNN+LSTM baselines, realizing a 6-fold decrease in model size with only a minor accuracy drop of 0.5% on the Kinetics dataset. Moreover, this model exhibits improved robustness to random pruning. We also demonstrate the capability of the $micro$-LSTM network to generate action proposals by training the network with class-balanced negative frames, leading to promising results. The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is often expressed through its effect on the mass-to-charge ratio of a particle. Another approach posits its fundamental expression is tied to the self-repulsive properties of a specific particle in long-range interactions. A new, closely related formulation suggests it could be formulated in terms of a particle's self-binding energy being non-negative. This new interpretation becomes particularly insightful within anti-de Sitter space due to its association with a conformal field theory, where a relationship involving the dimension of an operator exists and forms a convex function of the operator's charge under a U(1) symmetry. The novelty of this formulation allows it to bypass any reference to the theory's holographic duality and spacetime locality, thereby strengthening its status as a more fundamental conjecture. We explore the implications of this formulation in various scenarios, including systems of multiple particles where its convictions are maintained, and the scenario is analyzed in detail. We further demonstrate that this new formulation is equivalent to another recently proposed conjecture, known as the Anti-Wolf Conjecture. Moreover, we observe that both this conjecture and the Anti-Wolf Conjecture are valid in systems characterized by a first law of thermodynamics, and we investigate the limitations of this system in the absence of convexity. Finally, we propose that our formulation of the Weak Gravity Conjecture could be linked to another recently proposed theory, known as the Universal Bound Conjecture. A possible relationship between this conjecture and our formulation of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is explored in a scenario involving a system with multiple charges, where both convictions of this formulation and the Universal Bound Conjecture remain valid. However, in the absence of convexity, only the Universal Bound Conjecture remains valid, and we investigate the implications of this relationship for the charged black holes in anti-de Sitter space. Additionally, we discuss potential applications of this relationship to the Big Desert Conjecture. A potential connection between our formulation of the Weak Gravity Conjecture and another recently proposed theory, known as the Stringy Low-Energy Conjecture, is explored in a scenario involving a system with multiple charges, where both convictions of this formulation and the Stringy Low-Energy Conjecture remain valid. This model-space QITE method iteratively expands the model space while maintaining its orthogonality, enabling simultaneous description of multiple states. We enhance model-space QITE by integrating the quantum Lanczos algorithm, which boosts its convergence rate. In simulations, our approach outperforms both standard quantum Lanczos and the folded-spectrum QITE in calculating excited states. We show that spin contamination can be mitigated through an imaginary time propagator shift, efficiently obtaining excited states with specific spin properties without descending into lower-energy states with mixed spins. Additionally, we examine how the degree of unitary approximation within MSQITE influences its results. Our study paves the way for efficient quantum simulation of chemical systems with multiple electrons, necessary for applying quantum chemistry to realistic problems.

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the tight Hilbert function of that ideal. These criteria make use of various submodules of the tight Hilbert function's module counterpart, which are derived from the $e$-function of the ring's Frobenius homomorphism. These submodules also share connections with fractions of the ring's canonical module and its associated graded ring under the Frobenius homomorphism. Implementing these criteria, we establish instances of $F$-rationality on high-dimensional varieties resulting from cone constructions, and we establish relationships between these constructions and various forms of rationality on the original variety. Additionally, we establish a link between the tight Hilbert function's module counterpart and a specific module of the ring's associated graded ring under the Frobenius homomorphism, which enables us to derive new forms of the ring's canonical module. Given this context, our main contribution amounts to a simplified version of our initial criteria for $F$-rationality, which removes an earlier condition that relied on a specific form of the ring's $e$-function. This simplified version highlights the core principles of our approach. Our method also extends to analyzing the ring's Lorenzian property and its associated form factor with respect to the Frobenius homomorphism. The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA Python toolset for Power System Analysis. This model offers adjustable market parameters, agent-specific tactics, and thorough clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market, continuous intra-day trading, redispatch, and imbalance management. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validated the model and explored a redispatch design issue, revealing several key implications. The findings indicate that high-order redispatch designs can minimize costs by almost 50 when the network is highly connected and the redispatch rates are high. The study also showcases the model's capability to assess complex market phenomena and encourage further research by making its source code freely accessible on GitHub. R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the exceptional Lie algebra in fields of characteristic zero. Building on this, we explore a broader scenario involving fields of positive characteristic. Let $\sigma$ be the Galois automorphism of a finite regular extension $K$, and consider the polynomial $f(x) = x^d + a_1x^{d-1} + \cdots + a_d$, with coefficients $a_i \in K$, given by $\mathrm{gcd}(\mathrm{HT}_K(\sigma), d) = 0$. Here, $\mathrm{HT}_K(\sigma)$ represents the Kummer trace field of $\sigma$, obtained through the Kummer theory applied to the field $K$. We demonstrate that for a specific base field $F$, when the characteristic of $F$ does not divide $d$, the Galois group of the $n$-th iterate of the polynomial $f(x)$ over $F$ is isomorphic to an irreducible component of the exceptional Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}_2$, and this occurs for an infinite number of values of $n$. Additionally, we establish that if the base field $F$ satisfies $\mathrm{char}(F) = p$ and $p$ does not divide $d$, then there are infinitely many values of $n$ for which the Galois group of the $n$-th iterate of the polynomial $f(x)$ over $F$ is $2$-transitive and has order $(d^n-1)/p$. This represents a significant expansion on earlier work by J.J. Thomson. Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, but it took until the end of the summer for it to exhibit the temperature and chemical contrasts seen in the southern hemisphere during its own summer. The vortex in the north was found to be surrounded by a strengthening temperature gradient at 78 degrees latitude and displayed a hexagonal shape. This indicates that a particular type of atmospheric wave, previously thought to influence temperatures deep in the planet's atmosphere, has the ability to impact temperatures as high as 300 km above the clouds. The vortex in the north was also found to be surrounded by areas of the atmosphere that were both cool and dense, indicating the presence of massive polar vortices in the past that eventually broke down and were absorbed into the planet's atmospheric circulation. The breakdown of these vortices may have led to the formation of the swirling polar storm patterns seen in the southern hemisphere. The rates of formation and dissolution of the north polar vortex were found to be consistent with the theory that the formation of broad, warm vortices in the polar stratospheres of the outer planets is caused by the accumulation of vortices formed in the planet's troposphere as the atmosphere rotates at different speeds in different latitudes. The application of this research to the study of the outer planets is facilitated by the use of infrared spectroscopy to analyze the concentrations of specific atmospheric compounds, which provide a measure of the rates of formation and dissolution of the polar vortices in these systems. The discovery of the vortex in the north in infrared images of the planet taken during the Galileo spacecraft mission was the result of the activation of one of the spacecraft's instruments, which was set to prioritize the study of this feature in order to better understand its formation and characteristics. The analysis of data from the Galileo spacecraft also revealed that the vortex in the north had begun forming in the late spring of 1995, but it took until the end of the summer for it to exhibit the temperature and chemical contrasts seen in the southern hemisphere during its own summer

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign in the second derivative of variance. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that is relevant for solutions in this particular scenario. This approach also yields an additional result regarding the rate of blow-up. Another contribution of this paper is the establishment of an optimal lower bound for the energy required for solutions to collapse in a finite time. This is achieved through the development of a new approach, incorporating a different type of variance measure that takes into account the specifics of the nonlinear term. This new approach also provides a means to determine the blow-up criterion in a more direct manner. Lastly, this method may be applied to investigate the blow-up properties of related equations. In this case, it is demonstrated that solutions with negative energy will collapse within a finite time period, and an optimal lower bound on the energy required for this blow-up is equal to half of the critical power. This new approach to studying the Schrödinger equation can also be applied to related equations, such as the Klein-Gordon equation, under similar conditions. However, it is important to note that these results are optimal in the sense that they are achieved with equality in the relevant inequalities used to establish the lower bounds. Additionally, this approach allows us to demonstrate the concavity of a modified variance measure, which has a relevant derivative that is non-increasing for solutions with negative energy. This increase in the rate of concavity results in a faster rate of blow-up in this scenario. It is also shown that this approach can be applied to a broader class of nonlinearities, provided that the nonlinearity depends on the solution in a subcritical manner. Lastly, this approach yields an additional result regarding the rate of blow-up, which can be interpreted as indicating that the solution develops a singularity of a specific type, characterized by a frequency that increases over time

The manner in which the surface of materials is terminated has significant implications for their physical characteristics. Investigating the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films necessitates a deep comprehension of the effect of surface termination.  Our studies achieved varying surface terminations in V$_2$O$_3$ films using low energy electron diffraction and photoemission spectroscopy, which led us to a key finding - depending on the terminations, the metal-insulator transition may be significantly impeded or totally hindered near the surface due to distinct variations in electron distribution at different layers and altered screening length as compared to the bulk.  A considerable reorganization of spectral weight across the metal-insulator transition has also been observed, with an observable transfer of spectral weight across the entire energy scale from the high-binding energy regime to the low-binding energy regime, in contrast to our findings of unconserved total spectral weight across the metal-insulator transition, which indicates a failure in applying'sum rules of spectral weight',  a hallmark of systems with strong correlations.  Our data suggest that changes in hybridization, effective carrier density, lattice volume, and spin degrees of freedom, possibly all interlinked with the change in electron correlations across the metal-insulator transition, are responsible for such a shift in spectral weight.  Furthermore, our research demonstrates that in V$_2$O$_3$, the metal-insulator transition is fundamentally driven by correlation between electrons, with the effect of these interactions playing a pivotal role in determining the transition's occurrence.  Our studies also offer a greater insight into understanding the electronic structure of systems with strong correlations, underscoring the significance of factoring in surface-related effects while interpreting experimental data collected through surface-sensitive techniques such as resistivity measurement, as this has significant implications for comprehending physical characteristics. We find a specific scaling of Bose-Einstein condensation fractions in ground states that can be used to analyze quasi-condensation in weakly coupled quantum double dark-soliton states. We first demonstrate the precise time-dependent density profile of a quantum double dark-soliton state via the Bethe ansatz method. Next, we derive an effective macroscopic wave function for these states by calculating the amplitude and phase of field operator matrix elements. In the weak-coupling regime, these profiles resemble those of dark solitons. We then precisely examine the interaction between two notches in quantum double dark-soliton states. Observations suggest that quasi-condensation may play a significant role in quantum double dark-soliton dynamics, and that states with high condensate fractions should be well-represented by a quasi-condensation state that follows a mean-field model. Conversely, states with low condensate fractions might be better described by breaking down the double dark-soliton into two solitary waves that interact in a weak sense. One notable example of the latter scenario involves initial conditions that support two distinct condensate phases. Finally, we discover that deep-notch states with high condensate fractions exhibit distinct scaling and near-equilibrium behavior at longer times. In contrast, systems with low condensate fractions display different scaling and may approach equilibrium more quickly. These findings highlight the intricate non-equilibrium behavior of quantum double dark-soliton states. Moreover, they reveal the significance of quasi-Bose-Einstein condensation in these dynamics. This, in turn, could lead to a deeper comprehension of quantum dynamics in other systems characterized by multiple coexisting condensate phases. Consequently, the proposed explanation for our results remains speculative and would require validation through additional theories or simulations. We create a linearisation functor for full linearisation that transforms a graded bundle of degree k into a k-fold vector bundle. Our analysis defines the image of the full linearisation functor, resulting in a subcategory of k-fold vector bundles. These vector bundles are equipped with symmetric morphisms associated with the symmetric group Sn. A significant observation arises in the degree 2 scenario, where this added structure leads to the concept of symplectic double vector bundles. These have an opposite relationship with metric double vector bundles. The process of full linearisation is also used to extend N-manifolds and a superising method for a graded bundle. Consequently, this produces a natural extension of the full linearisation procedure for vector bundles of higher grades. Furthermore, our approach leads to the identification of a key transformation, describing how the full linearisation of a graded bundle is related to the full linearisation of a vector bundle that contains it. This relationship serves as a linearisation of the inclusion map. By utilising this relationship, we make use of known results about full linearisation of vector bundles to derive results about full linearisation of graded bundles. The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The knowledge gained through phase information also leads to accurate reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental data, a level of precision that cannot be achieved with other methods. Our approach provides a useful data analysis tool, offering a beneficial impact on x-ray quantum optics and M\"ossbauer spectroscopy that employs synchrotron radiation. Moreover, this approach may be applied to other systems that involve light-matter interactions and result in spectra displaying energy shifts and broadening. A simulation featuring a system with two-level components illustrates the algorithm's capability to accurately reconstruct both spectral components' lifetimes and concentrations. The implementation of this algorithm as a user-friendly data analysis tool is also described, along with the potential it holds for enhancing research in the mentioned fields. The algorithm has been made publicly accessible to promote the development of new applications that could arise from its use in fields related to x-ray quantum optics and quantum systems that interact with x-rays. The publicly accessible data set presented here is an example of the algorithm's performance and is accompanied by a paper that explains the associated data processing steps. The algorithm and related research are also discussed in an accompanying video. The algorithm is now available online.

This research provides a method for assessing the fundamental error thresholds of quantum error correcting codes, independently of any specific decoding strategies. We investigate a model for fractured porous media that incorporates varying fracture properties. Unlike traditional models, where fractures are categorized as either conductive or blocking based on permeability, this model considers the probability of a fracture's conductivity. This approach is similar to others suggested by Amar and Agueh, and Duray, respectively. Specifically, we analyze a single-phase flow model that involves evaluating the probability of a fracture's conductivity as fluid moves through the media. By applying the method of random walk, we analyze the scalability of the model and subsequently establish the asymptotic behavior of the model's scalar field as the number of fractures increases. However, our results indicate that the model's convergence is impacted by the probability distribution of fracture conductivity. Moreover, we establish the relationship between the model's conductivity and its corresponding scaling exponent. Finally, we compare our model's performance to that of the Weiss and Zhai model, and discuss its applicability to actual fracture media. Keywords: fractured porous media; permeability; scaling exponent; random walk systems; pullback attractors. Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online. Leveraging this code, along with the accompanying simulations, can help ensure the reliability of statistical inferences in cognitive science projects. The study's findings and proposed solutions for addressing the identified challenges are expected to benefit a broader range of statistical applications, extending beyond the realm of cognitive science. The developed framework is also expected to facilitate collaborative evaluation of Bayes factor analysis performance across different research areas, thereby sparking further methodological developments in cognitive science and beyond. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, resulting in novel relations and a comprehensive set of discourse indicators that are uniquely categorized into nine groups based on their inter-sentence connections. This approach yields 18 distinct indicators that were previously unidentified in large linguistic corpora and further research is needed to define their grammatical characteristics including their usage, positioning, and potential collocations. Some of these indicators hold promising potential for applications in text Inference, such as predicting relationships between unsentenced character mentions in a novel context. Moreover, this work introduces a newly annotated dataset that includes 60 character mentions with their inter-statement semantic connections, enabling the development of models that can infer the relationships between statements about characters. The existing discourse indicators were found to fail in predicting these new relations, demonstrating a need for more research in this area and the potential advancement of models through the identification of novel indicators. This innovative method of discourse indicator prediction is an exploratory study that is open to further development and invites participation from researchers to both use this approach to discover new indicators and to contribute to the existing catalog of indicators by labeling them in relevant contexts where they appear. We investigate the properties of a negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under high-temperature and vacuum conditions.  By combining optical detection of magnetic resonance (ODMR) and optical spectroscopy, we studied the spin resonances and radiative transitions at high temperatures.  Our findings indicate that increasing temperature leads to a reduction in the intensity of visible and infrared light emitted from the diamond, as well as a decrease in the frequencies of ODMR resonance and a shift in the emission line towards longer wavelengths.  By comparing our measured data to theoretical predictions, specifically from the Mott-Seitz model, we estimated that a significant nonradiative energy barrier has a height of approximately 0.24 electron volts.  In addition, we observed that at high temperatures, there are multiple emission peaks, which we attribute to the presence of two distinct nitrogen-vacancy centers in our diamond sample.  Our research demonstrates the usefulness of combining ODMR and optical measurements in analyzing the physical properties of nitrogen-vacancy centers within diamond.  We believe that our findings will contribute to the development of highly sensitive diamond magnetometry systems capable of operating effectively in thermally challenging environments.  Furthermore, we suggest potential applications for our technique in studying the properties of nitrogen-vacancy centers within resonating cavities or within biological systems, where temperature fluctuations are significant.  By manipulating the properties of these centers, we may be able to enhance their optical characteristics or change their spectral lines depending on the surrounding environment.  Ultimately, this research paves the way for improving the performance of diamond-based optical and magnetic sensing technologies.  We also examine the theoretical limitations of using diamond-based optical sensing systems, where we note that reducing noise from optical readouts can improve sensitivity.  We further investigate the possibility of controlling NV\^- spin resonance frequencies in response to changes in temperature, pressure, or chemical environment by altering the surrounding host material through laser heating of embedded optical cavities, where we estimate that a well-designed cavity can change the resonance frequency by over 10 MHz under moderate heating conditions. The backpropagation algorithm, though effective for training neural networks, has a significant drawback: it mandates the sharing of weights. This presents an insurmountable challenge to modeling brain function accurately. A new algorithm developed for two-layer networks overcomes this hurdle by doing away with explicit error calculation and backpropagation altogether. This algorithm remarkably translates to a neural network that closely mimics the brain's connectivity pattern and learning processes, and experiments show it rivals the performance of backpropagation across various datasets. Moreover, the algorithm is versatile and can be applied to transductive domains. The underlying theory provides valuable insights into the conditions necessary for an algorithm to be applicable to untrained data. The algorithm is called Branchless Policy Gradient, and it is now available as an open-source package. This could potentially lead to significant advancements in machine learning, given its potential to optimize a wide range of functionals. A new implementation of the Hartree-Fock (HF) method has been developed to efficiently achieve robust convergence for well-behaved central potentials. The method converts HF equations into a generalized eigenvalue problem by using a B-spline basis in a finite-size box and incrementally increases the strength of electron-electron interactions. The accuracy and performance of this implementation were verified through a series of benchmark tests, involving calculations of atoms and ions with central Coulomb potentials, electron gas confined by harmonic and uniform potentials, and alkali-metal clusters modeled by the jellium model. The results were compared to established methods, showing good agreement in terms of convergence patterns and energies for atoms and ions, electron energy and density for harmonic confinement, and dipole polarizabilities for sodium clusters, aligning closely with theoretical and experimental expectations. The developed framework is anticipated to contribute positively to the advancement of computational multiconfiguration wave functions methods. The implementation of this approach is made freely accessible via the MRCC 2018.01 program. The source code has been thoroughly reviewed as part of its development, in line with the guidelines established by the Research Institute for Advanced Computing (RIAC). The code has been tested on a range of multi-core computers and high-performance clusters. We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, providing a critical connection, and also establish an independent result regarding the convexity of geodesic balls under the Riemannian quotient geometry. Lastly, we verify our theoretical findings with numerical experiments using both synthetic and real datasets. The results demonstrate the efficacy of the plain gradient method for this matrix optimization problem. Notably, our analysis offers a theoretical justification for a recent success of plain gradient descent in practice. Our experiments examine how the geometric structure of force-free rigid swimmers interacts with different fluid properties: Newtonian and viscoelastic (specifically Boger fluids).  By changing the swimmer body and its helical tail dimensions, our findings reveal that viscoelastic properties' influence is largely dependent on the swimmer design, potentially amplifying its speed by as much as five times, or instead, diminish its velocity by a similar amount, or leave its locomotion mostly unaffected. Analysis and corresponding theoretical modeling suggest that viscoelastic forces on these swimmers are dictated by a similar'snowman effect' found with linear swimmers, in which asymmetry in the swimmer causes an elasticity-related force that may aid or impede propulsion. Moreover, our results demonstrate that in viscoelastic fluids, force-free swimming propulsion can be understood through a simple "elastic couple" mechanism, in which the interplay between different swimmer components drives traction forces that can accelerate the swimmer forward or backward. This research into viscoelastic swimming also raises intriguing questions about the possible existence of efficient force-free swimmers designed to take advantage of viscoelastic properties in elastic fluids.  Ultimately, our study paves the way for a broader examination of property-dependent swimmers that adapt their movement to respond effectively to varied fluid characteristics. The growing threat landscape in cybersecurity demands increased vigilance, 
wherein existing vulnerability information can be utilized to enhance knowledge 
and predictive analytics for risk mitigation. By structuring security 
knowledge as an ontology, anomaly detection and threat assessment become 
more feasible, along with other security operations. Nevertheless, 
traditional methods of enriching ontologies based on natural language 
processing and machine learning are hampered by issues in extracting contextual 
conceptual relationships from text. Therefore, sequential Deep Learning models 
capable of navigating through the semantic structures in language and pinpointing 
embedded security vulnerabilities are needed. Our approach employs a model 
called Bidirectional LSTM (Bi-LSTM) that simultaneously processes the left 
and right contextual features of each word to identify the underlying threats 
embedded in security vulnerability reports. By utilizing a dense ontology, 
we further refine the extraction of security concept relationships with features 
derived from the Bi-LSTM model and multi-task learning. As a result, our 
approach achieves a notable 77.8% accuracy in detecting hidden security 
concept relationships and thereby enriches the ontology with more meaningful 
concept relationships that are applicable across different domains. Moreover, 
our approach demonstrates the capacity to identify rare concepts with an 
F-score of 62.3%, indicating substantial potential for its utilization in 
the large-scale extraction of security concepts from text. However, the current 
approach is hindered by its reliance on pre-existing taxonomies and the use 
of dense ontologies, which limits its ability to extract distinct security 
concept instances. Consequently, further research is needed to address these 
challenges and overcome difficulties in handling ambiguous and contextually 
modulated concepts with subtle conceptual differences. Nonetheless, our 
initial findings offer a crucial starting point for the application of 
Deep Learning models to enhanced security concept recognition and the 
subsequent enhancement of security knowledge representation systems. As such, 
our approach can serve as a foundation for the advancement of cutting-edge 
methods and the improvement of a crucial aspect of security knowledge 
representation, namely the recognition of security concepts with high 
accuracy. Consequently, one notable achievement resulting from this work is 
the public dissemination of a high-accuracy Bi-LSTM-based security concept 
extraction model. Furthermore, all experimentally derived data utilized in this 
research is available for public access, thereby facilitating the 
progression of related research projects. Ultimately, this research aims to 
lay the groundwork for the collaborative development of innovative methods

The Ising model falls within the domain of equilibrium statistical mechanics, in contrast, the voter model represents a system out of equilibrium. Our analysis focuses on an opinion formation model, a hybrid of Ising and voter agents, with concentrations of $p$ and $1-p$. Notably, even though detailed balance is violated for $p<1$, it has been shown that on a fully connected graph the stationary state average magnetization for any $p>0$ follows the same equation as for the pure Ising model ($p=1$). This behavior is further confirmed by numerical simulations; however, the observed equivalence between pure Ising and hybrid models is limited to magnetization. While susceptibility diverges at the same temperature as magnetization, its values differ. Moreover, although both models exhibit ferromagnetic ordering at sufficiently low temperatures, this ordering can be achieved at significantly higher temperatures for the pure Ising model ($p=1$). Simulations on a random graph also reveal that the model can display competing order parameters, leading to spin glass-like behavior in the stationary state. This competition arises due to the coexistence of Ising domains in separate components of the network. Thus, the interaction between component Ising systems can result in distinct, non-Ising stationary states. Additionally, the temperature at which these competing order parameters emerge can serve as an indicator of the network's connectivity. In conclusion, hybrid models representing opposing phases of equilibrium and out-of-equilibrium dynamics can exhibit unexpected stationary states that resemble nonequilibrium phase transitions. Thus, they provide a potential tool for analyzing average opinion and its connection to individual beliefs. Lastly, our research demonstrates that even a minimal combination of Ising and voter agents can yield a level of complexity associated with more intricate spin glass and network models. This level of complexity gives rise to unique, nonequilibrium stationary states competing with an Ising stationary state. These competing states can be understood as a result of separate components of the network exhibiting their own unique stationary states. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the temperatures at which these competing order parameters emerge can serve as an indicator of the network's connectivity. In conclusion, our research offers a potential approach to analyzing average opinion and its connection to individual beliefs within opinion formation models. The COVID19 virus is spread through contaminated droplets expelled by infected individuals when they cough, sneeze, speak or breathe. Understanding how these virus-carrying droplets behave under changing environmental conditions is essential to tracking the infection's spread. To investigate this, we examine the movement of evaporating droplets influenced by gravity and varying weather, observing how they change in size until either settling on the ground or breaking down into small particles that can linger in the air. Our analysis reveals significant impacts of humidity and temperature on evaporation, with large droplets falling due to gravity's dominance despite evaporative losses and smaller droplets suspended in the air due to diffusive forces. The size of intermediate droplets is highly dependent on weather conditions and is critical to infection spread, underscoring the need for physical distancing and making face masks essential. Finally, our research suggests that surface disinfection can reduce but may not entirely eliminate the risk of infection from residual virus particles. Visualizations of our findings are available as supplementary material.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalence for a specific subclass of weighted directed trees. Moreover, this subclass excludes the phenomenon of symbolic vs. ordinary series equivalence seen in directed trees. Furthermore, the study also identifies the condition under which the symbolic and ordinary power series of oriented line segments exhibit distinct series. Additionally, the study demonstrates that the symbolic and ordinary power series of oriented stars exhibit equivalent series, and this series is akin to that of the corresponding co-directed star. Lastly, the study presents relationships between the symbolic and ordinary power series of oriented complete paths, as well as oriented complete trees, showing various equivalence relationships. This type of model has been proposed as a simple quantum system for testing various multimatrix quantum field theory formulations. By calculating the expectation values of various observables, we demonstrate their consistent behavior under the SU($N$)/U($N$) symmetry group for any finite $N$. Our findings further reveal the emergence of an effective large-$N$ continuum limit model, characterized by a continuous Wilkeberger function that is distinct for both SU($N$) and U($N$). A striking feature observed in our plaquette model is an unexpected discontinuity in the large-$N$ limit, leading to a separation of its large-$N$ spectrum into two groups with different scaling behaviors. The existence of an intermediate energy gap can also be identified by analyzing the model's thermodynamic properties. A comparison with related work involving double-Coleman-Mosaic-type unitary matrix models has been included in our study. There, we highlight the failures in establishing a continuous large-$N$ limit for those models, as well as the failure in validating their claimed universal scaling behaviors. Instead, we found that those models exhibit large-$N$ scale separations and model-specific scaling behaviors governed by mass parameters. Our research demonstrates that only models with massless behavior at large $N$ can realistically replicate the predicted large-$N$ continuum limit physics. Following the successful use of activation clipping, we have developed a prototype to demonstrate that range control can serve as a trustworthy error detection and prevention method for classifier CNNs, specifically against common memory errors leading to data corruption. We evaluate the accuracy of various CNNs, including the influential VGGNet, under controlled range constraints and compare them to their unclipped counterparts. We also examine the effect of range limits on error types, network architectures, and the potential for these findings to inform more substantial reliability interventions. The European Central Bank's definition of clearing or netting has far-reaching effects on a nation's economy, affecting transactions and business-to-business interactions. Essentially, netting represents a different method for companies to make payments to each other, involving an agreement in which each party deducts debts owed from debts owed to it. By combining the debts between parties, the usual payment process can be substituted with a direct settlement. In this research, we present a suite of graph algorithms capable of generating optimal netting solutions suitable for a national economy's scale, yielding efficient results in a timely manner. Our analysis utilizing Romanian Ministry of Economy invoice data demonstrates that conventional graph algorithms can still tackle highly significant contemporary challenges effectively. In this particular case study, finding the optimal netting solution for the country's debt took as little as 43 milliseconds. The developed algorithms can be found in the attached source code, ready for use in clearing and netting applications. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words and their clusters. Our model processes each word's character-level representation and its corresponding knowledge-based attributes to produce a rich feature vector. This approach significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods according to multiple evaluation metrics. Moreover, our results demonstrate substantial gains when using additional knowledge-based attributes and demonstrate the potential to leverage various other knowledge bases beyond the specific bases used in this research. Our work paves the way for enhanced cross-lingual knowledge sharing and a deeper understanding of how words are perceived as entities within their respective language spaces. Our construction of the multilingual semantic space, along with the features and methods employed, is made freely accessible for further research and applications. It is available online at https://github.com/zll989/mmspace. The initial production measurement of various particles such as pions, kaons, 
protons and $\phi$ mesons in midrapidity for mid-central ( centrality 33-44) 
LHC collisions is analyzed. This analysis is based on published data from the 
ALICE experiment at the LHC, using lead-lead collisions at an energy of 2.76 TeV. 
It finds that the radial flow pattern explained by the Fourier flow coefficients 
$v_2$, $v_3$ and $v_4$ depends on the charged-particle count in a way that differs 
substantially between different particle types. Furthermore, a larger initial 
viscous fluid profile is indicated, and the obtained data are compared with 
predictions from various model simulations, including several calculations of 
viscous fluid dynamics and particle production models that account for initial 
conditions and hadronization. The comparison shows that most of these models 
fail to replicate the observed data, with the main discrepancies arising from 
underestimated radial flow in some models and overestimated flow in others. 
The results also suggest that the initial condition differences between models 
are relatively minor, with the primary factors influencing radial flow patterns 
being associated with hadronization and viscosity. Ultimately, the findings 
highlight the importance of exploring radial flow patterns in high-energy 
collisions as a tool for gaining insight into the properties of the quark-gluon 
plasma and the hadronization process. The published data also provide a 
relevant reference for ongoing and future studies, such as those in the LHC 
with lead-lead collisions at 5 TeV and the NICA with heavy ions at 11 GeV.

The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly accelerated the study of dialogue state tracking, yet contains considerable annotation errors that significantly impede the robust training of models. The recent releases of refined datasets, MultiWOZ 2.1 to 2.4, are not entirely noise-free, especially in the training subset, rectifying them proves costly. Instead of addressing the issues of annotation quality in the current datasets, we develop a versatile framework named ASSIST that employs a diverse range of strategies to counter label noise in dialogue state tracking. This framework is tissue-friendly and allows for the simultaneous improvement of models on multiple datasets with minimal extra cost. We introduce a null model that trains high-performing dialogue state tracking models on mixed labels, resulting in an ash cloud model that is simple to train and serves as the foundation for several significant advancements, including an auxiliary model that switches between different training labels. The ASSIST framework, which combines the null and ash cloud models via an auxiliary self-correcting mechanism, achieves a notable 10.48% improvement in overall score on the clean MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset, outperforming the current state of the art by a significant margin. Moreover, the ASSIST framework is unaffected by the type of dataset, and a limited evaluation on the annotations of newly collected datasets demonstrates its potential to handle real-world challenges. In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. A tentative proposal is made to mitigate this constraint by introducing a theoretical model that could potentially address the challenge of modeling riots in closed spaces. A major shortcoming of this project is acknowledged, as no rigorous testing of its proposed modifications to the epidemiological model has been conducted. Nevertheless, this initiative aims to stimulate discussion and gather input from other researchers before exploring further developments in modeling urban unrest. However, the predictions are less accurate when considering all galaxies, which may be due to limitations in modeling other factors that influence the line measurement. Given its sensitivity to star formation rate and minimal impact of dust, the Brackett-$ eta$ line could be a valuable indicator for measuring the star formation rates of galaxies. In high-scale theories involving extra neutrino states, the standard low-energy matrix used for neutrino interactions may be invalid. We reevaluate how much this matrix can deviate from its expected unitary form, taking into account both direct experimental limits and indirect theoretical constraints from newly calculated closure terms. Specifically, we examine how much the currently allowed neutrino mixing parameters can vary, assuming either a typical "desert" geometry of extra dimensions or the scenario of large extra dimensions as described in the ADD model. Our analysis shows that in both scenarios, some neutrino mixing matrix elements can differ significantly from their expected unitary values, with differences of up to 1% needed to fit observed data. However, in the case of large extra dimensions, we find that neutrino oscillation parameters could be affected at a much greater level of up to 100%, but only if certain very tightly controlled conditions regarding both particle energies and experimental detection settings are met. We also derive a straightforward, model-independent formula for predicting how much neutrino state purity will decrease when observing neutrinos in experiments such as Tevatron, and suggest additional methods for deriving tighter constraints on high-scale theories based on data from these experiments. Finally, we suggest that future particle colliders have the potential to significantly increase their ability to detect neutrino state purity, potentially leading to much tighter constraints on high-scale theories. Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models using learning techniques, often rely on recurrent models that fuse multimodal information and process signals, although they have difficulty training and efficiency limitations. This study proposes an external memory attention learning-based VIO framework, capable of efficiently combining the data from both the camera and inertial sensors for state estimation, and demonstrates the algorithm's effectiveness by accurately estimating the pose in various challenging scenarios. Moreover, to enhance the algorithm's practicality, we also investigated its robustness when different sensor data sampling rates were used, and found that the proposed method successfully handled various sampling rates efficiently. To validate and compare the algorithm, we created the first public dataset containing real-world data recorded from a mobile robot equipped with both camera and inertial sensors, and successfully demonstrated the algorithm's performance on this dataset. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems. Furthermore, we predict that SHOWS will exhibit unusually robust anomalous Hall and magnetization. This breakthrough could lead to significant advancements in topological quantum electronics and potentially enable the development of topological magnets capable of supporting topological magnons. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their models. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student model to excel in a specific task without relying on a large, diverse dataset. To achieve this, the FedSA approach employs a custom method to calculate the aggregate function, ensuring that the student model can effectively utilize the information provided by the teachers. To evaluate the FedSA approach, we conducted comprehensive experiments using the IMDB text classification dataset and observed a substantial improvement in model performance compared to alternative federated learning methods. Moreover, we found that feeding the input text directly to the student model, rather than employing a neural processor like BERT, leads to better performance when using FedSA. To demonstrate the FedSA approach in action with more realistic models, we conducted additional experiments utilizing the BERT dataset and observed a notable improvement in model performance. Notably, when using the BERT dataset, feeding the input text directly to the student model resulted in poor performance; however, incorporating BERT yielded better performance than using BERT in isolation. Lastly, we successfully applied the FedSA approach to create a robust model for the classification of abusive offline content, achieving a notable improvement in model performance compared to alternative federated learning methods. The code and data utilized in this research are openly accessible at https://github.com/AlineRAZMIN/FedSA. The paper's findings have been posted on the arXiv platform under the identifier arXiv:2203.01746 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.01746). The paper's authors have also presented its research findings in the FedLearn 2021 workshop, which was hosted by the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM). The paper has undergone peer review with two reviewers. The paper's research has been supported by the Science Foundation Ireland (SFI) through the grant JFC. Approximately a decade ago, the existence of grid cells within the medial entorhinal cortex of rats was first identified. Researchers initially hypothesized that grid cells' unique firing patterns, linked to periodic locations within the environment, might serve as a spatial metric. Subsequent studies have since revealed significant new insights into grid cells' properties and the neural networks surrounding the parahippocampal-hippocampal region. As a result, existing models of grid cells require revision and refinement. This survey seeks to present an extensive summary of grid cell research conducted over the past decade, covering key aspects including grid cells' functionality and responsiveness to external stimuli as well as their underlying neural foundations. Furthermore, a comprehensive review of hypothesized theories explaining grid cells' functions and supportive evidence will be provided. Finally, potential future areas of research within this field are outlined. These reviews position me to tackle a previously unaddressed topic: a computational model that generatively devolops grid cells' characteristic firing patterns through a self-organizing process rooted in grid cells' intrinsic neural connections. This model showcases how grid cells' spatial metric properties arise naturally as a consequence of entorhinal cortex grid cells' recurrent excitatory interactions, unaffected by external spatial cues. As such, it offers a neural theory of grid cells' origins and suggests that grid cells' functional role in spatial navigation might be attributed to their underlying biophysical properties ensuring persistent coverage of environmental locations during exploration. Notably, this model anticipates the coexistence of grid cells with distinct scaling dimensions within a single neural network, a prediction amenable to experimental confirmation. As such, it is reasonable to contend that this model may serve as a foundation for investigating various grid cells subpopulations within diverse animal models and environmental settings. As we look ahead to future grid cells research, key considerations include integrating this model with existing approaches to spatial navigation, reconciling it with proposed theories of grid cells formation, and exploring its implications for understanding grid cells related disorders. Ultimately, this survey of grid cells research lays the groundwork for a comprehensive discussion of my proposed model and its potential to contribute meaningfully to this field. As such, it is my hope that this survey will spark engaging dialogue with other experts within this field.

Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slower equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this regime emerges during the main sequence and persists in slow rotators, it may influence the generation of magnetic fields through the dynamo process. Considering the possibility of alpha-quenching in these stars, we explore how magnetic dynamos might operate across various rotation rates. Given the effect of the Rossby number on turbulent mixing and the alpha-effect, we suggest that quenching could accelerate the transition from the slow and rapid rotation regimes in solar-type stars, potentially making it more challenging for anti-solar rotators to maintain their distinctive differential rotation patterns. As a result, we anticipate that anti-solar differential rotation will only survive in low-Angelo criteria rotating stars with minimal alpha quenching. This could have significant implications for global magnetic dynamos in solar-type stars. For example, anti-solar rotators might struggle to generate sufficient alpha-effect to sustain their differential rotation patterns, potentially leading to a decrease in alpha-effect strength and, consequently, a reduction in global magnetic field strength. This theory is supported by an examination of solar-type stars with generated magnetic fields, revealing a distinct class characterized by weak magnetic fields and slow rotation. These findings suggest that the surface magnetic field strength in solar-type stars may ultimately depend on internal differential rotation patterns, potentially influencing global magnetic dynamos through the alpha omega process. Consequently, we propose that quasi-stable magnetic cycles in solar-type stars could serve as a critical component of global magnetic dynamos, where short-period cycle variability might be an integral feature of these stars. We analyze the rank growth of elliptic curves from rational numbers to quartic extensions in the Galois groups $S_4$ and $A_4$, and investigate how rank varies in different quartic fields for a fixed elliptic curve. Notably, under specific conditions, we establish the existence of an infinite number of $S_4$ quartic extensions where the rank of an elliptic curve doesn't increase compared to its rank over the rational numbers. This achievement is made possible by our development of methods to manage the 2-Selmer rank of elliptic curves within certain quadratic fields, enabling control of the rank in families of $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions. This research is initiated by a question posed by David Chouquitt. The work includes an extension of Fouvry-Kopylov's results and contributes to understanding the Mordell-Weil groups of elliptic curves and their growth in rank over number fields. The research specifically examines the behaviour of the rank of $x^4 + ax^2 + b^2 = 0$ when b is squared, an equation with similar characteristics to the ones studied by David, Chouquitt, and his collaborators. The work also enables future research to tackle additional questions raised in the introductory section by considering more general polynomials and constructing genus 1 and 2 algebraic curves using 4th roots of rational functions, thereby facilitating the generation of elliptic curves with specific rank properties in quartic fields. The research is supported by an appendix containing newly developed methods that might be useful in other contexts. The work involves the use of localisation of endoscopes, particularly in 2-Selmer ranks within quadratic fields, allowing the management of 2-Selmer ranks in families of Galois groups $S_4$ and $A_4$, which is an innovation in the research. The paper is also accompanied by an appendix highlighting newly developed techniques that could be applied in other research contexts.
