A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis approach, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. With these guidelines, we determine the model's parameter space, identifying the feasible ranges for the adiabatic index, viscosity coefficient, and other parameters. A key aspect of our analysis is the determination of parameters that influence the model's behavior at different cosmological scales. Furthermore, we investigate the model's predictions for various cosmological transitions, including the Big Bang transition, the matter-dark energy transition, and the dark energy-like behavior at high energies. Through numerical calculations, we assess the model's predictions for various cosmological transitions, finding that it meets the observed cosmological transitions and behaves like dark energy at present. The model predicts a viscous fluid behavior during the Big Bang transition and during the matter-dark energy transition, which aligns with certain observational limits. The model also forecasts that the dark energy equation of state will continue to diminish throughout the universe's history. With the model's parameters set to their default values, we simulate the associated particle physics model, revealing that the model produces scalar particles with negative energies that could be responsible for the dark energy phenomenon. This implies that the model provides a theoretical framework that could address the cosmological dark energy challenge. Through numerical simulations, we investigate the model's predictions for the gravitational wave spectrum and the primordial power spectrum, finding that it conforms to the principles of the Planck satellite mission. Consequently, this model offers a theoretical framework that could address the universe's dark energy challenge. In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a vital preparation for a future where lifelong learning and skill acquisition will be increasingly essential.  Unfortunately, many school systems are undermining curiosity by focusing solely on test-taking.  However, educators are seeking innovative ways to spark curiosity in their students, as they recognize the importance of lifelong learning in an ever-changing world.  One understudied aspect of curiosity is its link to peer interactions.  Our study introduces a pioneering theoretical framework that combines cognitive and social factors to explain how peers can inspire curiosity through various observable behaviors and underlying states.  This framework distinguishes between two components of curiosity: personal factors and peer influences.  Our data analysis confirmed a significant, positive relationship between these factors and curiosity levels.  Additionally, our results highlighted key behaviors that contribute to curiosity in learning environments.  Building on these findings, we developed practical strategies that can be incorporated into learning technologies to identify, stimulate, and guide curiosity in real-time.  Our work is a significant step towards designing more effective learning technologies that recognize and respond to curiosity in collaborative learning settings and also paves the way for the development of computer support for other important cognitive and emotional skills.  We believe that our research will motivate further theoretical and empirical investigations in this area and is relevant to all designers of collaborative learning technologies who strive to give due consideration to the diverse psychological aspects of learners.  We are confident that our study will serve as a foundation for exploring other vital cognitive and emotional aspects of learning, such as motivation, attention, metacognition, and emotional intelligence in collaborative learning settings. We are confident that our study will be of great interest to you and that you will find it thought-provoking.  We are eager to engage in a dialogue with you and address any questions you may have.  We would be thrilled if you could join us in exploring this important aspect of learning and consider contributing to the ongoing discussion through a response to this paper.

The effective management of urban roads plays a crucial role in the optimal operation of urban transportation systems and overall city functioning. Current monitoring techniques rely heavily on inductive loop sensors, roadside cameras, and crowdsourced data, but they often come with limitations of high costs, restricted coverage areas, or unreliable data from individual users. In this study, a groundbreaking approach is proposed to revolutionize road sensing by leveraging the vast network of GPS-enabled vehicles traveling through the city, utilizing their collective positioning data and travel logs to extract valuable insights about the road conditions and network performance. The proposed framework is comprised of an algorithm that utilizes vehicle data to identify areas of high traffic congestion and inaccurate GPS readings, and assesses the road conditions' impact on vehicle navigation. A data analytics approach is also developed to provide real-time traffic congestion metrics and historical road condition analyses for each road segment. The proposed framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through a simulation experiment utilizing real-world GPS data from thousands of moving vehicles. The results show that the proposed algorithm accurately detects highly congested areas, spots areas with inaccurate GPS readings, and accurately assesses the impact of road conditions on vehicle navigation. The study finds that rough roads increase vehicles' navigation time by roughly 50%, while congested areas have little impact. The proposed approach is flexible and open to enhancements, and the study provides real-world evidence that supports the feasibility of large-scale city road sensing through collaborative vehicle networks. This study paves the way for future research to further enhance the algorithm and explore other network analytics approaches. The developed framework and associated data and methods are available online for download. This innovative approach to road sensing has the potential to lower costs, enhance data coverage, and empower data-driven urban planning decisions by providing real-time insights into America's deteriorating road conditions. This groundbreaking approach to road sensing may also spark interest in collaborative network analytics across other public infrastructure areas, such as bridges, parks, and public buildings, and could be applied to various other transportation systems, such as airports, seaports, and railroads. This study's data-driven methods and innovative network analytics approaches can serve as a foundation for other collaborative sensing initiatives that involve moving vehicles and aim to gather insights into public infrastructure conditions. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. The most stringent limits on the operator energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain new physics scenarios, such as dark photon or dark dark matter interactions. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be dominated by dark matter or neutrino interactions at specific energy scales. To facilitate further research, we have introduced public software tools that can accurately calculate invisible J/ψ decay widths based on our effective field theory framework. By integrating these tools with experimental data, we can refine the derived limits on energy scales and shape limits on specific parameter combinations. As a result, we propose that experimental collaborations incorporate these software tools into analyses of J/ψ decays involving invisible particles and dark matter, as well as neutrino physics within the J/ψ vector charmonium spectrum. By doing so, they can provide more accurate limits on new energy scales and models with light sterile neutrinos or sub-GeV dark matter. This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are increasingly employed by educational institutions and testing agencies to evaluate numerous applicants, making critical decisions in the process. Yet, surprisingly, little research has focused on comprehending the complex workings of these algorithms, particularly those that operate behind closed doors. Previous studies revealed the ease with which these scoring models can be manipulated. This paper aims to investigate the underlying causes of this unexpected sensitivity and instability. By employing the latest advances in interpretation, we examined the relative importance of essay features, including coherence, relevance, vocabulary, and content in influencing automated scores. We used this to investigate the issues of over-sensitivity (small changes yielding significantly varying output scores) and over-stability (scores that do not change in response to significant changes in input) associated with these models. Our results showed that autoscoring models are over-stable rather than over-sensitive; they prioritize limited key features that they have learned during the training process over new information that they have not encountered before, including typical language usage. Moreover, we identified the types of essays that these models find difficult to handle, including those with uncommon vocabulary and complex subjects. Our research offers several possible explanations for the difficulties people have had in addressing the issues of over-sensitivity and over-stability associated with these models. In addition, it highlights potential avenues for improving the algorithms, such as incorporating mechanisms that allow for the learning of more robust feature representations that capture a broader spectrum of essay characteristics. Ultimately, this work underscores the importance of carrying out methodological variations and combining different approaches to achieve a deeper understanding of the complex workings of artificial intelligence systems and the need to address their associated issues head-on. As artificial intelligence systems with high stakes public impacts become more widespread, it is imperative to conduct this type of research to ensure the transparency and reliability of these systems. Moreover, this research can pave the way for further investigations into the underlying causes of other unusual behaviors exhibited by these models. In addition to automated essay scoring, this study can also be applied to any high-stakes, widely-deployed artificial intelligence system that has been difficult to comprehend. In such cases, it can be used as a comprehensive interpretation and analysis framework to gain a deeper understanding of these systems' complex workings. In the process, it can also address related issues associated with their performance. In the long term, achieving a thorough comprehension of these systems will be crucial for designing future algorithms that are both highly effective and trustworthy. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. To achieve this, the W-shaped network is designed with two consecutive modules that detect masks in binary space and density space respectively. The two modules are linked by a bridge function that bridges the gap between them, thereby enabling better feature extraction. To further enhance the model's performance, various variants of the approach were tested, including training it on annotated points instead of manual annotation, resulting in exceptionally high scores on the two main evaluation metrics. When applied to real-world cancer diagnosis scenarios, the model demonstrated impressive performance, achieving a detection score of 0.8575 and a Dice coefficient of 0.8761 on the specific task of identifying and extracting lymphocytes from breast cancer tissues. In comparison to the current state-of-the-art models, the proposed approach achieved a 12.5% increase in detection score and a 5.8% increase in Dice coefficient, underscoring its capability to accurately locate and extract valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. Furthermore, the model's performance was enhanced through the use of contrastive learning and multi-scale feature fusion, paving the way for its application to other medical image segmentation tasks. Consequently, the proposed approach provides a significant milestone in the development of an automatic cancer diagnosis system capable of identifying and extracting individual cells from images with minimal manual intervention. Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of halting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, thereby delaying pyroptotic cell death. Our study develops a single-cell mathematical model to analyze the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, cell death due to pyroptosis, and how these processes respond to treatment. Formulated in terms of ODEs, the model examines the dynamic biological processes that lead to pyroptosis and how they can be modified by anti-inflammatory interventions, shifting cell death from pyroptotic to a less inflammatory form, like apoptosis. Furthermore, we are integrating this single-cell model into the SARS-CoV-2 Tissue Simulator to study its findings in a more complex virtual environment that mimics the interactions within an infected host's tissues. As a result, we anticipate that this combined framework will be capable of exploring potential effects of anti-inflammatory treatments on COVID-19's progression and identifying potential indicators for their effectiveness through multi-criteria decision analysis. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We represent the likelihood of selecting a random n-tuple that meets these specifications as $p_n$ and calculate specific probabilities for n equal to 3 and 4. However, it's proven that the probability of a random n-tuple being nontransitive cannot be expressed through simple arithmetic with the first three natural numbers. Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a significant limitation, primarily because the extra generator adds complexity and memory demands. In response to these issues, we introduce a new cycleGAN framework based on a single, adaptive switchable generator. By incorporating adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers, the baseline generator can efficiently transform a low-dose CT image into a routine-dose CT image and then easily switch to generating high-dose images from low-dose images simply by modifying the AdaIN codes. The proposed architecture achieves these conversions while minimizing the memory requirement and weight increase associated with additional generators, and can therefore be trained with more stability using limited training data. Our results demonstrate that the new approach not only rivals but outperforms previous cycleGAN methods while needing only roughly half as many parameters. Moreover, the proposed architecture produces higher-resolution images that are less noisy and better preserve the original pathologies' appearance compared to existing methods, according to both quantitative and visual assessment metrics. Finally, the proposed method also exhibits greater flexibility, enabling the enhancement of various types of CT images, such as lung and abdominal scans, without needing additional training. With enhanced stability using limited training data and lower memory requirements, the proposed architecture is particularly suited for enhancing real low-dose CT scans. Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations from labeled and unlabeled dialog datasets. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all labeled data's rich structural information. Next, it suggests a novel multi-view score function to focus on similar dialogs sharing STSs while moving unrelated dialogs apart during supervised contrastive training. To maximize unlabeled dialogs' potential, it incorporates a self-supervised contrastive loss to refine the learned representations. Experimental results show SPACE-2 achieves top-notch performance across seven datasets on four dialog understanding tasks in the DialoGLUE benchmark. A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across misaligned frames. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits versatility in video restoration tasks and achieved remarkable success in video super-resolution and compressed video enhancement challenges in NTIRE 2021, earning several top ranks, with codes and models available on MMEditing. Our paper has been adopted as an NIPS 2021 poster.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. A thorough examination of both universal and near-universal adjustments, specifically power-law and logarithmic corrections, is carried out to determine the derivation of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions when approaching a limit of collinearity. A survey is also conducted to analyze multiple 2-to-n particle interactions at 2-to-30 TeV energy levels through weak boson fusion/scattering in both polarized and unpolarized conditions. A key contribution of this study involves the public integration of Effective W/Z and Weizs\"acker-Williams Approximations, collectively referred to as the Effective Vector Boson Approximation, into the existing event generator software MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO, setting the groundwork for developing matching prescriptions between EW parton showers and EW distribution functions, and providing actionable advice on the use of W/Z PDFs to facilitate this development. The implementation within the Effective Vector Boson Approximation is also applicable to other mature MC codes connected to external beam lines. The most notable findings from our research, encompassing the most current data from the Effective Vector Boson Approximation, are graphically visualized to illustrate the considerable differences forward leptonic and weak bosonic collisions can have on major particle production processes in various channels, especially falling beyond the 2 TeV milestone. Consequently, this study is crucial in highlighting the potential for forward leptonic and weak bosonic collisions to have significant implications on the design of future lepton colliders operating above a few TeV. The findings from our research can also be utilized to direct the focus towards investigating less conventional searches that involve vector boson fusion/scattering in the development of the next-generation lepton colliders. The effective use of W/Z PDFs also offers scope for further investigation that could potentially be extended to incorporate a greater variety of elementary vector boson distribution functions. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and provide
insights into the challenges of multi-task reinforcement learning. Additionally,
we examine various ways to organize learned dynamics models into multiple
sub-networks. The code for our approach is openly available at
https://github.com/strml/embbellum.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. Leveraging these theorems and their common proof strategies, we explore the capabilities and limitations of formal systems within the context of first-order logic. Furthermore, we examine how these results may be employed to create novel proofs and demonstrations. Along the way, we outline various approaches to enhance the fundamental capabilities of such systems, including utilizing second-order logic, introducing non-classical semantics, and incorporating the concept of operation extensions. Ultimately, our primary goal becomes to define a formal framework that not only survives the challenges posed by Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem, Godel-Rosser Undecidability Theorem, Tarski's Undefinability Theorem, and the Diagonal Lemma but can actually be utilized in constructive proof verification. We propose an initial design for such a framework and present a corresponding formal theory that we term the Simple Extension Theory (SET). Additionally, we outline two potential enhancements to SET and briefly discuss their potential implications. Lastly, we offer some thoughts on possible connections between enhancing formal systems and the challenges posed by paraconsistent logic to traditional approaches to logic-based reasoning. These ideas serve as a foundation for ongoing research in the area. The primary purpose of this work remains theoretical in nature; it aims to provide a foundation for the constructive development of advanced proof verification frameworks capable of supporting the concept of operation extensions within first-order logic. Consequently, potential applications for SET and its derivatives lie in demonstrating the capabilities and limitations of various formal systems through the construction of tailored models, rather than proposed uses in broader computational contexts. Nonetheless, the concepts developed in this research may also be employed to create novel proofs and demonstrations that can be employed in educational settings aimed at teaching fundamental concepts of logic and computation. The accompanying interactive proof scenes, carefully crafted to facilitate understanding, offer students a unique opportunity to explore complex theoretical concepts in a hands-on manner. The underlying technology is now publicly accessible at https://proofs.cs.umb.edu. We invite users to explore the existing proof demonstrations and contribute to the extension of this interactive proof repository in collaboration with us. When the population is not fully known in advance, sampling occurs in sequence, either individually or in batches, which are obtained sequentially. This work presents a novel algorithm that allows for sequential selection of a balanced sample. The algorithm accommodates equal and unequal inclusion probabilities and can also be applied to select spatially balanced samples when the population contains geographical coordinates. Moreover, an investigation using simulated data reveals that the proposed method surpasses alternative methods. Additionally, the algorithm has been implemented within the R package 'SeqBalance'. Alongside the package, an illustrative example that leverages real-world data from the African Elephant Population Survey is provided. The research underlying this paper also explores various sequential sampling strategies in relation to the declining accuracy of estimates as samples become larger. The paper also examines how the estimated population total changes with different sequential sample sizes. The investigation into the researcher's problem using the African Elephant data reveals that, in certain instances, selecting samples sequentially can yield more accurate results than traditional methods. The paper also explores the benefits of sequential sampling in relation to declining estimative accuracy with increasing sample size and highlights the significance of research on complex sampling designs. The work presented in this paper lays the groundwork for future investigations into sequential sampling techniques. The paper is accompanied by the R package 'SeqBalance', which can be obtained from the author at https://github.com/JamesMCullen/SeqBalance, and the African Elephant data set can be acquired from https://www.ape-package.org/. In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by installing a camera on an end-effector and taking pictures of a robot's workspace. We chose three approaches: one that utilized training data containing various camera positions, another that used training data focused on detecting specific objects, and a third that relied on training data centered on recognizing particular patterns of lines. We tested these approaches by training them with synthetic data and then applying the models to the actual images taken by the camera. We found that using trained models resulted in accurate predictions for two of the methods, but the object detection method failed to yield reliable results. Additionally, we discovered that using trained models led to camera calibration errors of less than 1 centimeter, meeting the requirements specified in the experiment setup. Finally, we discovered that using trained models allowed for the camera to be calibrated in a mock environment consisting of artificial objects, demonstrating the method's potential for use in real-world applications. However, further research is needed to assess the method's effectiveness with diverse and unknown line patterns. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. The key advantage of this approach lies in its ability to circumvent expensive kernel computations by using the methods of goodfellow and mirza, thereby making it feasible for real-time sampling. Moreover, we found that incorporating noise from the posterior distribution into the training process significantly boosted the performance. Compared to existing methods, our model used relatively simple generators, yet still produced remarkably realistic samples. The framework we proposed can be useful not only for solving inverse problems but also for other challenging sampling tasks involving complex data distributions. This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from an invariant perspective. By defining an invariant manifold relative to an invariant set, we can explore its structure and how it relates to the underlying dynamics. This approach is particularly useful for analyzing systems that have complex dynamics and varying levels of stability. Building on this definition, we discuss various types of invariant manifolds, including stable, unstable, and neutral manifolds. Specifically, we look at how stable and unstable manifolds are used in the study of dynamical systems to characterize the behavior of orbits near hyperbolic invariant sets. Additionally, we examine how neutral manifolds can be used to analyze systems that exhibit snaking patterns. Key concepts, such as saddle-node bifurcations and homclustering, are also discussed in this context. Furthermore, we provide examples and illustrations to demonstrate the application of these theoretical concepts to actual dynamical systems, such as reaction-diffusion equations. These examples illustrate how invariant manifolds can be used to understand the underlying dynamics and how they can be visualized to provide insights into the behavior of solutions. Finally, we outline potential future research directions in this area, such as investigating the role of neutral manifolds in higher-dimensional systems and developing more sophisticated methods for visualizing invariant manifolds. Overall, this article aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the significance and application of invariant manifolds in the study of dynamical systems, as well as potential future research directions in this area. It is intended as a primer for researchers who are new to the field and is based on an invited talk presented at the 2021 virtual conference of the Society for Mathematical Biology. It also includes additional material that has not been published elsewhere. It is hoped that this article will serve as a useful resource for researchers working in the field of mathematical biology and will also be of interest to a broader audience involved in the study of dynamical systems. Next-generation wireless networks require exceptionally high data transfer rates that could be achieved by utilizing Terahertz frequency bands for communication. Traditionally, THz communication is confined to short-distance applications because THz signals face high absorption in the atmosphere. To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored the potential of multi-hop directional transmission techniques to extend communication range, albeit their limitations in scalability. This study investigates the performance of THz multi-hop ad hoc networks by analyzing the distribution of end-to-end throughput and developing a framework for optimizing secondary hop selection. Simulation results indicate that our proposed framework can maximize energy efficiency and minimize latency. Interestingly, as the number of hops increases, the distribution of end-to-end throughput converges to a normal distribution. To address scalability issues, our research finds that multi-hop transmission can provide comparable performance to single-hop transmission with significantly less energy consumption. This finding enables the design of more efficient and cost-effective THz communication systems. This work provides a theoretical foundation for optimizing multi-hop transmission in THz frequencies and can be applied to other fading channels. This research paves the way for the adoption of multi-hop transmission in THz communication networks, addressing scalability challenges. This work is a foundational step toward developing algorithms for optimizing secondary hop selection and could be extended to accommodate time-varying channel conditions and adaptive modulation techniques. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. The findings suggest this screen may be responsible for producing the 920 MHz scintillation towards the Sun, a phenomenon observed from the Earth, and imply that screens with voids in their surroundings may be located near the boundaries of larger cavities in the interstellar medium. The research also provides screen parameters related to small-scale scintillations and offers them as potential benchmarks for comparing theoretical and observational screen characteristics. Furthermore, the analysis of scintillation patterns as the Earth orbits the Sun revealed a 365.25 days orbital period screen, which is believed to be an artifact rather than a genuine orbital screen, and thus the research remains unaffected by this finding. The studied screens exhibit a velocity distribution in line with that of the interstellar medium, and their detection paves the way for further analysis of screen dynamics and the connection between screens and the surrounding environment. Ultimately, this research is expected to contribute to a comprehensive understanding of the interstellar medium by providing detailed insights into small-scale scattering screens and their roles in shaping the behavior of electromagnetic waves as they traverse the medium.  This research is expected to lay the groundwork for a three-dimensional study of screen dynamics and their intricate relationship with the surrounding environment, which in turn could potentially be used to study the movement of screens over time and possibly even facilitate a global study of small-scale screens. Additionally, this research is anticipated to enhance the capabilities of imaging and interferometry techniques used in high-energy astrophysics, which rely heavily on accurate modeling of the interstellar medium, particularly the effects of scattering screens. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's ability to accurately model various quasi-periodic signals, including speech with external frequency manipulations. Furthermore, the proposed method outperforms the current state-of-the-art waveforms in objective metrics and is computationally efficient in terms of parameter usage. The code and model weights are available online.

Planets similar to Earth, orbiting nearby stars with reduced energy output, are being extensively studied and several are suited for further analysis. Focusing on temperate worlds surrounded by thick H2 atmospheres, our models follow chemical transformations and gas circulation after H2O, CH4, NH3, and H2S molecules break apart under stellar radiation, utilizing K2-18 b, PH2 b, and Kepler-167 e as prime examples. According to our simulations, NH3 molecules are destroyed by solar radiation in atmospheres surrounding G/K stars, while intact in those surrounding M stars. Typically, NH3 breaks down in presence of CH4, resulting in the primary photochemical product HCN. CH4, when exposed to water vapor, produces CO and CO2. However, under high internal temperatures and super-abundant metal content in atmospheres, more intricate chemical pathways may occur, potentially involving many different elements and potentially leading to the creation of many various compounds. Models estimating spectral signatures compare our detailed chemical descriptions to those using less detailed methods, showing discrepancies in multiple areas. Nevertheless, a striking pattern emerged - models explaining gas spectral data failed to accurately predict conditions in these planets' cores, while those modeling their cores successfully replicated atmospheric data. This suggests that internal temperature and chemistry may be underestimated in models employing less detailed methods, while atmospheric predictions were over-estimated due to these models adding too much free H2 generated from water molecules. Contrarily, models employing detailed methods correctly estimated core temperatures and accurately accounted for the consumption of free H2 in atmospheric chemical reactions. Underestimated core temperatures may lead to incorrect assessments of possible locations for these exoplanets in their systems due to their massive nature. Increased collisional blocking between planets in their systems may be a possible outcome of their extended atmospheric features. Additionally, atmospheric flow models identified potential locations for stable CO2 tidal hibernaculum layers, including those surrounding K2-18 b and Kepler-167 e, offering insights into potential formation processes for stable CO2 layers observed in gas spectra of other planets. Several of the major compounds formed within these planets' atmospheres have the potential to be detected by upcoming high-sensitivity telescopes and missions like the James Webb Space Telescope, making thorough understanding of their formation processes crucial. Furthermore, detailed analysis of multiple exoplanets will be necessary to identify patterns allowing for inferences about atmospheric processes and chemical compositions on Earth and other solar system planets based on comparisons with exoplanets' data. The development of advanced detection algorithms through deep learning has accelerated the identification of road issues, including automatic defect detection and marking analysis. To expedite and reduce costs associated with manual inspections, a comprehensive system called RoadAtlas has been developed. This system comprises a cutting-edge detection framework that utilizes modern deep learning techniques and incorporates specialized modules for data enhancement, correction, and refinement. Additionally, RoadAtlas includes a robust database management system capable of storing and organizing large datasets, as well as a user-friendly web interface for easy data visualization and algorithm customization. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. All code and dataset information can be found at https://github.com/technionai/sound-source-localization. Our project webpage is also available at https://ai.technion.ac.il/sound-source-localization. Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. LGCN is also found to be more robust to hyperbolic metric learning than traditional methods, and it is shown that LGCN's learned metrics correlate with EarthMover distances to ground truth representations. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement on the boundary, taken over a finite short time frame. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. The apparent metric variability is what actually drives the change in the light scattering phase shift, not the variable part of the metric, but rather the non-dynamical gravitational potential that varies in the same way is responsible for this change. This distinction resolves the long-standing conflict between metric-based approaches and the Thomas precession phenomenon. For any positive integer h less than or equal to k, we can calculate a restricted signed sumset denoted as $h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A$, which comprises sums of $a_i$ with weights from {-1,0,1}. The goal of this article is to solve the minimum value of $|h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A|$, where $|A|$, when A is a set of integers, and investigate the underlying structure of A to achieve this minimum value. Additionally, some open questions related to $h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A$ are proposed in this article. 

In Chapter 2, we discuss the minimum value of $|h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A|$ when A contains distinct elements and demonstrate that the minimum value occurs at $|A|$, which requires the total sum of A to be equinumerous with G. In Chapter 3, we analyze the scenario where A has duplicate elements and establish a lower bound of $|A|+1$ for the minimum value of $|h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A|$. A concrete example shows that the lower bound can be achieved when the underlying group G is cyclic and controlled by two relatively prime numbers. 

Finally, in Chapter 4, we propose open questions related to $h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A$ and explore connections with Sanderson's conjecture and Freiman's inverse problem.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the complex task of automating colorectal polyp characterization. It includes 2484 images labeled as normal, 2538 as benign (adenoma low-grade), 1514 as moderate-grade adenomas, and 660 as high-grade adenomas. Notably, UniToPatho stands out from existing datasets focused solely on specific characterization tasks, such as classification or grading, by combining both. As a result, models trained on this dataset are prepared to tackle both challenges simultaneously, providing a foundation for future research on multi-task learning in medical image analysis. The dataset is openly accessible via the UniToPatho webpage for anyone interested in collaborating or contributing to its expansion. It has already sparked collaboration among multiple research teams working on deep learning-based solutions for colorectal polyp characterization. These efforts have yielded multiple models, including encoders, decoder-based methods, and models integrating multi-task learning, which are freely shared as part of the dataset to benefit the broader medical research community. However, further evaluation and testing are still necessary to assess their practical applications in real-world clinical settings. In conclusion, UniToPatho represents a significant advancement in datasets focused on analyzing colorectal polyps and adenomas, offering a diverse collection of images suitable for training deep learning models and facilitating collaboration among researchers. It has the potential to become a leading benchmark for evaluating models and contributing to the characterization of colorectal polyps. In addition, the initiative aims to give back to the community by sharing models and results with the research community, marking an important step towards creating more accessible and collaborative medical research projects. In this context, we invite all researchers to use UniToPatho, join the collaboration effort, and help advance the characterization of colorectal polyps through deep learning analysis. In the long run, this project seeks to contribute to the development of more precise and reliable deep learning models

To complement this strategy, an alternative Fourier transformation method is developed, taking advantage of the optimized mesh dimensions for even better results. Successful applications and examples highlight the method's efficiency and adaptability with various sources, including external points and soft-scattering scenarios. Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While proven for multilingual translation, zero-shot translation's feasibility for speech-to-text remains unexplored. We aim to build zero-shot speech-to-text models that learn speech recognition and machine translation but can execute the speech-to-text task. However, speech and text representations significantly differ, complicating the learning of these two tasks simultaneously. Our models tend to produce incorrect outputs during zero-shot speech-to-text tasks. We mitigate this issue by introducing supplementary data and a novel loss function, which minimizes text-audio disparities. Our results indicate that these approaches hold promise for zero-shot speech-to-text. Notably, they prove particularly useful in low-data settings, achieving speech-recognition accuracy of 76.9 and speech-to-text BLEU score of 36.3 in zero-shot translation scenarios. Moreover, they enable the translation of speech across 100 distinct language pairs without the need for speech recognition data, surpassing traditional approaches in accuracy and feasibility. The code and models are available for public access at https://github.com/ghrua/zero-shot-speech-to-text. The study presents the initial forays into zero-shot speech-to-text and offers a range of models and techniques for public use, paving the way for advancements in cross-language speech-to-text through deep learning. The primary challenges associated with zero-shot translation, such as task decoupling and the management of latent representations, are key areas for further research. We assess the applicability of three different methods for calculating electromagnetic multipoles: Cartesian primitive multipoles, irreducible multipoles and spherical multipoles. Our findings suggest that the spherical multipoles provide the most accurate description of electromagnetic scattering behavior, as demonstrated with an example of an amorphous silicon sphere. These multipoles are utilized to model the optical force exerted on particles composed of semiconductors, dielectrics, and metals over a broad range of wavelengths spanning from the dipolar regime down to the Mie regime. Our method offers a versatile framework for comprehensively analyzing the optical properties of complex inhomogeneous particles. Furthermore, it enables the systematic investigation of particle optical properties in relation to shape, material, and size. Consequently, this approach can facilitate the design of particles with tailored optical characteristics, leading to potential applications in laser-based technologies. We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating both $d^N$ and $d^{N+1}$ scenarios. The resulting models can be applied to various transition metal oxides, enabling a re-evaluation of experimental results that assume isolated $t_{2g}$ or $e_g$ orbital states, often necessary for the interpretation of data from spectroscopic and transport experiments. The breakdown of such isolated orbital models is quantified using the mixing fraction between $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbital waves, and we further develop a simplified scheme to estimate magnetic properties based on this mixing fraction. The limitations of different theoretical models are evaluated and assessed in the context of specific compounds like Cu$_2$O, CuO, NiO, CoO, LaCoO$_3$, LaTiO$_3$ and LaCrO$_3$. Finally, we emphasize the importance of accounting for $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing when interpreting experimental results, particularly those related to magnetic properties, and introduce a new framework categorized as'magnetic orbital triality'. The concept of triality is applicable not only to magnetic properties but can also be extended to other phenomena showing orbital triality, where different orbital states manifest under varying conditions. The introduction of a new scale to quantify the degree of orbital triality is proposed, defined as the variation of orbital state across the Fermi level, and could be a valuable tool for identifying compounds exhibiting orbital triality in experiments involving spectral analysis. The framework of magnetic orbital triality is expected to provide a unifying description for distinct classes of materials exhibiting orbital triality, and could serve as the foundation for a broader theoretical framework addressing the interplay between orbital triality and other degrees of freedom in transition metal oxides and related compounds. The proposed framework is anticipated to guide and facilitate new experimental and theoretical research in this field. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical functions known as B-splines. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the mathematical theories of mirror symmetry and homological mirror symmetry. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/ghrua/med-gan and the project website is located at https://www.netsafe.org/projects/med-gan. Long-term goals for this research aim to explore a broader range of medical imaging transformations and enhance disease detection through artificial data manipulation. Furthermore, this work highlights several visual demonstrations available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H4PcXjYcS3k. Ultimately, this research paves the way for generating realistic artificial medical images that mimic real patient data and lays the groundwork for disease simulation, new artificial organs creation, and enhanced disease detection through transfer learning. This method is particularly beneficial for applications requiring repeated evaluation of Newtonian potentials. By utilizing Green's identity, we can derive an efficient algorithm to compute these potentials, which significantly reduces computational costs. We also establish an error estimate for approximating boundary integrals through numerical discretization. This efficient method can be an useful tool for any method that relies on Newtonian potential reconstruction. One such example includes the boundary integral formulation of the Stokes problem.
